## Name the unique mechanism so your product isn't a commodity
Use when: Merchandising a PDP, VSL or ad where the product is easily price-compared against near-identical alternatives.
- Identify one distinct feature or construction and give it a name (the source points to named systems like 'Money Magnet System').
- Frame it around the common failure of cheaper competitors — the source's vacuum example is a V12 engine that doesn't lose suction as the bin fills, versus weaker one-cylinder machines.
- Draw the commodity-versus-mechanism contrast: a plain winter tire gets bought on price, a 'rubber stud technology' tire supports a higher price because it isn't the same thing.
- Use the mechanism to answer the implicit objection — the source's resistance-training example explicitly addresses 'why wouldn't I just use free weights?'
- Keep the claim grounded in a real product feature; the source's examples are invented for illustration, and a fabricated mechanism is a legal and trust risk.
Caveat: The purpose is differentiation, not deception — name a real feature, don't invent the feature.
Caveat: This is a copywriting frame and does not by itself make a product superior.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, positioning, offer-design, product-page, creative-strategy
Source: 8 Hour Copywriting Course For Beginners.docx

---

## Use a standard VSL structure from call-out to offer
Use when: Scripting a flagship VSL or long-form sales page for a hero product or premium bundle.
- Call out the specific avatar and their urgent problem; the source's example opens with 'attention online fitness coaches' and a big promise with a dollar figure.
- Show what most people do and why it doesn't work — throw stones at alternatives with proof and analogies so the comparison is easy to understand.
- Deliver the belief shift: what actually works, why it's better, and how to use it.
- Present the unique mechanism's two to three pillars and explain why your way is effective while alternatives are inferior, using analogies throughout.
- Stack proof: results, testimonials, borrowed authority, stats, then your own credibility and cost narration (what you spent to learn the method).
- End with a CTA and, where appropriate, the unique selling proposition — tell them what to do and why now; the source notes a VSL is essentially a collection of emails in one asset.
Caveat: The example VSL is for a coaching business; adapt the audience, problem and proof to your product category.
Caveat: Testimonials show what others achieved — they are not a promised result.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, video-sales-letter, copywriting, creative-strategy, offer-design
Source: 8 Hour Copywriting Course For Beginners.docx

---

## Sell the mechanism that sells the product
Use when: Writing any sales asset where the product looks like every other option in its category.
- Define the system or mechanism the product delivers and make it the centerpiece of the copy, not the product name alone.
- Walk through why the mechanism works — the source shows the VSL spending most of its runtime explaining the named system before asking for the purchase.
- Contrast it with the common alternative (cheap substitute, DIY version, inferior material) and name the specific reason those fail.
- Once the reader believes the mechanism works, the offer becomes a lower-friction decision — the source describes this as the point where buying becomes a no-brainer.
- In ecommerce terms: sell the reason your formulation, sourcing or design works before selling the SKU, so price comparison loses its grip.
Caveat: The source's example is a high-ticket coaching funnel; the ecommerce application is a transfer of the principle, not a demonstrated result.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, positioning, offer-design, product-page, creative-strategy
Source: 8 Hour Copywriting Course For Beginners.docx

---

## Do avatar and problem research before writing the VSL
Use when: Starting a new VSL, landing page or ad for a category you don't know intimately.
- Define exactly who the offer is for, and research their fears, obstacles, wants and desires; write out what their day might look like.
- Identify the urgent problem your product solves in their life — not a general benefit.
- Define the dream outcome the product helps them achieve.
- Lay out the step-by-step process to that outcome, then build two or three pillars of the unique mechanism explaining why this way works and alternatives are inferior.
- Use analogies throughout the mechanism section so the explanation is simple to understand.
Caveat: The source gives no specific research methods; fill this out with your own customer data (reviews, support tickets, surveys).
Caveat: Avatar assumptions should be checked against real buyer data rather than guessed.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, customer-research, avatar, video-sales-letter, creative-strategy
Source: 8 Hour Copywriting Course For Beginners.docx

---

## Be a stat shower, not a claim-maker
Use when: Any ad, PDP or email line that asserts quality, speed, results or superiority.
- Identify every unsupported claim in the draft ('it works', 'best formula') and flag it.
- Replace each with proof the reader can see and check — a number, a result, a demonstration or a testimonial.
- Use borrowed authority (quotes, credible sources) and stats that support the exact point you're making.
- Frame testimonials as evidence of what others achieved rather than claims you make yourself.
- Keep proof specific to your own genuine results; the source's figures (125 coaches, five over $1M) belong to that business and shouldn't be borrowed.
Caveat: Do not fabricate statistics, reviews or results — use only verifiable proof from your business or legitimately cited third parties.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, copywriting, social-proof, creative-strategy
Source: 8 Hour Copywriting Course For Beginners.docx

---

## Use AI to improve and generate ideas, not to write the copy
Use when: Speeding up drafting for emails, PDPs, ads or VSLs without producing obvious AI output.
- Write the copy yourself first, then prompt 'make this better / funnier / more clever' and keep only the lines that are actually better than yours.
- Use prompt patterns like: 'what are some questions you can ask me that can get me the best result', 'give me one-line analogies that explain how X is as [adjective] as Y', 'give me quotes that explain X', and 'give me stats that prove why X'.
- Iterate with refinement prompts — 'make them shorter', 'add some funny ones too', 'make them more simple, one-liners' — before using anything.
- Keep prompts simple rather than hunting for elaborate prompt chains.
- Never paste long-form AI output about your product or customers directly into a send — the source warns against it on quality and credibility grounds; treat AI as a tool that needs your skill, like a calculator needs a mathematician.
Caveat: The presenter states AI will not replace copywriting skill and describes what was, at the time, ChatGPT's weak copy output; model capabilities and best prompts change, so re-test.
Caveat: Fabricated or recycled analogies and stats must be checked for accuracy and fit before publication.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, copywriting, ai, creative-strategy, email-marketing
Source: 8 Hour Copywriting Course For Beginners.docx

---

## Strip telltale AI analogs and clichés from store copy
Use when: Editing any AI-assisted or self-written ad, email or PDP copy before publishing.
- Scan for overused analogy families — the source flags magic wands and baking a cake as the ones AI reaches for most.
- Cut robotic openers like 'I hope this message finds you well' — the source points out no friend texts you that way.
- Remove generic hype that shifts no belief and gives no value ('imagine having a steady stream of clients').
- Rewrite so the copy sounds like a person speaking to a friend, which is what the source says copy is for.
- Read the copy aloud and flag anything you would not actually say to a customer in person.
Caveat: If AI-assisted phrasing survives editing because it fits your voice, the source's concern is unedited paste-in, not AI use itself.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, copywriting, ai, creative-strategy
Source: 8 Hour Copywriting Course For Beginners.docx

---

## Build a store landing page with blocks, background and readable text
Use when: Building a product signup page or campaign sales page without hiring a designer.
- Choose the page's one goal — signup (opt-in page) or purchase (sales page) — and remove extra navigation like About or Contact.
- Build with drag-and-drop blocks: hero section at top, then two-column text, then closing text and form. Add a video block and a form block as needed.
- Add a background image rather than leaving the page plain white or black — the source searched '4K black and red background' and used that, favoring pages with a subtle gradient or visual treatment.
- Layer a dark color over the background with reduced opacity so the headline text stays readable while the image stays visible; increase opacity toward solid for maximum contrast.
- Edit directly in the blocks — text, fonts, sizes — the source compares it to editing a Word document and insists no coding is involved.
- Apply the ladder: every block should move the reader toward the single goal, not add side quests.
Caveat: The source notes plain white backgrounds have made millions for some businesses — the background treatment is the presenter's preference, not a proven rule.
Caveat: The interface shown is ActiveCampaign's builder; other tools differ, so verify the current UI.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, landing-page, product-page, conversion-optimization, tools
Source: 8 Hour Copywriting Course For Beginners.docx

---

## Match your page builder to budget and feature needs
Use when: Choosing the page-builder stack for a store's campaign or launch.
- Use Miro to map the funnel visually before building pages — the source describes it as a funnel mapping tool.
- Consider Carrd for a limited free option, or Google Docs to sketch a page's visual layout when nothing else is available.
- Use Kajabi or ClickFunnels when you need the most common, feature-rich options — the source calls them somewhat expensive at roughly a couple hundred dollars a month, far less than a top-tier ESP.
- Don't let cost deter you: the source argues page builders are drag-and-drop and anyone who can use Zoom or Discord can build a page.
- Skip AI landing-page generators — the source finds editing generated pages slower than starting from scratch.
Caveat: Pricing and feature summaries are the presenter's at time of recording and should be re-verified.
Caveat: Free options like Carrd have very limited features.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, landing-page, tools, conversion-optimization
Source: 8 Hour Copywriting Course For Beginners.docx

---

## Map the sequence to lead temperature, cold to hot
Use when: Planning the timeline of a new-subscriber or post-purchase email series for a store.
- Sketch a simple timeline: day one welcome, day three value, day five soft sell, day eight hard sell — the source's illustrative model.
- Track lead temperature conceptually: cold subscribers don't know you and won't buy; hot subscribers know you well and might.
- Pair with automation branching: openers can skip ahead to the soft sell while non-openers get more value first.
- Increase promotion only as engagement rises — the source's principle is that more engaged subscribers are more susceptible to promo, and less engaged ones should be promoted to less.
- Apply the same cold-to-hot logic to any automation, not just welcome sequences.
Caveat: The day markers are an illustration, not a tested cadence — treat them as a starting skeleton.
Caveat: The engagement-to-promotion relationship is a stated principle, not a measured finding.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, email-marketing, automation, conversion-optimization, retention
Source: 8 Hour Copywriting Course For Beginners.docx

---

## Map Your Store's Sales Ladder Before Optimizing It
Use when: You're diagnosing why ad spend isn't turning into revenue, or planning where to insert an email capture, bundle or upsell in the buyer journey.
- List every acquisition channel you run (paid social, video, organic content, email) and mark how they feed each other — the source's model has each channel directing followers to the others so audiences compound.
- Choose one free entry point that all channels funnel into, such as a newsletter or free guide, and give it a specific qualifying promise rather than a generic 'subscribe'.
- From that entry point, route subscribers through email to a low-priced first purchase that a landing page is written for.
- Attach an upsell at checkout, ideally a one-click add so no new card details are needed; the source's stated psychology is that people are far more likely to say yes once they have already said yes.
- If the upsell is declined, still deliver the first product fully and promote the higher tier from inside the product content — the source calls this a content sales funnel.
- Redraw the ladder whenever you change price points or add a channel; the source's point is that every business has some version of this whether or not it was ever written down.
Caveat: The prices used in the source's example are illustrative, not benchmarks; set tiers from your own margin and category.
Caveat: The source says there are countless funnel variations — treat this map as one common shape, not the only valid one.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, funnel-design, upsell, offer-design, customer-journey, email-marketing
Source: 8 Hour Copywriting Course For Beginners.docx

---

## Use Four Funnel Metrics to Locate Where Ad Spend Leaks
Use when: Evaluating whether a paid campaign or funnel is working and identifying which stage — traffic, opt-in, purchase or upsell — is the bottleneck.
- Cost per lead: divide ad spend by opt-ins. In the source's worked example, $100 spend producing 1,530 signups works out to about 6 cents per lead.
- Lead conversion rate: divide buyers by leads. The same example has 92 buyers from 1,530 leads, roughly 6%.
- Average order value: combine the front-end price with the upsell take rate. The example adds $7 plus 15% of buyers at $77, contributing about $11.55 for an AOV near $18.55 — the source calls this the 'would you like fries with that' effect.
- Return on ad spend: multiply buyers by AOV for gross revenue, then divide by spend. The example gives about $1,706 from $100, roughly 17x.
- Translate ROAS into scale: the source treats 17x as meaning $10,000 in ads would notionally return about $170,000 under the same assumptions.
- Use this vocabulary consistently when reading ad platform dashboards so you're comparing the same stage across channels.
Caveat: These figures are a teaching example and the presenter jokes about his own math — treat them as illustration, not benchmarks for your store.
Caveat: Recalculate with your own real data; do not reuse these inputs.
Caveat: Keep lead conversion rate (leads to buyers) distinct from purchase conversion and from a sales close rate — the source uses the lead-to-buyer definition.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, measurement, roas, average-order-value, lead-conversion, paid-ads, unit-economics
Source: 8 Hour Copywriting Course For Beginners.docx

---

## Gate a Discount Behind Email Capture at the Buy Moment
Use when: Setting up store acquisition and deciding what a new visitor is asked for first, especially on a PDP or cart entry.
- Place the email capture in front of checkout, offering a small discount in return — the source's example offered 10% off ahead of a $45 purchase.
- Recognize the two payoffs: you get the address, and if the visitor leaves without buying you can reinitiate contact and remind them they didn't finish.
- Match the discount depth to your margin; the source observes stores commonly using 5% or 10%, but gives no tested conversion differential.
- Treat the resulting list as core infrastructure rather than a side channel — the source describes email as a huge part of the business in his example and for essentially every business.
- Make sure the discount code is actually delivered immediately after opt-in, since the reminder-emails play depends on the visitor feeling they have something waiting.
Caveat: The source presents this as an observation across many businesses, not a verified lift for any specific discount level.
Caveat: No data is given comparing a gated offer with an ungated one, so test depth against your own margins rather than copying a number.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, email-marketing, lead-capture, discounting, acquisition, retention
Source: 8 Hour Copywriting Course For Beginners.docx

---

## Add a Post-Purchase Offer to Raise Average Order Value
Use when: You sell a product with an obvious companion item and want more revenue per existing buyer without raising ad spend.
- Place the offer immediately after the order confirmation, framed as a companion or gift rather than a hard sell — the source's example put a $50 blueprint after a $45 order under the heading 'we have a special gift for you'.
- Keep it to one item and one decision; a menu of add-ons reintroduces the deliberation the buyer has already finished.
- Use a one-click acceptance so no card details are re-entered, which is the structural reason this slot converts better than a fresh checkout.
- Do not screen the offer on your own taste. The source personally found the example offer 'kind of dumb' and still describes the play as legitimate.
- Measure the incremental AOV across all buyers, not the accept rate alone, since the source's stance is that the minority who say yes make the front end more profitable.
Caveat: No conversion rate or AOV lift is given; this is a structural play, not a proven number for your category.
Caveat: An offer that feels unrelated to what was just bought can damage trust — keep it genuinely complementary, and note that the source offers no data on this risk.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, upsell, average-order-value, checkout, post-purchase, offer-design
Source: 8 Hour Copywriting Course For Beginners.docx

---

## Point Every Channel at One Shared Front-End Offer
Use when: Planning acquisition creative and deciding what the offer, qualifying line and landing target should be across platforms.
- Pick a single free entry offer, such as a newsletter or resource, and make it the shared destination for all front-end traffic.
- Write the ad with two parts: who it's for, and the outcome plus free mechanism. The source's example reads 'Fitness coaches, if you want to learn how to reach six figures per month, I'll show you how in my free newsletter — sign up absolutely free.'
- Run that same offer in paid social and video ads and in organic content, rather than creating disconnected destinations per channel.
- Have each platform explicitly send its audience to the others, so followers on one channel become followers on the next.
- Route every entrant into an email sequence, because that is where the paid offers are introduced later.
Caveat: The source's headline is an example of qualification and structure, not a claim you should replicate in an unrelated niche — substitute your own specific audience and outcome.
Caveat: The model assumes a landing page and emails will be written after the ads; budget that production work if you're doing it in-house.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, acquisition, paid-ads, creative-strategy, email-marketing, front-end-offer
Source: 8 Hour Copywriting Course For Beginners.docx

---

## Choose Where the Next-Tier Offer Appears in the Journey
Use when: Deciding where to introduce your next price tier and how to recover buyers who decline the first upsell.
- Option A, at checkout: present the next tier while the buyer is already in a buying state. The source's reasoning is that they have already said yes once, they don't re-enter card details, and accepting is just a checkbox.
- In the source's example the at-checkout ladder runs from a low-priced purchase to a mid-priced upsell, then to a high-ticket application for those who accept the upsell.
- Option B, inside the product: if the buyer declines and only wants what they originally came for, deliver that product at full value and promote the higher tier from within the content — the source calls this a content sales funnel.
- Sequence the two rather than choosing one: attempt the checkout upsell first, then use the in-product path to recover decliners toward the top tier.
- Keep the entry product genuinely valuable in Option B, since the in-product promotion depends on the buyer still being engaged with the material.
Caveat: The specific price ladder in the source is illustrative, not a recommended structure; adapt to your margins and category.
Caveat: The source notes many businesses run these sequences without ever having mapped them, so mapping is a diagnostic aid, not proof that any particular layout works.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, upsell, funnel-design, checkout, customer-journey
Source: 8 Hour Copywriting Course For Beginners.docx

---

## Treat Copy as One Layer of a Working Marketing Stack
Use when: Deciding what to learn or build next for your store's marketing, and whether copy alone is enough to move revenue.
- Accept the section's argument that copywriting is effectively an introduction to digital marketing as a whole, not a standalone deliverable.
- Inventory the components a working direct-response system needs: email sequences, email automations, video or page sales arguments, landing pages, offers and the funnel that connects them.
- Build them as one integrated machine rather than isolated projects, since the source says funnels are what bring the components together end to end.
- Prioritize breadth deliberately. The source's stated rule is that increasing the number of skills you hold increases your worth, and that marketing and sales are the two hardest to go without — copywriting sits at their intersection.
- Get comfortable reading numbers, because the source's position is that marketing is heavily numeric and that interpreting metrics well is where the money is.
Caveat: This is the presenter's opinion about skill stacking and earning potential, not a measured result, and it is framed for freelance copywriters building a service business.
Caveat: The source explicitly warns copywriting is not an easy money glitch — it's a skill with failures along the way, and no income claim should be read as a forecast.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, skill-stacking, funnel-design, email-marketing, career-development
Source: 8 Hour Copywriting Course For Beginners.docx

---

## Write a one-paragraph messaging strategy before any copy
Use when: You are about to write or rewrite PDP copy, homepage copy or ad creative for a store and need a shared standard for what the copy should do, especially when several people or freelancers touch it.
- Before writing any copy, write down the guiding principles your copy must follow as a short document. Joanna Wiebe's example for Page99Test.com is a single paragraph: copy is 'short, friendly and to the point', assumes visitors want to read book excerpts not marketing copy, keeps words to a minimum, and wherever a screenshot, press logo, button, video demo or icon can be used it should replace copy without sacrificing clarity.
- Pick the principles that matter for your store from the source's list of candidate principles: let copy guide design because good writing is good design; some visitors want to read a lot and some don't, and both are customers; support messages with social proof like testimonials or media reviews; support key concepts with video demonstrations; just because you say it doesn't make it true, so prove it; strive for clarity above cleverness; let the message match the medium at an exact point of need; all visitors can be persuaded to join or upgrade; engage visitors with content, experiences or mobile/app options.
- Treat the document as a living document, not etched in stone: update it as you learn your customers' language and as you add or change products.
- Share the strategy with designers, developers and freelancers so they understand your brand and messaging approach before they produce assets.
- Draft your own version in one sitting without censoring yourself, then edit afterward rather than trying to reach a final version on the first, second or third try.
Caveat: The source frames this for startups; a longer or more detailed strategy is not required for it to work.
Caveat: The strategy governs copy, not formatting or layout — establish messages before formatting bullets, headlines and buttons.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, messaging-strategy, copywriting, positioning, brand-voice, landing-page, product-page
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Do customer research before writing a single word of copy
Use when: You are preparing PDP copy, ad creative, taglines or a homepage and are tempted to start from internal assumptions about why people buy.
- Accept the source's core rule: every message you write needs to be a message your ideal visitors want to see. What you like hearing does not matter; copy that only 'wordsmiths' your internal message can fail to convert no matter how much the team loves it.
- Gather customer intelligence instead: if you have an email list from lead gen or pre-launch signups, send a short survey and ask about them and what interests them in the service. The source notes that asking people to do you a 'favor' (and using 'please') can raise response rates, and says to test it.
- Alternatively talk to people directly: the source argues that recruiting 8 people at a coffee shop — even with $25 gift cards — is cheaper than a formal focus group and yields real conversations that stick better than a report. Focus groups are also prone to groupthink where a dominant personality skews the data.
- Or listen online: participate in forums relevant to your category with the intent to listen to what potential customers discuss and engage only when mutually beneficial — not to spam a launch announcement and leave.
- Do not ask customers to approve your copy. The source states that the moment people are aware of copy, everything changes for them, so approval is not a valid test of message.
Caveat: The recommendation against asking customers to approve copy refers to reviewing finished copy, not to gathering research from them.
Caveat: Survey response-rate tips are the source's observed claims, not guaranteed numbers.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, customer-research, messaging-strategy, copywriting, surveys, positioning, product-page
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Define your primary target segment before writing copy
Use when: You are deciding who your homepage, PDP or ad messages should speak to, or you suspect your copy is trying to please everyone.
- Challenge your assumed market. The source's example: a photo-sharing startup may assume its market is the early-adopter tech crowd that upvotes the launch post, but research may show the prevailing users are teenage girls, teenage 'EMO' boys, new moms and retired women. Messages that work on tech geeks are unlikely to work on those groups.
- Collect demographic and behavioral details for each candidate market: age group, marital status, number of children, education, annual income, average consumer debt load, favorite websites, favorite pastimes, shopping preference (online vs retail vs print catalogue) and tech-savviness.
- Segment the market into manageable groups rather than marketing to everyone. The source's chosen segment is the group that will visit with the most frequency and be most likely to compensate you — with money paid or with referrals.
- Let the segment shape the message. Example: for married young stay-at-home moms with household income under $55K, high credit-card debt and high tech-savviness, lead with affordability and do not spend message space on ease. For middle-aged career-oriented women with low debt, high income and time on Skirt.com and Oprah.com, do not talk about affordability — the source suggests pricing and messaging might play into high prices equalling better solutions, and ease may be relevant if that segment is not tech-savvy.
- Test segment fit with PPC ads targeted at each candidate segment and see which segments click through.
Caveat: The income and debt figures in the source's examples are illustrative persona details, not benchmarks.
Caveat: Costs money to buy segment test traffic; the source treats that as money well spent only if it identifies the best-fit segment.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, customer-research, segmentation, positioning, messaging-strategy, pricing, acquisition
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Run a 12-interview pain-point research round
Use when: You need to identify the pains your product copy and ad hooks should address, and are weighing interviews against focus groups.
- Recruit 12 to 15 people from your target segment for one-on-one interviews. The source, citing Pain Killer Marketing (2008) by Chris Stiehl and Henry DeVries, says this generates about 80% of all possible pain points for the segment — the same as 7 focus groups of up to 12 participants each.
- Run them as conversations rather than questionnaires, so you capture what people reveal about themselves beyond direct answers.
- After at least 12 respondents, document and analyze everything. The source warns explicitly not to use this to validate your assumptions — look for new information, and highlight both the surprising and the repeated findings.
- Cross-check the pains you hear through other channels: audit competitor sites to see which pains they hit on, use the Google Adwords keyword tool for phrases your audience searches, run PPC ads testing different pain points to see which get clicked most, monitor your segment on Twitter and their blogs, and find out what websites they commonly visit.
- Translate each confirmed pain into how your product addresses or eradicates it, and use that in copy.
Caveat: The 80% figure is the source's citation of a specific 2008 book, not a measured law; treat 12–15 as a starting heuristic.
Caveat: Keyword tool names and interfaces may have changed; verify the current tool.
Caveat: Sources disagree on methods — the source prefers interviews and casual conversations over formal focus groups.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, customer-research, pain-points, interviews, keyword-research, copywriting, messaging-strategy
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Separate pain targeting from motivation reflection in copy
Use when: You are drafting headline and hero copy for a PDP or landing page and need to decide whether to hit pain or aspiration.
- Recognize the two sides of crafting a message: targeting pain, and reflecting motivation including values. Your product must either address and neutralize or eradicate a critical pain, or pinpoint a key motivation.
- Write motivation copy by reflecting, not describing, what drives the visitor. The source's example: Teresa, 39 and 65 pounds overweight, goes to a weight-loss site. Her real motivations are to prove herself against the skinny neighbor, attract an ideal partner, earn her mother's respect and love what she sees in the mirror — but she tells herself she wants information about weight loss. A million sites give information; the smart copy reflects the motivation, e.g. 'Embrace the Woman in the Mirror', supported with photos of two friends smiling coming out of a dressing room, testimonials from real women who love shopping now, and video and print case studies.
- Do not write the raw motivation literally (the source rejects 'Become the Size Zero You See in Magazines' as too blunt) — write useful copy that reflects it.
- Do not confuse motivation with discount or urgency: the source states that motivation is not a discount or a limited-time offer, and is not your value proposition, because a value proposition speaks to your unique solution while motivation speaks to the customer's pain.
- If competitors or a broader category have already created the motivation, piggyback on it rather than recreating it. Example copy given: 'Americans who use software to manage their money sleep better at night', 'Find out where you're leaking cash so you can save more money & invest in your future', 'Categorize your expenses!'
- Back any factual claim with a source, such as a link to the article where the research was published.
Caveat: Motivation copy may not convert every visitor; the source's stated goals for it are to confirm the solution is what they thought it was, remind them they need a solution, keep them on the page, get them nodding, and move them to the next step.
Caveat: Pain and motivation lists in the source are illustrative, not exhaustive.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, messaging-strategy, pain-points, positioning, landing-page, product-page, copywriting
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Target 20–35% of visitors instead of 100%
Use when: You are writing or revising a homepage headline, PDP headline or ad hook and feel pressure to keep it broad so it does not exclude anyone.
- Reject the neutral-house theory for stores. Real estate agents depersonalize a house because they need one buyer for one house; you need hundreds of buyers, which tempts you to neutralize your site into a 'beige blob'. The source's counter-argument: if you try to make every visitor happy you say nothing compelling enough to make anyone buy.
- Write for your most qualified traffic — the source's band is 20–35% of visitors, and it states that even 22% is fine to write for.
- Do the conversion math as the source frames it: if only 20% of visitors are in the segment and you convert half of them, your conversion rate becomes 10%; converting a quarter of that segment yields 5%, which the source describes as more than double the average for untargeted large-company sites.
- Use direct-mail precedent: a piece promoted with 'How to Legally Rob Slot Machines in ANY Casino!' converted well enough to be mailed repeatedly in 2005 by taking the risk of being highly desirable to a select few rather than appealing to everyone.
- Revise existing copy to speak directly to that segment. Make headlines more specific at minimum. The source's test: the more neutral and bland your copy is, the more likely you are not targeting a segment.
- Take the segment-specific headline pattern from startups the source cites: CampaignMonitor 'Email marketing software for designers and their clients' (any industry could use it, but designers arrive most and are influencers), CollegeBudget 'Student-only deals, delivered daily', Reach.ly 'We connect hotels with guests in real time', Trulia 'Homes and local scoop for the real estate obsessed'.
- Once the message is right for the segment, buy more traffic for that segment — the source expects better ROI than sending untargeted traffic to a targeted page.
Caveat: The source's conversion arithmetic is illustrative, not a benchmark; the 20–35% band is the source's heuristic.
Caveat: Do not let narrow targeting lock you out of expansion — the source notes that Reach.ly-style focused messages can be expanded as the business grows.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, segmentation, positioning, conversion-optimization, messaging-strategy, acquisition, landing-page
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

## Build a product positioning document with five columns
Use when: You are preparing to write PDP copy, comparison content or in-product messaging and need one source of truth about what your product does and why it matters, or you sell multiple products and need one document per product.
- Create a table with five columns: Features, Unique to Us, Customer Pain Solved, Benefits, Priority.
- In Features, list every single feature and leave nothing out. Even a feature you consider small — the source's example is a light switch on a lamp — may be the bullet that puts you above a competitor in someone's mind. Do not start writing copy or toying with words at this stage.
- In Unique to Us, check the box when only your solution offers the feature; if a competitor offers it, list each competitor; if it is similar to a competitor's feature, briefly describe the similarity.
- In Customer Pain Solved, use your earlier customer research to note which pain each feature solves or addresses, and tag which segment it solves for when you have several.
- In Benefits, assign at least one express benefit to every feature; some features have several. If a feature has no express benefit and you have to stretch to make one fit, cut it from the list — the customer does not need to learn about it on your site.
- Set Priority per row — the source uses high, medium, low or numbers or color-coding — to know what to emphasize versus subordinate when writing.
- Create a separate document for each product variant, and reuse the document for every page, email and in-product message.
Caveat: The source recommends spending real time making this document thorough and 'possibly ugly' — it is a listing exercise, not a wordsmithing exercise.
Caveat: Benefits of how you do what you do (e.g. FSC-only paper, a playful bookkeeping look-and-feel, donating to 1% for the Planet, vegan-certified materials) sit outside features and need their own rows.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, product-page, positioning, messaging-strategy, feature-benefit, copywriting, product-catalog
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Distinguish features from benefits and write the customer's outcome
Use when: You are writing PDP bullets or benefit blocks and keep restating specifications instead of outcomes.
- Use the source's working definitions: a feature is a part of your product that does a unique thing (a light switch on a lamp); a benefit is the outcome of what that feature does — the value the customer derives (you can easily fill a room with light or darken it).
- Avoid the common mistake of treating the purpose of a feature as its benefit. Example: for an online cake service, gluten-free flour that prevents flare-ups for people with celiac and aligns with whole-food or vegan diets is still a description of the feature, not the benefit.
- Ask who the buyer is, because the benefit changes per segment. For a grandmother who feels deep satisfaction when loved ones enjoy a meal, the benefit of a gluten-free cake is watching her granddaughter with celiac enjoy her birthday party like every other kid. For a teacher bringing a celebratory cake to school under gluten restrictions, the benefit is rewarding her students while keeping the principal and the PTA happy.
- Judge a benefit by whether it tells the customer what is in it for them — how they will feel after using it and what improves in their lives — not merely what the feature will do.
- Remember the source's ordering rule for copy: your copy is first about what the user wants, and second about how your product satisfies those wants.
Caveat: Benefits that tap into motivations are described as powerful, but the source gives no measured lift figures for benefit-framed versus feature-framed copy.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, feature-benefit, product-page, copywriting, messaging-strategy, segmentation
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Choose whether to lead with a benefit or a feature per audience
Use when: You are deciding what goes in the hero headline and first bullets of a PDP or landing page for a specific shopper type.
- Treat the top-priority message as your 'lead'. The source reports having seen a headline focused on a new product feature outperform a headline showing an expected benefit, so the decision is situational, driven by what your customer base needs at that moment.
- Match the lead to shopper type. Some shoppers are suspicious of soft marketing messages — which many benefits unfortunately become. Others jump straight to comparison charts and catalogues to check the features. Others signed up because they heard about one cool feature. The source states none of these types would want you to lead with the benefit.
- Whatever you lead with, support every feature with a benefit and every benefit with a feature or a related support point — the source's example of support is a snapshot of the interface design backing a benefit of enjoyable software.
- Look at AnyNewBooks as a working pattern: the headline leads with the core benefit, the subhead supports it with the service feature of weekly notifications. The source derives at least three explicit benefits from that one feature: no cost so cash stays in your pocket; weekly cadence means no spam and no wasted seconds deleting emails; the emails come to you so you don't hunt for new books and risk missing something you would love.
- Use a mix as Mint does on its How It Works page: the page headline speaks to features while addressing the overarching value proposition of power and simplicity, and the chunk headlines vary between benefits ('See all your accounts in one place', 'stay safe and secure') and features (autocategorization of transactions), each supported by a clear visual.
Caveat: The source's cross-reference of feature-led versus benefit-led headline performance comes from the author's own observation, with no dataset, so it does not establish a general rule.
Caveat: Do not summarize to fit a tight space: the source says a constrained copywriter should choose shorter, tighter words rather than dilute the message, because a summary is neither noticeable nor memorable and specifics stick.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, product-page, feature-benefit, copywriting, conversion-optimization, merchandising
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Show don't tell: let design and visuals carry part of the message
Use when: You are building a PDP, How It Works page or feature section and deciding what to write versus what to show.
- Adopt the source's 'show don't tell' reading of Mint: rather than telling visitors the software is design-focused, the site's clean visual design demonstrates the benefit of easy, clean design.
- Support each message chunk with a visual that either gives proof of the claim — the source's example is showing interface screenshots — or reinforces the message, as with a sign saying the service is free.
- Where a screenshot, press logo, button, video demo or icon can replace copy, let it, but only without sacrificing clarity.
- In the product positioning document, pair benefit rows with their support points (e.g. an interface snapshot supporting the benefit of enjoyable software) so writers know what asset to place next to the copy.
- Note that good writing is good design in the source's framing — copy should guide design, not be squeezed into a template afterward.
Caveat: The source's examples are drawn from Mint and AnyNewBooks as observed at the time of writing; page layouts have since changed.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, product-page, landing-page, visual-hierarchy, copywriting, conversion-optimization
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Audit competitor and search language to skip wordsmithing
Use when: You need headline and value-proposition language for a PDP or ad set and are deciding between internal wording and market wording.
- Pull language from three external sources rather than from internal assumptions: exact search keywords your audience uses, phrases that appear in reviews, and competitor audits.
- Use the Google Adwords keyword tool (verify the current tool name, since interfaces change) to find phrases your audience is searching, as the source recommends for uncovering pain points.
- Audit competitors' sites to see which pain points they hit on and which features they claim, and record the overlaps in the Unique to Us column of your product positioning document.
- Borrow motivation that competitors or the broader category have already created instead of building it yourself. The source's example: personal finance tools benefit from Intuit, major banks and TV shows like Til Debt Do Us Part having already convinced people they need to manage their money, so the store only has to remind people why they need the solution.
- When you make a factual claim in the resulting copy, link or cite the research source — the source suggests this can be as simple as a link to the article where the research was published.
Caveat: The source warns against 'wordsmithing' — rearranging internal messages — but does not claim external language alone produces conversion lift.
Caveat: Competitor copy is itself unverified; treat competitor claims as language input, not as proven positioning.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, keyword-research, competitive-research, positioning, messaging-strategy, copywriting, acquisition
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Plan messaging for launch traffic waves
Use when: You are sequencing store launch content, early landing pages or ad campaigns and deciding which message to show as traffic sources shift.
- Map the waves the source describes: wave 1 is beta signups from friends, contacts and family who join the email list; wave 2 is media coverage sending specific segments such as developers from Hacker News and technophiles from TechCrunch who also join the list; wave 3 is launch day, when the email list floods the site and many visitors like the site on social networks while niche or foreign press sends a range of traffic; wave 4 brings invitations, blog posts and social recommendations — the 'Lookie Lous'.
- Write to the dominant motivation of the current wave. In wave 1, visitors — including a mom who wants to support you and an ex-coworker who wants to pick apart the idea — are looking for the basics of what you are doing. Wave 2 visitors want more specifics. Waves 3 and 4 want to learn about the solution, learn about the company, and identify whether the solution solves X pain for them.
- Expect that a value proposition alone may not cover the wave-specific motivation; the source says you will likely have to write lines of copy specifically focused on reflecting visitor motivation.
- Write the copy to confirm the solution is what they thought it was, remind them they need a solution like yours, keep them on the page longer, get them nodding, and move them to the next part of the experience where conversion work continues.
Caveat: Wave descriptions come from the source's 2011 startup context and media landscape; the sequencing pattern is transferable but the named channels are dated.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, launch-planning, messaging-strategy, landing-page, acquisition, copywriting
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Test names and creative with cheap ad or shelf experiments
Use when: You are choosing a product name, collection name or ad creative set and want market evidence instead of internal preference.
- Use paid ad testing to decide naming. The source describes Ferriss buying PPC ads and testing various titles, then using the winning ad's title as the book's name.
- Use physical placement to decide creative. Ferriss printed different covers and placed them on other books in a bookstore to see which ones customers gravitated to; the cover that attracted most people became the book's cover.
- Translate to ecommerce: test candidate product names or collection names in ad copy and compare click-through; test hero creative variants by exposing them to traffic and watching what people engage with.
- Treat these as cheap directional tests rather than definitive design decisions, and rely on the same PPC-through-click testing discipline the source recommends for segment testing.
Caveat: The source presents these as examples of low-budget research, not as controlled experiments with reported lift figures.
Caveat: Ferriss' result — the winning title became the book name — is a case example, not a guarantee that ad-tested names always outperform.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, experiment-design, creative-strategy, naming, acquisition, testing
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Fix headlines that target no one
Use when: You are auditing an existing homepage or PDP headline and it reads generic or interchangeable with competitors.
- Check for the failure pattern the source documents: LikeALittle's headline 'Hello! Welcome to LikeALittle! Connect with people near you' describes a campus-only anonymous flirting service but could be confused with any social network's headline. LearnVest's 'Take Control. Afford Your Dreams.' helps women organize their finances yet never mentions women on the homepage — the source calls this a miss.
- Contrast with the targeted pattern: CampaignMonitor names designers, CollegeBudget names students, Reach.ly names hotels, Trulia names the real estate obsessed.
- Apply the fix: make headlines more specific at minimum. The source's diagnostic is that the more neutral and bland the copy is, the more likely it is not targeting a segment.
- Watch for the internal reason for vagueness — being too close to the project, deadline pressure, or believing investors won't fund something too narrow — and treat it as a risk rather than a reason to stay broad.
- Recognize the value of being the company that 'gets' a segment: the source argues that if your product is built for one small market segment, own that and speak directly to it.
Caveat: The cited sites and headlines reflect their state at the time of writing; some may have changed.
Caveat: When testing ad copy rather than a durable headline, a broader hook may be appropriate for demand capture — this guidance is about segment-specific messaging, not a ban on any broad ad.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, messaging-strategy, positioning, segmentation, landing-page, copywriting, conversion-optimization
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

## Decide whether to write copy in positive or negative framing
Use when: You are writing PDP or ad copy about a problem the product solves and are choosing between pain-first and positive-outcome-first framing.
- Name the tension explicitly: most marketing messages are based on the idea of solving customer pain, which the source calls inherently negative, but marketing managers want messages written in positive ways.
- Ask which side of the message you are writing. If you are targeting pain, your job is to neutralize or eradicate a critical pain for the segment. If you are reflecting motivation, the copy should express the desired outcome the visitor is already chasing — the source's example rewrites a blunt desire into 'Embrace the Woman in the Mirror' rather than naming the size-zero aspiration.
- Do not substitute discounts or limited-time offers for genuine pain or motivation: the source states motivation is not a discount and not a limited-time offer, even where customers are price-sensitive.
- Choose framing based on the segment's shopper type — the same audience that distrusts soft benefit language may respond better to a direct problem statement, while a motivation-led buyer responds better to outcome language.
- Keep all claims factual and supported. The source notes that when making claims you must have support, such as a link to where the research was first published.
Caveat: The source does not resolve the positive-versus-negative question with a rule; it presents the conflict without prescribing one side.
Caveat: No measured comparison of positive versus negative copy is provided.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, copywriting, messaging-strategy, pain-points, product-page, creative-strategy
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Run a research survey and select your target segments
Use when: You are starting from limited customer knowledge and need to pick which segment your store copy and ads should speak to.
- Field a survey by email if you have the list, by phone, or in person at a real location.
- Ask questions that get people to reveal themselves — demographics, favorite services and products, and motivations.
- Collect at least 12 responses, then document and analyze everything. The source stresses you must not simply validate your assumptions; look for new information that helps you write copy to build the business rather than your ego.
- Highlight both the surprising findings and the repeated findings.
- Shortlist a segment by two conditions together: they visit your site frequently, and they compensate you with cash or referrals and likes.
- Then buy PPC ads on Google targeted to each candidate segment and see which segments click through, accepting that the test costs money but is worthwhile if it pinpoints the single best fit.
Caveat: 12 responses is the source's stated minimum for this exercise, not a statistical standard.
Caveat: Asking respondents to do you a favor and adding 'please' is claimed to raise response rates; the source says to test it.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, customer-research, surveys, segmentation, experiment-design, acquisition, messaging-strategy
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Show Don't Tell: Convey Benefits Through Design and UI
Use when: Designing a PDP, landing page or app onboarding where a core benefit (simplicity, speed, cleanliness) can be demonstrated visually instead of claimed in text.
- Identify one benefit you currently state in copy (e.g., 'clean, easy design', 'fast checkout', 'simple setup').
- Ask whether the page itself can demonstrate that benefit rather than assert it: a stripped-back layout for a design-forward product, a 2-field checkout for a simplicity claim, an instant-loading demo for a speed claim.
- Apply the Mint example as the pattern: Mint shows clean, easy visual design through their own web design instead of telling visitors they are design-focused.
- Recognize that some of the strongest messages never appear as text on the page; audit your key pages for benefits you claim in words that could instead be embodied by the page experience.
- Where the product or interface can't demonstrate the benefit directly, keep the copy claim but support it with a visual proof element (screenshot, before/after) rather than leaving it as a bare assertion.
Caveat: Works best when the claimed benefit matches something the page itself can physically do; not every benefit is demonstrable this way.
Caveat: Design-as-message still needs to be legible to a first-time visitor who doesn't know what to look for.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, product-page, landing-page, creative-strategy, positioning, visual-proof
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Build a Product Positioning Document Before Writing Copy
Use when: Starting copy for a new product page, landing page or ad campaign and needing a documented, ranked source of messages before writing.
- Create a table with columns: Feature, Unique to Us?, Customer Pain Solved, Benefit, Priority.
- List every feature of the product or offer, and mark which ones are genuinely unique versus table stakes in your category.
- For each feature, write the specific customer pain it solves, then translate it into a customer-facing benefit (not a restated feature).
- Assign a priority rank to each benefit; this ranking becomes the basis of your messaging hierarchy for every page you write.
- Keep this document as a living reference and revisit it before each new page or campaign so copy stays consistent across sessions that may be weeks apart.
- Source (Joanna Wiebe, Copy Hackers) insists this document is critical to writing compelling copy; treat completing it as a prerequisite, not an optional exercise.
Caveat: Priority ranking is a working judgment, not a formula; revisit it as you learn from customer research and testing.
Caveat: Unique features may still rank low on priority if they solve a pain few customers feel.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, positioning, product-page, messaging-hierarchy, offer-design, customer-research
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Choose Positive vs Negative Framing Based on What's Working
Use when: Deciding how to frame a headline, ad hook or landing page message around a customer pain versus a desired outcome.
- Recognize that many marketing managers demand only positive copy (avoiding 'don't', 'never', 'get rid of') while negative framings like 'DreamBox Gets Rid of SPAM' or 'Bankers Don't Want You to Use This Free Banking App' often capture attention more sharply.
- Compare the paired examples directly when drafting: 'Now You Can Use Your Smart Phone to Reduce Your Bank Fees' vs. 'Bankers Don't Want You to Use This Free Banking App'; note that both classic positive campaigns (VW 'Think Small') and negative ones (Apple '1984') are remembered as historically great.
- Test both framings on your page rather than picking on principle, per the source's advice that no one has made a definitive case for either.
- The key warning: avoid creating a negative image and then tacking your brand on as the solution. If your solution can't decisively erase the negative feeling, hint at the negative rather than dragging it to the surface.
- Do not rewrite existing negative copy that is already converting; the source's rule is 'if it ain't broke, don't fix it' — only revise negative copy if conversion rate is low or bounce/exit rate is high.
- A hybrid can work, as in Miller Lite's 'Tastes great, less filling' — pair a positive and negative frame in one message.
Caveat: The source explicitly refuses to declare a universal winner between positive and negative; treat any choice as testable, not settled.
Caveat: Revise copy only on evidence of underperformance (low conversion, high bounce/exit), not on stylistic preference.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, copywriting, headline, creative-strategy, conversion-optimization, experiment-design
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Use Keyword Research to Source Customer Language for Copy
Use when: Writing headlines, subheads, meta titles, demo scripts or button copy for a product or category page and needing the customer's own vocabulary.
- Open Google AdWords keyword tool and enter at least one primary keyword or phrase you believe fits your product.
- Review the global and local monthly search volumes to find higher-traffic related phrases; the source's example is Patrick McKenzie researching 'bingo card creator' and finding 'printable cards' has roughly 100x the traffic.
- If a higher-traffic phrase is a genuine fit, write a landing page targeting that phrase (the source presents this as McKenzie's approach, not a universal mandate).
- Record the keywords and use them to shape copy in H1 headlines, H2 subheads, URLs, meta titles, meta descriptions, demo scripts, screenshot captions, and the second line of multi-line buttons.
- Treat AdWords keywords as often the exact phrases customers want to see on the page — the language they use and that resonates when they land.
- The tool interface and availability change over time; verify the current keyword research interface before building a workflow around it.
Caveat: The specific traffic multiplier (100x) is a single illustrative example, not a benchmark.
Caveat: Keyword fit must be judged; not every high-volume phrase matches the product, and forcing it can distort messaging.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, keyword-research, copywriting, landing-page, seo, customer-research
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Run a Home-Page-Only Competitor Content Audit
Use when: Planning a new home page, category page or landing page and needing to know what messages prospects have already seen from competitors.
- Take your top keyword phrases, search them, and note the top 3 organic and PPC results for each; the companies ranking for your keywords are your competitors (source: what shows up at the top of SERPs for your keywords IS your competition).
- Limit the audit to the home page of a maximum of 10 competitors.
- For each, capture a screen of the home page and on a second page record five things: (1) the value proposition/headline, (2) top messages, (3) primary calls to action — language, visual design and page position, (4) special reasons to buy such as guarantees and assurances, (5) anything else seriously cool that wows you.
- Work in a slide deck with two pages per site; the source uses PPT with a screen capture page and an audit page.
- Synthesize: build a value proposition table (competitor, value prop, benefits highlighted such as 'security', 'ease', 'affordability'), a top messages table with tickmarks and a totals column, and a CTA table with tickmarks and totals.
- Use the totals to identify messages that are either white noise from overuse or baseline expectations visitors hold — for example, the source's audit found 'Accept credit cards', 'Low/Competitive rates & fees' and 'Support' were widely used.
- Remember the audit only describes what competitors say, not what works; assessment and testing of the messages comes later.
- Optionally, recruit users through a usability testing service (source cites about $29 per user in 2010) to review competitor pages on a budget; verify current pricing.
Caveat: The audit cannot tell you which competitor messages are effective; it only reveals what exists and is repeated.
Caveat: A message common across competitors may be a necessary baseline expectation or may be exhausted white noise — the audit alone cannot distinguish these.
Caveat: Pricing cited is from 2010 and should be verified.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, competitive-research, content-audit, home-page, messaging-hierarchy, customer-research
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Build a Messaging Hierarchy Tied to Where Users Look
Use when: Laying out a landing page, home page or PDP and deciding which message goes above the fold, near buttons, or further down.
- Start from the priority ranking of features and benefits in your product positioning document.
- Understand that hierarchy is not about ordering messages top-to-bottom on the page; it's about knowing where users look and putting the messages they need to see there.
- Lead with the biggest point for your visitor (the reason they landed), then position supporting messages as they're needed — first they land for X, then you tell them Y, then you close the deal Z.
- Make sure two things are true: messages are clearly organized so copy draws visitors through the page toward a primary CTA ('Learn More', 'Buy Now', 'Sign Up', 'Get Started'), and messages are logically positioned. Emotional decisions still require logically fed information to happen.
- Audit a high-traffic page: are the messages you want people to see — strong social proof, a stellar benefit — near eye-catching elements like buttons, icons or images? If not, reorganize and test.
- Write the hierarchy down if your team is less confident or copy sessions are spread out; the longer the gap between writing sessions, the more the hierarchy keeps you on track. Small startup teams may be able to hold it in their heads.
- Consider the gaze-direction research: usability specialist James Breeze (UsableWorld) used eye tracking to find people follow the gaze of a person in a photo; if you have a stock photo of a person near a button, test having that person look toward the button.
Caveat: The 'woman looking at button' effect is presented as testable, not proven for your page; the source frames it as worth an experiment.
Caveat: Hierarchy exists to prevent drift across sessions, not to prescribe a rigid template for every page.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, messaging-hierarchy, landing-page, product-page, conversion-optimization, layout, social-proof
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Simplify Ambiguous Offers Into One Concrete Statement
Use when: Writing or revising an offer headline, promo banner, pricing page or loyalty/checkout message that currently contains vague terms.
- Identify whether your offer message contains ambiguity on any of these axes: what exactly is reduced/offered, what the qualifying amount or condition is, and which account or product the condition applies to.
- The source's example: Fidelity's reduced-fee message was ambiguous on all three ('What sort of reduced fees? What is a certain amount? Is it checking, savings, or both?').
- Rewrite as one concrete statement: 'No Fees If You Keep $400 In Your Savings Account.'
- Per the source, customers in that program quadrupled within just 4 months after the simplification — treat this as a case example, not a promised result for your store.
- Apply the same test to your ecommerce offers: shipping thresholds, bundle discounts and subscription terms should state the exact amount and exact condition in the headline itself rather than requiring a click or a FAQ visit.
Caveat: The quadrupling result is a single reported case from a financial services program, not a benchmark for ecommerce or for every simplification.
Caveat: Simplifying does not mean overpromising; keep the concrete terms accurate to what the offer actually delivers.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, offer-design, pricing, headline, conversion-optimization, cart-checkout
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Write Unbelievable-but-True Copy and Back It With Credibility
Use when: Drafting a bold claim or hook for a PDP, landing page or ad where the benefit sounds too good to be ordinary.
- Recognize that longform sales copywriters routinely write lines that are almost impossible to believe, and this can work to your benefit.
- Enforce the critical distinction: a nearly-unbelievable line is acceptable; an impossible-to-believe line is not.
- Always support the almost-unbelievable message on the same page with clear examples that build credibility — proof, specifics or demonstrations.
- Balance against the related insight that customers want to keep believing there are magic cures, that they deserve them, and that those solutions require little effort while saving time; people are willing to believe you have the miracle product.
- The source's stance: do not exploit that willingness, but also don't hold back if you genuinely have a product that will rock their socks off — roll with the inertia of their desire to believe.
Caveat: The credibility-support step is not optional; the source explicitly says an almost-unbelievable message should always be supported by examples.
Caveat: This is the source's expressed opinion about customer psychology, not a measured result.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, copywriting, product-page, landing-page, creative-strategy, social-proof
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Leverage Related News for a Time-Sensitive Landing Page
Use when: An industry news event or competitor failure creates momentary interest your store can respond to with a landing page or campaign.
- Watch for news items related to your category that you can use in a non-nasty way; the source's criterion is explicitly that the use must not be nasty.
- The example: a client's competitor made a major blunder, a national newspaper picked it up, and the team cited the article in a long-form 'open letter' page designed to lure people away from that competitor.
- Combine a long-form page format with the news hook; the source states the long-form helped, but the motivation created by the news item was critical to the campaign's success.
- Per the source, that campaign sold nearly double the forecast — treat as a case example, not a guarantee.
- Move fast, since the motivation is tied to a news cycle; keep the page honest and cite the source rather than misrepresenting the event.
Caveat: The nearly-double result is a single case study, not a benchmark.
Caveat: The source insists on non-nasty use; using a competitor's misfortune in a way that reflects badly on you can backfire.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, landing-page, creative-strategy, copywriting, campaign-planning, competitive-research
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Overwrite, Then Cut Vigorously — Long Copy Works If Interesting
Use when: Drafting a long-form landing page, sales page or product story and deciding how much to write and how hard to edit.
- Start with 10x more information than you need and write it out; per John Caples (quoted by the source), if you need a thousand words, write two thousand.
- Then trim vigorously — the source states the second half is just as important as the first; write through the night, then spend the day editing.
- Do not fear long copy: fact-packed messages carry a wallop, and if the ad is interesting, people will be hungry for all the copy you can give them; if it's dull, short copy won't save it.
- Apply to ecommerce contexts such as PDP descriptions, long-form landing pages and email sequences: abundant specific facts plus aggressive cutting beats a thin page padded with filler.
Caveat: Long copy only works when it remains interesting; length alone is not the goal.
Caveat: The Caples quote is attributed secondhand and presented as a principle, not a tested standard.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, copywriting, landing-page, product-page, editing, long-form
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Don't Over-Explain; Assume Less Analytical Readers
Use when: Deciding how much explanation and justification to include in page copy, descriptions or ad text without bloating it.
- Account for the fact that people make hundreds of thousands of decisions daily without thinking and blindly accept things because questioning everything is exhausting.
- Because of this, you do not need to explain every statement you write; you can state a benefit without a supporting rationale for each line.
- Yet the source pairs this with an explicit boundary: do not take advantage of this tendency — the following tip states clearly 'Don't take advantage of this.'
- Practically, this means cutting unnecessary hedges and justifications, keeping copy tight, while still being truthful about what the product or offer does.
Caveat: This sits in tension with the tip to support almost-unbelievable claims with credibility examples; the resolution is that bold claims need support, ordinary claims don't need exhaustive justification.
Caveat: Assuming readers are less analytical is a heuristic, not a license for deceptive copy.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, copywriting, product-page, editing, audience-psychology
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

---

## Treat Positioning as the Highest-Leverage Copy Decision
Use when: Before writing any product page, category page or ad campaign — when deciding what your product fundamentally is in the customer's mind.
- Accept the source's claim that the most important decision you will make is how you position your product or service.
- Study the cited repositioning examples: Ogilvy & Mather positioned Merrill Lynch not as a stockbroker but as a total financial services centre, and positioned American Express Travelers Cheques for domestic use as well as foreign travel.
- Do research first — talk to customers, business contacts, anyone who will answer questions — to determine how to position.
- Decide positioning before you write a word; the source argues that although you can change later, there's no reason to start on the wrong foot when you can start right.
- Apply to ecommerce equivalents: deciding whether your store is 'cheapest', 'fastest to receive', 'the specialist for a specific use' or 'the bundle that removes decisions' is a positioning decision that should be made with customer input, not copywriting momentum.
Caveat: The cited repositioning examples are historical agency cases, not ecommerce experiments; adapt the principle cautiously.
Caveat: Positioning can be changed later, but the source recommends starting from a researched position.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, positioning, customer-research, product-page, campaign-planning
Source: COPY HACKERS.docx

## Write Ads to Trigger the Life-Force 8 Biological Desires
Use when: Choosing the core angle for a PDP headline, ad creative or launch campaign when deciding which emotional benefit to lead with.
- Reference the Life-Force 8: (1) survival/life enjoyment/life extension, (2) enjoyment of food and beverages, (3) freedom from fear, pain and danger, (4) sexual companionship, (5) comfortable living conditions, (6) to be superior/winning/keeping up with the Joneses, (7) care and protection of loved ones, (8) social approval.
- Pick the single LF8 desire your product most credibly satisfies, then make that the dominant appeal across headline, hero image and first lines of body copy.
- Treat the nine learned/secondary wants (be informed, curiosity, cleanliness, efficiency, convenience, dependability/quality, beauty and style, economy/profit, bargains) as supporting, not leading, arguments—the source argues they are far weaker because they are learned, not hardwired.
- Test which LF8 angle your buyers respond to (see the Haldeman-Julius example: the same book retitled 'Quest for a Blonde Mistress' jumped from 5,000 to 50,000 copies, and 'How to Argue Logically' tripled sales) by running the same product under different LF8-framed headlines and comparing click-through and purchase conversion.
Caveat: The book-title lift figures are a 1920s mail-order example, not a modern ecommerce benchmark.
Caveat: Pick the desire your product genuinely satisfies—the source warns that appeals your product cannot deliver will fail.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, customer-research, offer-design, creative-strategy, positioning, copywriting
Source: Cashvertising.docx

## Direct Mental Movies With Specific Visual Words
Use when: Writing product descriptions, ad body copy, landing page sections or video scripts where a generic benefit statement is falling flat.
- Start from a vague line ('Go somewhere and do something') and progressively add specificity: location, object, action, then sensory detail (the source's progression: go to the kitchen / open the oven / pull out the pizza / pull out the freshest, crispiest pizza you've ever eaten).
- Use action verbs and concrete nouns so readers picture themselves performing steps with the product, not just reading a claim.
- Add 'positive visual adjectives' (PVAs) sparingly at key moments to intensify the image.
- Apply this to ecommerce PDPs: instead of 'high-quality nonstick pan', write copy that walks the buyer through the first meal they'll cook in it.
- For video ads, script the sequence of images the viewer should see in their mind rather than listing features; the source's framing is that 'the first use of any product is inside the consumers' minds'.
Caveat: Whitman's claim that imagery increases desire is a persuasion principle, not a measured conversion lift—test copy variants against your own baseline.
Caveat: Overwriting dense imagery can hurt readability; the source also recommends clear readability formulas and simplicity.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, product-page, creative-strategy, landing-page, copywriting, video-ads
Source: Cashvertising.docx

## Lead With 'What's In It For Me?' Benefits
Use when: Reviewing product pages, about sections, ad copy or brochures that currently describe the company, factory or product specs.
- Audit each asset for self-serving content: company history, staff counts, square footage, equipment photos, 'unusual camera angles'. The source cites Daniel Starch's research showing readers ignore factory-focused ads.
- For each feature listed, write the corresponding consumer benefit and lead with the benefit.
- Put the single biggest benefit in the headline.
- Batch benefits throughout ('Bombard Your Readers With Benefits') rather than relying on one strong claim.
- Use the Flesch readability ease concept and clear layout so benefit statements land fast.
Caveat: This is the book's core 'advertising should move people to act' doctrine—it is a direct-response stance, not a brand-awareness stance; brand campaigns may weight emotion and imagery differently.

## Build Fear Appeals With All Four Required Components
Use when: Writing ad copy or a landing page for a protective or problem-solving product (security, insurance, hygiene, safety gear, health supplements).
- Confirm your product genuinely resolves the fear; if it doesn't, the source says the appeal will fail.
- Include all four elements (Pratkanis & Aronson, Age of Propaganda): (1) scare the prospect, (2) offer a specific recommendation to overcome the threat, (3) make the action seem effective, (4) make the prospect believe they can perform it.
- Target existing, widely recognized fears rather than inventing new ones—e.g., sun damage sells sunscreen; UV damage to laundry does not sell detergent.
- Support the solution with credibility boosters: testimonials, demos, free trials.
- Use deadlines and scarcity ('limited offer', 'while supplies last') as a fear-of-loss variant, but still provide the clear path to buy.
Caveat: Too much fear can paralyze rather than motivate (the source's 'deer in headlights' analogy).
Caveat: The source explicitly ties ethical use to having a truly effective solution.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, creative-strategy, copywriting, landing-page, scarcity, positioning
Source: Cashvertising.docx

## Use Ego Morphing to Sell Identity, Not Just Function
Use when: Merchandising lifestyle, luxury, apparel, beauty or status-adjacent products where functional copy underperforms.
- Identify the desirable characteristic society associates with the product: physical attractiveness, intelligence, economic success, sexual prowess.
- Show imagery of aspirational customers—per the source, perfume ads show attractive models who never even wear the product.
- For stores without celebrity customers, create association: the book's example suggests giving free product to recognizable local figures, then referencing who uses your service.
- Apply the social-proof version for B2B/service contexts: name the most rigorous clients ('why local bank presidents choose us') to transfer credibility to the average buyer.
- Avoid heavy persuasion copy in these assets; let the image do the ego work.
Caveat: This mostly applies to goods whose value is largely symbolic; commodity purchases usually need functional benefit copy.
Caveat: False or misleading customer references would be deceptive—only state genuine relationships.

## Pair the Scare With a Credible, Easy Solution
Use when: Designing acquisition creative for problem-solution products like sanitizers, supplements, insurance or safety items.
- Diagnose your market's preexisting anxieties: for hand sanitizer, the source shows GOJO used surveys about unwashed hands and dirty money to make bacteria a foreground concern.
- Lead with concrete facts about the risk, then present your product as the accessible fix (the source notes Purell's travel bottles made the solution easy).
- For product pages, add a clear call to action with a low barrier (free shipping, sample, easy return).
- Use deadline mechanics—'one-day sale', 'while supplies last'—to nudge action on the fear of missing out.
- Validate the fear's credibility by targeting existing, widely-recognized fears rather than fringe concerns.
Caveat: The book's sanitizer and mint ads are historical examples of positioning, not proof of your product's efficacy.
Caveat: Exaggerated health or safety claims can breach advertising standards; keep claims substantiated.
