## Structure branded traffic separately before scaling
Use when: Cleaning up campaign segmentation in a Google Ads account before increasing spend.
- Create a dedicated Branded Search campaign with absolute impression-share targeting to protect your brand terms and block competitor bids.
- Create a separate Branded Shopping campaign distinct from your prospecting shopping.
- Keep the rest of your budget (the source says 80-90%) on cold traffic, so branded terms don't soak up spend that was already going to convert.
- Split prospecting from retargeting campaigns, and split branded from non-branded, so spend is directed at cold customers rather than easy conversions.
- Watch for the distortion effect: if branded terms sit in prospecting campaigns, Google will spend on the easiest converters and starve the cold terms where new customers are.
Caveat: The 80-90% cold-traffic split and absolute targeting are the source's recommendations; the right split varies by brand.
Caveat: The source says competitor brand bidding is generally a waste because well-protected brands neutralize it.

## The cold customer magnet funnel structure
Use when: Designing the full Google campaign architecture for an ecommerce store.
- Top of funnel (demand generation): YouTube ads (shorts and in-stream), non-brand search, display; use advertorials, listicles, VSLs or quiz funnels as landing pages.
- Middle of funnel (demand capture): Performance Max, Standard Shopping, and Dynamic Search Ads to show products where demand already exists — this is where most ecommerce revenue comes from.
- Bottom of funnel (conversion): Branded Search, Branded Shopping and Dynamic Remarketing in Merchant Center to convert high-intent visitors and maximize revenue.
- Connect the layers: add-to-cart drop-offs are dynamically retargeted back to homepage or product page; brand-aware users get routed through branded search/shopping.
- Verify the structure matches your current stage — brands relying only on a single campaign type will remain vulnerable to competitors.
Caveat: The claimed 3-5x return applies to the source's example accounts, not a guaranteed outcome.
Caveat: Fully building out this system takes roughly 1-4 months per the source; it is not an overnight setup.

## Know the role of each ecommerce Google campaign type
Use when: Choosing which campaign types to launch for a store at its current scale and deciding which to prioritize.
- Performance Max should be your biggest spender, combined with Standard Shopping to cover the shopping placement and win first-position auctions in your category.
- Non-brand search targets high-intent queries plus problem statements and investment statements.
- Branded search and branded shopping capture already-aware users cheaply and stop competitors bidding on your terms.
- YouTube sits at the top of funnel to generate search volume and can run its own funnel simultaneously.
- Dynamic remarketing ties it all together, re-targeting anyone who visited your homepage, product page or add-to-cart.
- Only add YouTube and cold search campaigns once branded search, shopping and Performance Max are established.
Caveat: The source warns Performance Max is black-box and must be controlled properly to avoid wasted spend.
Caveat: Recommended ordering assumes a baseline of conversion data already exists.

## The three phases of ecommerce Google Ads growth
Use when: Deciding what to build first when launching or rebuilding a store's Google Ads account.
- Phase 1 (30-60 days): launch branded search, branded shopping and prospecting shopping; set up conversion tracking and analytics; use manual bidding to control spend while waiting for at least one conversion per day over 30 days.
- Phase 2 (roughly months 2-6): shift to max conversions or tROAS based on margins and break-even ROAS; remove low-performing keywords; add retargeting and audience segmentation; launch YouTube and Performance Max.
- Phase 3 (after ~6 months): increase budget on high-performing campaigns; expand to new search/shopping keywords using collected data; use Performance Max to scale with control.
- Once the core is mature, add cold search and display if you have extra spend to build out the account fully.
- Expect full build-out of a Google system covering ~90% of the inventory you'd bid on to take roughly 1-4 months.
Caveat: The 30-60 day, 2-6 month and 6-month windows are the source's heuristics, not fixed rules.
Caveat: Manual bidding in phase 1 assumes you can monitor and adjust spend regularly.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, google-ads, account-structure, scaling, conversion-tracking, bidding
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Trust Google's automation but set guardrails
Use when: Deciding how much manual control to keep over keywords, bidding and targeting in a store's Google Ads account.
- Let the creative do the targeting: go broad on keywords and audiences, and avoid over-restricting to preset signals so Google can find new converting terms.
- For standard shopping and branded search, keep tighter control — the source recommends absolute impression-share targeting on brand search.
- Use automated bidding (tROAS/tCPA) only on campaigns where it makes sense, since Google bids in real time more efficiently than manual for those.
- Set clear constraints: run negative keyword scripts to filter low-intent searches, and manually prune via search term reports daily.
- Turn off Google's automated recommendations, and scale based on your own performance data, not Google's suggestions to spend more.
- Where engagement metrics are weak (high bounce, low session duration), fix the landing page — Google can't fix bad conversion rates.
Caveat: The default-to-automation advice is the source's opinion; some accounts may need more manual control.
Caveat: Negative keyword automation still needs manual review of search terms.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, google-ads, automation, bidding, negative-keywords, campaign-structure

## Scale as a process, not an event
Use when: Managing an existing store's Google Ads account and deciding when and how much to increase spend.
- Daily: review search terms and add negative keywords; monitor impression share and adjust bids toward the source's 50-60% impression-share target.
- Weekly: scale winning campaigns against your break-even ROAS/CPA KPIs; optimize landing pages based on session duration and conversion performance; A/B test new ad copy and landing pages; do Weekly Merchant Center optimizations.
- Monthly: increase budgets only if new-customer acquisition and blended ROAS are stable; run a full account review to catch disapprovals or gaps missed during daily/weekly work.
- After each increase, confirm KPIs stay stable at the higher spend before scaling further.
- If performance declines, fix the leak before increasing budget — the source stresses that scaling is about spending better, not just more.
Caveat: The 50-60% impression-share target is the source's stated sweet spot, not a universal benchmark.
Caveat: Session duration and conversion metrics should be read together, not as standalone signals.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, google-ads, scaling, measurement, landing-page, budgeting

## Cut poor SKUs and cap brand spend for efficiency
Use when: Reviewing a store's product-level ad spend and branded campaign budgets to eliminate waste.

- Cut poor-performing SKUs rather than advertising every product; not all SKUs are scalable on Google per the source.
- Cap branded campaign spend at a maximum of around 10% of monthly spend; the source prefers 3-8%.
- Use tROAS/tCPA bidding to keep spend focused on efficient, converting traffic.
- Target the goal of increasing acquisition without increasing waste, reviewing SKU-level and brand-level spend regularly.
Caveat: The 10% maximum and 3-8% range are the source's heuristics; overspend thresholds vary by brand maturity and brand-name search volume.
Caveat: Cutting SKUs should consider whether those products support cross-sell or LTV.

Use when: Setting up ongoing optimization for a store's Google Ads and PDP/landing pages.

- Test landing-page variants too: different layouts and messaging flows, using conversion data to decide.

## Make the offer the centerpiece of Google ads
Use when: Designing ad copy and promotions for a store competing in comparative Google search and shopping results.
- Because Google is a comparative shopping platform, decide what makes your offer visibly better than the alternatives shown alongside you.
- Use shipping thresholds and frame free shipping as 'shipping on us' so customers feel they already have it.
- Test offers like buy-one-get-one, buy-two-get-one, percentage off, or for high-AOV products (above roughly $100) a dollar amount off like $50 off.
- Put the offer everywhere in the ad so it appears in the context shoppers compare.
- Consider bundling to differentiate and simultaneously raise AOV, which gives more margin to advertise.
Caveat: The above-$100 AOV suggestion and 'shipping on us' framing are the source's tips, not universal rules.
Caveat: Offer strength must pair with a congruent landing page, or clicks won't convert.

## Diagnose weak performance via landing page congruence
Use when: Troubleshooting a store's Google Ads where impressions and clicks are strong but conversions are low.
- Separate the ad's job (get the click) from the landing page's job (make the sale).
- Check average session duration as a proxy for whether the page matches what the ad promised.
- If people bounce quickly, the page likely isn't relevant to what they clicked for — fix page relevance rather than the ad.
- Confirm the offer shown in the ad also appears on the landing page so the shopper's expectation is met.
- Only after ruling out page and congruence issues should you treat it as a targeting or ad-copy problem.
Caveat: Average session duration is a rough proxy for congruence, not a definitive metric.
Caveat: The source recommends prioritizing impression share, CPC, CTR, conversion rate and conversion count before session duration.

Use when: Evaluating whether a store has the margin to run and scale Google Ads.

- Rather than focusing first on lowering COGS, the source argues to raise AOV because it offers more leverage without risking product quality or supplier relationships.
- Increase AOV through stronger offers and bundles.
- Factor LTV into how much you can afford to pay: a strong LTV may let you go break-even or slightly negative (the source gives a 0.8 example) and recover it over the next 12 months.

## Diagnose Google Ads health in the right order
Use when: Your Google Ads spend is rising but profit is flat, and you need to decide whether to fix creative, landing page, offer or campaign setup before scaling budget.
- Pull six metrics: impression share, average CPC, CTR, conversion rate, number of conversions, and average session duration.
- Read them in that priority order — the source treats impression share as the leading indicator: low impression share predicts high CPC, low CTR, low conversion rate and few conversions.
- Treat average session duration as the congruence check between ad promise and landing page; short sessions suggest the ad and page are saying different things.
- Only after those site/offer-level numbers look sound, move to Google Ads mechanics (conversion tracking, structure, creative, bids).
- Interpret the benchmark contextually: lower impression share means competitors are outbidding or out-converting you, which is a spend/offer problem, not just a bidding problem.

## Set up Shopify-to-Google Ads purchase conversion tracking
Use when: You are launching Google Ads or your reported conversions do not match Shopify orders and you need trustworthy purchase data before scaling.
- Install Google Analytics 4 via the Shopify Google & YouTube app first, then in Google Ads go to Goals > Settings and switch on enhanced conversions using the Google tag method.
- In Goals > Conversions > Summary, create new conversion actions for purchase, add to cart, begin checkout and product view (page view).
- For the purchase action: add to account-default goals, mark as primary, use different values per conversion, count every conversion, and set click-through window to 90 days and engage-view and view-through windows to 30 days.
- Set attribution to data-driven and manage conversions through the Google tag.
- Import the prebuilt Google Tag Manager container, then paste the conversion ID and each of the four conversion labels into the matching GTM constants and publish the workspace.
- In Shopify admin > Settings > Customer Events, add a custom pixel, paste the GTM customer-event code, set your country code and insert your GTM container ID, then save and connect.
- Finally, edit add to cart, begin checkout and product view to Secondary (observe only) so they do not drive bidding; keep purchase as the account default goal.
Caveat: The exact menu paths and prebuilt container are from the source's 2025 workflow; verify current Google Ads and Shopify interfaces before following step by step.
Caveat: Turning non-purchase events to secondary assumes purchase is your optimisation event — different goals may justify a different primary.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, conversion-tracking, shopify, google-tag-manager, measurement, pixel-setup
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Structure campaigns by funnel stage and start at the bottom
Use when: You are planning a Google Ads account architecture or reworking an account where branded and non-branded results are blended and unreadable.
- Top of funnel: YouTube Shorts and static assets run through Demand Gen, fed by your Meta winners at roughly $50/day, running fully broad with the creative doing the targeting.
- Mid funnel: cold search, competitive search (only if it works well), Performance Max and cold Shopping.
- Bottom funnel: branded search, branded shopping and dynamic remarketing.
- If you are just starting, begin at the bottom of the funnel to accumulate conversions, then add one mid-funnel campaign — for ecommerce usually Shopping and PMax — and only move up-funnel once smart bidding is viable.
- Exclude all customer lists from cold campaigns and exclude your brand from PMax so branded conversions do not inflate cold performance.
- Keep branded search and branded shopping in separate campaigns so cheap branded conversions stay identifiable and marketing spend stays efficient.
Caveat: The source's rule of thumb for smart bidding eligibility is about one conversion per day sustained over 30 days — treat as a heuristic, not a Google requirement.
Caveat: Running your Meta winners as YouTube statics/shorts is a transfer assumption; test rather than assuming parity.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, campaign-structure, google-ads, funnel, performance-max, branded-search, demand-gen
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Write Google ads from audience research, not keyword lists
Use when: You are writing search ad copy, shopping titles or a YouTube short for a cold audience and need angle and language direction.
- Before writing anything, map the audience: the language they use, psychographics, problems, pains, goals, desires, why they buy and why they buy from you specifically.
- Ask explicitly: what type of person searches this, what pain are they in, what problem are they solving, what desire or goal does the product fulfil.
- Write search headlines, descriptions, images, callouts, site links and snippets that echo that language, since on Google the searcher is seeing every competitor's ad simultaneously.
- In shopping ads, carry the same language into the title (for targeting) plus the promo extension, ratings and social proof that visually differentiate the listing.
- For YouTube Shorts use heavy direct response: make the CTA explicit (click here, search this, tap the screen) and state the big offer and next step, because the platform is less purchase-oriented than Meta.
- The source argues resonance, connection and offer are what make you stand out — not just being cheapest, since margin constrains price competition.
Caveat: The claim that cheap price would win all else being equal is the source's framing; margin reality often prevents it.
Caveat: Heavy-direct-response guidance is the source's opinion about YouTube's buying sophistication, not a measured universal rule.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, customer-research, ad-copy, shopping-ads, youtube-ads, positioning, offer-design
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Let Shopping and PMax discover your converting keywords
Use when: You need real, purchase-confirmed search phrases for search campaigns, shopping titles or landing page copy.
- Launch Shopping and PMax broadly and let Google test a wide range of search terms automatically rather than pre-selecting keywords.
- Read the search term report inside Google Ads and rank queries by impressions, CTR, conversions and CPC.
- In Shopping, this also reveals what your product title is actually matching against, which tells you what your feed title is communicating.
- Extract converting queries into exact and phrase match keywords in search campaigns — start with exact for proven winners, phrase for close variations.
- Push the same winning phrases into product titles, PMax assets, YouTube angles, offers and landing page copy.
- Exclude the low-performing and non-converting search terms to raise efficiency, then repeat: the loop is a flywheel, not a one-time task.
- Example: a shopping feed surfaces 'best marathon shoes for flat feet' as converting, so you'd otherwise never have intuited that query and can now target it exactly and build copy around it.
Caveat: This inverts traditional keyword-first research; the source recommends manual keyword research only for your very first search campaigns or when you need control.
Caveat: The source claims broad will not work in search campaigns unless you are explicitly testing — validate data elsewhere first.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, keyword-research, search-terms, performance-max, shopping-ads, search-campaigns
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Use manual keyword tools only for the first rung
Use when: You have no conversion history and must launch a first search campaign or decide initial product title targets.
- Use Google Keyword Planner on your main product category to find general product-level search phrases with high search volume and reasonable CPCs.
- Use paid tools (Ahrefs, Semrush) to reverse-engineer competitor keywords, and SpyFu to see what competitors are bidding on.
- Treat competitor bidding as weak evidence: the source says assume competitors may be bidding on terms that do not work for them.
- Note the limitation: third-party data gives search volume and competitor behaviour but no purchase confirmation for your product.
- Use these keywords only to seed, then let Shopping/PMax conversion data replace and refine them over time.
- Best combined approach per the source: start broad with method one (let Google optimise for speed and scale), then layer traditional research for extra optimisation.
Caveat: High search volume without buyer intent is a poor target; the source stresses buy intent over volume.
Caveat: Keyword Planner and third-party tool interfaces change frequently — verify current functionality.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, keyword-research, google-keyword-planner, competitor-research, search-campaigns
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Set bids and budgets from unit economics, not habit
Use when: You are setting bid strategy and daily budget for branded, shopping, PMax or cold campaigns.
- Work backwards from unit economics: how much can you afford to spend per acquisition to beat competitors, and how much are you willing to spend to test versus scale.
- Match strategy to campaign type: branded search runs on target impression share (the source calls it absolute target impression share); branded shopping runs on manual CPC where you control max CPC.
- Mid-funnel and cold campaigns use smart bidding: maximise conversion value for ecommerce (more value per purchase), maximise conversions when you want volume, plus tROAS and tCPA variants.
- Choose maximise conversions over value only when you know your break-even CPA and simply want as many actions as possible; otherwise value-based bidding is the ecommerce default per the source.
- The source treats bids and budget as the last optimisation area — after creative, structure, tracking and offer — though it still matters.
- Budget levels depend entirely on brand specifics: goals, KPIs, COGS and desired scale; there is no universal number.
Caveat: The source explicitly gives a non-specific answer on budget size because it depends on individual brand economics — do not copy another brand's budget.
Caveat: Smart bidding requires sufficient conversion volume to learn; bid strategy names and settings change, so verify in the current Google Ads interface.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, bidding, budgeting, unit-economics, smart-bidding, branded-search
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Enrol the four GMC add-ons
Use when: You are setting up or auditing Google Merchant Center before running Shopping, PMax or remarketing.
- Go to Merchant Center Settings > Add-ons and check the Discover tab for programs you are not enrolled in.
- Enable dynamic remarketing — the source says it is essential for the whole Google Ads system to function for ecommerce.
- Enable Google customer reviews and product ratings to add trust signals that the source claims noticeably raise CTR and conversion rate on ads.
- Enable promotions so your discount appears in the Shopping ad itself; the source argues a visible better offer wins the click and increases purchase likelihood.
- Verify each add-on is actually active, not just available, before spending on feed campaigns.
Caveat: CTR and conversion-rate lifts from reviews/ratings/promotions are stated by the source without specific measured figures — treat as directional.

## Complete GMC business info and branding to survive review
Use when: You are onboarding a store to Merchant Center or your account has warnings and you want to reduce suspension risk.
- In Business Info, enter details that exactly match your website: verify and claim your online store, provide your checkout link, accepted payment methods, and business logo and colours.
- In the same screen use Edit logo and colours to upload square and rectangular logos plus a main and accent colour, so Shopping ads look on-brand and Google sees a complete, legitimate business.
- Verify your website branding, payment methods and policies are genuinely consistent with what you enter — the source warns Google is ruthless about mismatches that lead to account suspension.
- If in the US, enable business identity attributes: category options include woman-owned, veteran-owned, black-owned, Latino-owned and small business.
- The source recommends selecting small business even for larger companies, citing the Bureau of Labor Statistics threshold of under $40 million annual revenue as qualifying as small.
- Add social profiles (Instagram, Facebook and others) to make business information as complete as possible.
Caveat: The small-business threshold is the source's interpretation of Bureau of Labor Statistics classification, not a Google eligibility rule — verify current Google criteria.
Caveat: Identity attributes are flagged as a minor CTR/social-standing factor, not a major performance lever.

## Lock shipping and returns as manual in GMC
Use when: You are configuring Merchant Center shipping/returns or your store changes shipping rates and you fear feed or policy mismatches.
- In the Shopify Google & YouTube sales channel, under product feed settings, set shipping settings to Manual setup in GMC so changes in Shopify do not auto-update Merchant Center.
- The source's reasoning: a random sync change can create a mismatch with your stated shipping policy and a flag can escalate to account suspension.
- In Merchant Center > Shipping and returns, add policies for every country you ship to, including differing speeds and methods (the example brand runs both US and Canada).
- Enter an accurate ship-from location.
- Add your returns policy inside GMC, link directly to the specific returns policy page, and ensure it mirrors what is on your site.
- Treat a clear, strong return policy as effectively a requirement to run Merchant Center today, and as something Google checks when deciding to suspend.
Caveat: Keeping settings manual means you must update GMC yourself when shipping genuinely changes — do it as part of the routine maintenance cycle.
Caveat: Google's policy and feeds interfaces change; verify that manual-mode options still exist before relying on the workflow.

## Audit feeds and fix 'needs attention' errors
Use when: You are diagnosing why feed ads underperform, or onboarding a store whose products are disapproved or warning-flagged.
- In Merchant Center settings, open Data sources to see every feed; with the Shopify Google & YouTube app the primary feed comes via the content API.
- Identify your primary feed and any supplemental feeds, confirm the primary is updating, and note that promotions sources can also live here.
- Go to Products > Needs attention to see Google's per-SKU issues; the example shows approved products missing an age group.
- Work through the list systematically, fixing red errors and yellow warnings using Google's own stated fix instructions.
- Make this a weekly routine: revisit Products and diagnostics each week and clear new red or yellow flags before they accumulate.
Caveat: The source notes many brands never do this and blame Google Ads for what is a feed problem — expect meaningful time cost with large SKU counts.

## Build product titles with the 130–150 character formula
Use when: You are rewriting Shopping/PMax feed titles to raise relevance and win more qualifying impressions.
- Write titles of roughly 130–150 characters including: highest-volume keyword, product details (colour, size, quantity), second highest-volume keyword, differentiating angles/USPs, and brand name.
- For a small brand pushing cold traffic, frontload the high-volume keywords and place the brand name at the end.
- For a big brand that can leverage recognition in Shopping, place the brand name first and the high-volume keywords after.
- Cover variant fields — colour, size, weight, format — so searchers know exactly what they are buying.
- Apply the difference between high-volume keyword (the most product-aware term everyone uses), variants, USPs/angles and brand name in that structure.
- Edit titles in Merchant Center > Products by opening the SKU and using Edit product, or manage them in a data feed tool like DataFeedWatch.
- You can paste the formula and your product info into ChatGPT to generate a draft, then edit the keyword choices yourself.
Caveat: The 130–150 character target is the source's recommendation; verify current Google title length limits before publishing.
Caveat: The example 'Apple Watch band' title shows the pattern but is a case illustration, not a performance promise.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, product-feed, product-titles, shopping-ads, keyword-research, seo-copy
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Write feed descriptions that survive policy review
Use when: You are optimising feed descriptions for a store that simply imports Shopify product copy into Merchant Center.
- Check your current description: if it is auto-pulled from the Shopify product page, assume it is not optimised for feed targeting.
- Write roughly 1,000 characters covering key features, USPs, a call to action and useful product information.
- Frontload high-volume keywords at the start, in the style of an SEO article, because Google uses the description for targeting.
- Exclude promotional text such as discount claims, because the source states that violates Google's policies.
- Treat description as secondary in impact to the title, but still worth the effort because it expands the terms your product can match against.
Caveat: The source calls the description less leveraged than the title — prioritise titles first.
Caveat: Promotion language belongs in Merchant Center promotions, not the description; policy details can change, so verify current rules.

## Choose feed images for context and standout
Use when: You are choosing or testing primary feed images for product pages and Shopping/PMax assets.
- Select the highest quality, most attention-grabbing image available for each SKU as the primary feed image.
- Test the product alone on a clean background against the product in context: a sofa in a well-lit living room setup, golf clubs mid-swing on the green, an Apple Watch band shown on an actual Apple Watch.
- Show a product in the context it was made for when the item alone is confusing — the Apple Watch band only makes sense attached to a watch.
- Supplement with lifestyle images of people using the product for other placements.
- For this source's example brand, the product-focused image performed best; treat that as their finding and run your own test rather than copying it.
Caveat: The source is explicit that the best-performing image style is brand-specific — do not assume product-only wins for your category.
Caveat: Main image choice can affect eligibility and performance simultaneously; check policy requirements alongside conversion appeal.

Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Fill product identifiers, categories and attributes accurately
Use when: Your feed shows warnings about identifiers or missing attributes, or you want products to appear under Shopping filters.
- Never change the product ID or SKU; let them import consistently from Shopify or a feed tool, because changing them disrupts history and targeting.
- Provide GTIN, UPC, EAN, JAN or ISBN if your product has one — ask your supplier and register the barcode in the feed; custom-made products may legitimately lack one.
- Set product type and Google product category for every SKU (the source suggests asking ChatGPT for a first draft), condition to new unless genuinely used, plus accurate price and availability.
- Complete detailed attributes used in Shopping filters: colour, size, size type, sizing system by country, gender, material, pattern, age group for apparel; bundle status, adult and energy class where relevant.
- Leave shipping and returns to pull from Shopify or the policies configured in GMC.
- Add custom labels (e.g. label 1 for small bands, label 2 for large bands) so you can target and report on cohorts inside Google Ads.
- Keep COGS, sell quantity and currency fields filled where applicable, though the source calls these minor for performance.
Caveat: Missing correct identifiers create performance-limiting warnings rather than outright ban in most cases — still fix them early.
Caveat: Attribute requirements and identifier rules vary by category and country; check current Merchant Center requirements.

Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Never edit price or availability inside GMC
Use when: You are updating product pricing or stock and deciding where to make the change.
- Make all price, availability and sale price changes in Shopify (or your store platform), never directly in Merchant Center.
- Let the change flow back into GMC through the feed so the value matches what a shopper sees on your site.
- Understand the risk: Merchant Center checks for mismatches between the site price and the feed price, flags a warning, and repeated mismatches compound account risk.
- Treat this as part of weekly and monthly maintenance: review feed values against the live site during routine checks.
- If a value genuinely must change in GMC for a feed-only reason, confirm the source-of-truth logic first so the next sync does not overwrite or re-flag it.
Caveat: The rule applies to price, availability and sale price specifically; other attributes such as titles and descriptions are edited in the feed.
Caveat: This is the source's stated best practice for avoiding suspension — enforcement behaviour can change, so keep site and feed aligned regardless.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, google-merchant-center, pricing, inventory, account-compliance, shopify

## Run a weekly and monthly GMC maintenance rhythm
Use when: You run feed campaigns continuously and need an operating routine that prevents gradual account decay or suspension.
- Weekly: go through Products and diagnostics, fixing any new red errors and yellow warnings.
- Monthly: briefly review your website shipping and returns policies against what is configured in Merchant Center and correct any drift.
- When a new sale or promotion starts, add it to GMC promotions and set a proper end date; when the sale ends, make sure the promotion expires or is removed.
- Keep the go-to-market discipline of never editing price, availability or sale price in GMC, so maintenance stays focused on feed hygiene rather than correcting mismatches.
- Treat this as the ongoing layer on top of the one-time setup phases: account and business setup, shipping/returns/tax, feed health, and trust/visibility.

## Reduce Merchant Center suspension risk deliberately
Use when: You are auditing an account for suspension risk or your store has received warnings, mismatches or policy flags.
- Prioritise the most common triggers the source identifies: inaccurate business information, mismatched shipping and returns policies, and price/availability mismatches between site and feed.
- Keep business info, checkout link, payment methods and branding accurate and consistent with the live site at all times.
- Set shipping settings to manual in GMC and maintain policies per country with an accurate ship-from location.
- Link directly to a real returns policy page and mirror the policy in Greenhouse Center configuration.
- Clear feed errors and warnings weekly rather than letting them stack, and never edit price, availability or sale price inside GMC.
- Recognise the stakes: a ban blocks feed ads, Shopping ads, and the strongest part of PMax for an ecommerce brand, so prevention work outranks other optimisation.
Caveat: This is a prevention checklist, not an appeals process — a suspended account needs its own remediation path.

## Product Feed Optimization Basics for Google Merchant Center
Use when: Optimizing your Google Merchant Center product feed so Shopping and PMax ads can serve correctly and convert.
- Do not overcomplicate feed titles, descriptions or images; the source argues keeping them simple and accurate works best and that most people overcomplicate this.
- Never change your sale price inside Google Merchant Center itself — leave pricing to sync from your store so no mismatch can appear.
- Make availability dynamic to real stock: anything out of stock must be marked sold out, or Google will flag you for showing 'in stock and ready to ship'.
- Do the same pass across every SKU; note that scaling this is mostly manual work if you have many SKUs, but once correct it improves Shopping results.

## Payment and Checkout Compliance Checks for GMC
Use when: Preparing or auditing your store checkout to avoid Google Merchant Center suspension or promotion disapproval.
- Maintain SSL on checkout pages — confirm the checkout URL starts with HTTPS, which Google requires for secure transactions.
- Test every payment method you list (PayPal, cards, crypto, Afterpay, etc.); listing a method that doesn't actually work at checkout is a GMC error and can suspend the account.
- Verify final price transparency: taxes, state-level sales tax, and shipping fees by destination must all be reflected before payment and match the Shopify and GMC data. Run test orders to confirm calculations.
- Test discount code functionality. A promotion won't go live in GMC unless the code applies at checkout; if an approved promotion stops working, that is a big flag.
Caveat: GMC's checkout audit behaviour is described from the presenter's experience, not official documentation; verify current policy.
Caveat: Promotion approval rules and deadlines change — check GMC help docs.

## Listing Accuracy Checklist: Claims, Reviews, Links, Pricing
Use when: Auditing product listings and product pages before scaling Google Shopping or PMax spend.
- Review product claims for accuracy and remove exaggerated or unverifiable claims; stick to factual benefits. If making scientific claims, provide credible resources in listings, descriptions and on the landing page.
- Verify review authenticity and recency. The presenter warns against fake reviews; he recommends a real review flow and pushing a review feed into GMC so star ratings show on Shopping listings.
- Mark out-of-stock items as sold out and keep availability dynamic to real inventory — showing 'in stock and ready to ship' on an out-of-stock item is a violation.
- Check every link, especially product page to shopping listing; broken or mismatched links can be flagged as a scam and lead to suspension.
- Ensure listed price matches checkout price and discounts apply accurately; mismatches cause abandoned carts and GMC disapprovals.
Caveat: The source calls unverifiable claims 'the biggest thing that hits brands' — his experience, not a published statistic.
Caveat: Claim rules vary by category (e.g. health); confirm current Google misrepresentation policy.

## Shipping, Returns and Contact Info Sync for GMC
Use when: Setting up or maintaining shipping, returns and contact sections to prevent GMC suspension.
- Match website shipping settings to GMC shipping and returns sections, including shipping cost and delivery times. The source shares a client case where shipping cost dropped after a courier change but GMC wasn't updated, causing a week-long suspension.
- Name the courier services you actually use (UPS, FedEx, DHL) in both your shipping policy page and GMC shipping policy.
- Confirm order tracking functionality works and that the courier provides tracking; customer service will feel it otherwise.
- Write clear step-by-step return instructions in both your site returns policy and GMC, and link GMC to the site returns page. Missing returns, shipping or terms pages guarantees suspension per the source.
- Update refund processing timings monthly, keep return periods current, test return links, and verify return address and timing monthly.
- Verify physical business address monthly, test the customer service phone number, use a branded domain email (not Gmail), and cross-check contact details match across GMC, Google Ads and all Google accounts.

## Build a Reusable Brand Context Profile with AI Before Writing Ad Copy
Use when: Preparing to generate Google Ads assets, Meta copy, landing page copy or emails and needing consistent brand context.
- Give the AI a role, context, task, examples, constraints and desired output — the source calls this the best way to prompt anything.
- Use a prompt casting the AI as a world-class direct response copywriter for ecommerce cold traffic, and feed it a PDF of a product page (e.g. save the page as PDF from the browser).
- Have it audit the page for value proposition, emotional and logical persuasion, CTAs, voice of customer, proof mechanisms, offer positioning, copy structure, conversion blockers and missed psychological levers, plus optimization suggestions.
- Run a second prompt casting it as an elite advertising strategist/deep researcher to map product intelligence, customer psychographics, competitors, keyword and intent mapping, and market positioning.
- Save the resulting context profile offline or in Drive so you and your team can reuse it for any asset type.

## Convert Research into JSON Context Profiles for Consistent Copy
Use when: Structuring brand research so any AI session can instantly understand your store before generating copy.
- Prompt a strong writing model (the source uses Claude Sonnet 4) as a world-class AI prompt engineer and brand strategist, feeding it the full deep research document.
- Have it produce four outputs: a customer avatar JSON, a market context JSON (pricing tiers, direct and indirect competitors, target keywords, competitive landscape), a brand context JSON, and a full combined context profile.
- Use the combined profile as the paste-in context for any model when generating ad copy, landing pages or emails.
- Keep the JSON files in Drive so your whole team can reuse them; note that long responses may pause and require 'continue'.
- Expect detail like avatar psychographics, competitor mapping and offer positioning — the point is precision, not brevity.
Caveat: JSON is used because it maps variables clearly for LLMs; it is a workflow choice, not a Google requirement.
Caveat: Model names and best-model recommendations may change.

## Generate All Google Ads Assets from a Context Profile
Use when: Building Google Search or PMax campaign assets at scale without starting from a blank page.
- Load the full context profile into a fresh model session together with the Google Ads asset JSON template.
- Prompt simply: create all the Google Ads assets needed for my brand.
- Review outputs organized as Search and PMax assets — headlines (including long ones), descriptions, sitelinks, callouts, structured snippets, price extension suggestions, and asset variations by awareness level (problem, solution, product, most aware) plus competitor and responsive search ad examples.
- Ask for a product feed Shopping title when needed; the model returns primary and alternative titles, keyword-optimized and competitive variations, promotional titles, and explains why they work.
- Manually edit weak or off-brand lines — the source flags examples like 'aerospace grade materials' as bad and 'stop buying cheap wallets' as possibly off-brand.
Caveat: The source says AI gets you roughly 80–90% of the way; human judgment supplies the rest.
Caveat: The '$10M new customer revenue' figure is the agency's claim about its workflow, not a guaranteed result.
Caveat: Verify character limits and current asset requirements in Google Ads.

## Set Up a Branded Search Campaign to Protect and Capture Demand
Use when: Launching or optimizing paid search on your own brand name to capture searchers who saw you elsewhere.
- Create a Search campaign, optimize for the purchase conversion, name it clearly (agency + brand + 'search brand').
- Use impression share bidding, not conversions, and set 'absolute top of search' to about 95%, with a max CPC around $3. In the source's experience brand clicks then cost about 1–2 cents, at most around 50 cents.
- Turn off search and display network partners, target your own country using presence (not presence or interest), set English, and add observational audiences like customer list and GA traffic.
- Add exact-match brand keywords such as [brand], [brand reviews], [brand discount code]; optionally add phrase match versions of best exact-match keywords for extra scope.
- Write RSAs with brand + 'official site' + offer headlines and sales copy descriptions; add logo and business name; set a daily budget like $25.
- Optimize by raising max CPC only if the budget won't spend, and never switch away from absolute top of search.
Caveat: The source says you are often paying for some conversions that might have happened organically, but argues the space, defence and cheap conversion-data benefits justify it.
Caveat: The $64 spend returning $1.5K and $858 returning 24 orders are specific examples, not benchmarks.
Caveat: CPC and bidding options change — verify current Google Ads settings.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, branded-search, google-ads, conversion-optimization, bid-strategy, brand-defence
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Why Every Ecommerce Brand Should Run a Branded Search Campaign
Use when: Deciding whether to spend on your own brand terms in Google Ads.
- Take up more SERP space: paid ad at top plus organic results plus Shopping results leaves searchers surrounded by your brand.
- Defend your branded term from competitors who may bid on it with 'us vs them' ads; the source says running early helps Google give you ad rank as the official advertiser.
- Induce purchases from people who discovered you on Facebook or organic content and then search your name — an offer in the ad can move them from research to buying.
- Feed your purchase conversion action with cheap, high-intent conversions that improve performance of Shopping, PMax and other campaigns.
- Add buying-journey safety: a sponsored 'official site' result helps searchers trust they are on the real store rather than a knockoff or scammer.
Caveat: SAS is where the source says competitor brand-bidding is most prevalent; ecommerce less so.
Caveat: The source concedes most brand conversions would often happen organically anyway — the case is marginal gain and defence, not pure incremental revenue.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, branded-search, google-ads, conversion-data, brand-defence, acquisition

## Set Up and Automate a Branded Shopping Campaign with Scripts
Use when: Adding a high-leverage, fast-to-launch Shopping campaign to lift account efficiency and cheap sales.
- Duplicate or build a Shopping campaign structure, then exclude all non-branded terms so it only serves on branded queries.
- Use a negative keyword script to automatically keep non-branded queries out of the campaign as search terms accumulate.
- Match product feed titles and descriptions to brand naming so the campaign surfaces on brand searches.
- Monitor and adjust exclusions regularly to prevent non-branded spend leaking into the branded campaign.
- The source says this can be set up in a couple of clicks and lift ROAS and spend efficiency within about 24 hours.
Caveat: The claim of uplift within 24 hours is the presenter's description, not a measured benchmark.

## Branded Search & Shopping Campaigns: Structure, Bidding & Exclusions
Use when: Setting up or auditing paid search structure for a store that already gets branded searches and wants brand protection plus cheaper conversion data.
- Create a separate shopping campaign for branded traffic only (New campaign > Sales > conversion goal Purchases > Shopping > connect Merchant Center > choose Standard shopping, not Performance Max). Name it by brand + campaign type.
- Set bidding to manual CPC with a low budget (the source uses ~$50/day) and high campaign priority. Turn off the search network; set locations to where you actually sell and set location options to 'Presence' only, never 'Presence or interest'.
- Create a product group/ad group (e.g. all products in one group if the brand term applies to the whole catalog) with a ~$1 starting bid, then subdivide by product only when products differ enough that you want to see separate average CPCs.
- Automatically exclude all non-branded terms via a Google Ads script (Tools > Bulk actions > Scripts) so only brand terms remain in the shopping listing. Verify the current script UI before copying anything.
- Optionally run a parallel branded search campaign so a branded query shows both shopping and search ads, taking more of the above-the-fold SERP.
- In the branded campaign, exclude your existing-customer list: export the customer list from your store backend, then Google Ads > Audiences > Exclusions > upload and exclude. Rationale: repeat buyers searching your name are buying, not browsing, so paying for that click is waste.
- Optimize only via manual bids — do not switch to automated bidding; if search impression share is low, raise the max bid slightly instead.
- Check whether you are paying for conversions that would have happened organically: the presenter states you usually are, and argues it is still worth it for brand protection, cheap conversion data feeding prospecting, and conversion data that Google uses to steer smart bidding.
- Do not expect the campaign to stay clean on its own — continuously exclude non-branded terms and keep the Merchant Center feed optimized, since feed quality drives cost, visibility and click share.
Caveat: Source is a Google Ads agency owner with a commercial interest; his 'you always need one' position is his opinion, not a measured benchmark.
Caveat: Data showed competitors ranking on brand terms; the presenter notes this is mainly seen in software but applies to ecommerce too.
Caveat: Branded campaigns mostly capture demand that already exists; treat them as protection and data harvesting, not incremental growth.
Caveat: Automated keyword-removal scripts require account-specific edits and may change — verify the current script interface.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, google-ads, branded-search, shopping-campaigns, campaign-structure, bidding-strategy, brand-protection, measurement
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Cold Search Campaigns: Capture Problem-Aware Demand, Not Product-Aware Demand
Use when: Planning acquisition for a store whose product solves a specific problem and whose product-aware search demand is exhausted or too expensive.
- Set up a search campaign on the Google network only, objective Sales, single primary conversion action, campaigns optimized for purchase conversions.
- Choose bidding: the source uses Maximize Conversions with the AI Max feature on for cold problem-aware terms. He reserves Maximize Clicks for testing product-market fit with broad investigative terms. Turn brand exclusions on so branded queries stay out of this cold campaign.
- Set locations with 'Presence' (not presence or interest) limited to countries you actually ship to; set a daily budget you can hold for at least a few weeks of testing.
- Build the ad group from many problem-phrased keywords, mixing exact and broad match; the source explicitly avoids phrase match. Start broad to see the full range of queries the market actually types.
- Read the search terms report: mine converting broad queries, then promote proven ones to exact match so Google can optimize around them, and pause/remove terms with clicks but no conversions.
- Judge terms on click-through rate, CPC and conversion rate together. In the case study, 'how to lower blood pressure' had a 7.5% CTR at 38p CPC and ~2.3% conversion; 'blood pressure supplements' had a higher conversion rate but also a higher CPC; 'how to reduce high blood pressure' had a ~9% CTR with few conversions.
- Once a term proves itself, change the final URL for that keyword so the ad points to a page written for that exact query, rather than the generic default landing page.
- Build out the ad with price extensions, structured snippets, callouts, sitelinks and a business logo to occupy more of the SERP.
- Use dynamic keyword insertion in the headline so the searcher's own phrase appears in the ad (set a sensible default headline for when no keyword is inserted) and pin it; the source credits this congruence for an 8.32% cold CTR.
Caveat: Case-study metrics (8.32% CTR, 3.82% cold conversion rate, ~£3.5k spend, £7.6k reported return) are from one UK supplement account over ~3 weeks and are examples, not benchmarks.
Caveat: The presenter says Google-reported return figures are unreliable and recommends a third-party attribution tool as source of truth.
Caveat: Broad match floods in irrelevant queries; it requires ongoing search-term review and negative work.
Caveat: Send problem-aware cold traffic to an advertorial/educational sales letter, not a product page with a buy box — the source states you cannot present an offer to someone who is only problem-aware and brand-unaware.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, google-ads, cold-traffic, keyword-research, search-terms-report, landing-page, dynamic-keyword-insertion, acquisition
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Build Mini-Funnels Per Search Term for Cold Traffic
Use when: Deciding how many landing pages to build for paid search and where to spend page-creation effort on problem-aware traffic.
- List the problem-aware phrases in your niche with their monthly search volume (the source cites ~3.6k for 'how to lower blood pressure' as an example). Treat each phrase as a separate mini-funnel.
- For each phrase, check the three constraints: can the ad get a strong CTR, what CPC can you tolerate at your COGS, and what conversion rate can the page achieve.
- Apply constraint thinking: if CTR is already strong (the source reached ~8%) and CPC is acceptable, the biggest lever is conversion rate, so invest in the page for that phrase rather than rewriting the ad.
- Create a landing page congruent with the phrase — e.g. for 'how to lower blood pressure' build an educational article/sales letter that lays out the problem and solutions, then presents your product as the solution. Avoid a generic advertorial when the phrase implies a different intent.
- Point the keyword's final URL to that page (not just the default ad URL) so the same campaign can hold several mini-funnels.
- Keep phrases you have not built a page for yet running to the default page; add pages only for phrases with real search volume and converting signal.
- Expect different CPCs by intent: product-aware phrases ('blood pressure supplements') cost more per click than problem phrases, but the problem phrase can still have a lower cost per conversion because it is more congruent with the page.
- Because volume is capped per phrase, treat each page as longevity infrastructure — a page converting at 10% CTR on ~4,000 views a quarter compounds over years of the brand's life.
Caveat: Search volume limits reach per phrase; this is a demand-capture play, not a way to create new demand.
Caveat: The conversion-rate estimates in the source are projections from a 3-week test, not a proof that page changes lift conversion.
Caveat: Distinguish conversions at the page level (purchase conversion rate) from click-through rate on the ad; improving one does not automatically improve the other.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, landing-page, google-ads, cold-traffic, conversion-optimization, search-intent, advertorial
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Performance Max: What It Is and Where It Fits in the Google Funnel
Use when: Deciding whether to add Performance Max to a store's Google account and what budget share and role to assign it.
- Understand the incentive: the source argues Performance Max exists partly to force advertisers into YouTube, Display, Discovery and Gmail inventory that previously could not be monetized from search and shopping alone — so it is built to give Google revenue, but still useful to you.
- Position Performance Max as the middle-of-funnel catch-all: it covers auctions and placements your search and shopping campaigns lose, and it retargets cold traffic from Meta, TikTok or organic that landed on the Google network via page-view/product-view signals.
- Leave a separate top of funnel (YouTube shorts, in-stream, demand gen, display) and bottom of funnel (branded search, branded shopping, product-aware search and shopping).
- Allocate roughly 20–30% of budget to Performance Max as a healthy share — the source's heuristic, not a calculated optimum. Use Performance Max as a core engine, not the entire vehicle.
- Feed it strong signals before expecting performance: clean Merchant Center feed, optimized product titles, proper purchase conversion tracking, and high-quality creative assets.
- Use it as a remarketing mechanism for cold visitors, but exclude brand terms so it does not claim your branded conversions.
- Give it both demand capture and demand generation credit: it can catch existing searches/shopping intent and retarget cold visitors across placements within one campaign.
Caveat: The source explicitly warns Performance Max is not set-and-forget; he has audited accounts with 90–100% of budget in 11 Performance Max campaigns.
Caveat: Performance Max has limited reporting transparency, auto-bidding with no manual CPC control, and reduced placement control unless you add exclusions.
Caveat: Applies to stores with clean feeds, proper conversion tracking and enough volume to satisfy smart bidding; otherwise the source recommends manual search and shopping first.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, google-ads, performance-max, campaign-structure, budget-allocation, retargeting, feeds
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Qualify Your Store for Performance Max Before Launching
Use when: Assessing whether a store is ready for Performance Max or should stay on manual search and manual shopping.
- Check the feed: is the Merchant Center product feed clean, complete and optimized? A poorly optimized feed disqualifies the store in the source's view.
- Check tracking: is there one primary purchase conversion action firing accurately (Google & YouTube app for Shopify or Google tag), with no competing primary actions?
- Check volume: can the store generate roughly 30–50 conversions per month, which the source gives as the minimum for smart bidding strategies to learn?
- Check budget: does the store have at least $50–$100 per day available; the source treats tiny budgets as a bad fit and recommends manual search and manual shopping instead.
- If any check fails, do not force Performance Max. Run manual shopping/search, fix the feed and tracking, then revisit.
- When you do launch, accept that Performance Max may only be able to generalize from your conversion data — weak data means weak automation.
Caveat: $50–$100/day and 30–50 conversions/month are source-specific readiness heuristics, not universal thresholds.
Caveat: Being 'on shopping' matters because a store with no shopping presence has no feed signal for Performance Max to work with.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, google-ads, performance-max, feeds, measurement, budget-allocation, qualification
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Set Up a Performance Max Campaign: Bidding, Locations, Devices, Exclusions
Use when: Building a new Performance Max campaign inside a Google Ads account.
- New campaign > Sales > optimize for Purchases > Performance Max, connect Merchant Center, name with a clear convention.
- Choose bidding: the source almost always uses Maximize Conversion Value with a target ROAS derived from the store's break-even ROAS, computed from COGS, gross margin and unit economics; the alternative is Maximize Conversions with a target CPA. Do not copy another brand's ROAS target — it is meaningless without their margin.
- Leave the 'customer acquisition' bidding option off (source preference). Instead pursue new customers through offer, ad congruence and audience signals, and measure new-customer ROAS/CPA in a third-party attribution tool such as Triple Whale or Northbeam.
- Set locations to the countries you sell in and the correct language; ignore EU political ads if outside the EU.
- Add UTM parameters in campaign URL options (or set them post-publish in your attribution tool) so multi-channel reporting is clean.
- Turn off tablets and TV screens (source: tablets never; TVs only for dedicated demand gen) and check device splits — mobile usually converts best; keep computers only if their metrics hold up.
- Add brand exclusions; the source notes this is not foolproof.
- Import customer lists, in-market audiences, custom-intent audiences based on high-intent keywords, competitor brand names and specific websites as audience signals.
- Verify current Google Ads interface and feature names before following these steps, as this setup changes frequently.
Caveat: Break-even ROAS/CPA is store-specific; there is no universal 'good' ROAS.
Caveat: Performance Max only offers automated bidding (Maximize Conversions or Maximize Conversion Value), so you cannot control max CPC.
Caveat: Brand exclusions in Performance Max are described by the source as incomplete protection; verify with brand queries in reporting.
Caveat: The source's aversion to the customer-acquisition bidding toggle is an opinion, not a tested rule.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, google-ads, performance-max, bidding-strategy, measurement, budget-allocation, audience-signals
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Structure Performance Max Around Signal Density, Not Campaign Count
Use when: Deciding how many Performance Max campaigns a store should run and how to split products and geographies.
- Split into separate Performance Max campaigns only where audiences and products are genuinely different (e.g. wallets vs luggage) — the source's rule of thumb is that if a shopper would search these separately, they belong in separate campaigns.
- Also split by country or region when advertising in multiple locations; never run two locations in one Performance Max campaign.
- Otherwise put everything into one campaign and use multiple asset groups inside it for collections or product types.
- Match each asset group's targeting, messaging and audience signals to that specific product segment.
- Avoid fragmenting signals across many campaigns and hoping Google optimizes at account level — the source states it does not.
- Continually review product performance and remove SKUs that burn budget without converting.
- Audit regularly for the failure pattern the source describes: 90–100% of budget concentrated in many Performance Max campaigns with misfired signals, and branded conversions costing $5–$10 per click.
Caveat: The 'one campaign per category/country' guidance is a heuristic from the presenter's agency experience, not a controlled benchmark.
Caveat: Asset-group-level reporting is limited compared to search and shopping, so mis-allocation can hide inside a campaign.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, google-ads, performance-max, campaign-structure, audience-signals, product-selection
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Select Products for Performance Max: Scalers, Zombie Asset Groups and 80/20
Use when: Building or pruning the product list inside a Performance Max campaign.
- Apply the Pareto principle: first find the 20% of products generating 80% of revenue, and even the 4% generating 96%; start Performance Max there.
- Pick the product that best leads on cold traffic as the primary scaler, i.e. the offer a brand-unaware buyer can be sold on.
- Regularly review performance and remove SKUs that consume budget without converting.
- For larger catalogs, create 'zombie asset groups' that group only underperforming products, so they can be tested without dragging down the main scaling campaign.
- Do not neglect dedicated product pages for those zombie products, and still optimize them — some products simply do not work on Google, and the goal is to keep them from hurting your scalers.
- Keep impressions and clicks concentrated on proven high-converting products because every impression and click in Performance Max is a budget decision.
Caveat: This is the source's strategy, not a tested attribution model; the 80/20 and 4/96 splits are illustrative distributions.
Caveat: Removing products from Performance Max does not mean they cannot sell elsewhere (email, organic, other channels).

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, google-ads, performance-max, product-selection, budget-allocation, feeds
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Handle Performance Max's Reporting, Placement and CPC Limitations
Use when: Auditing an existing Performance Max campaign for wasted spend or unreliable reporting.
- Use a third-party attribution tool (Triple Whale, Northbeam) as the source of truth because Performance Max can take credit for sales originating in other marketing channels.
- Where campaign-level granularity is missing, apply a third-party reporting script (the source names Mike Rhodes'/Microscript as the gold standard) to get placement, cost and conversion detail inside the campaign. Note that Google is rolling out some equivalent transparency, but the source says it is not yet close.
- Audit landing pages and placements Performance Max is serving to; if you see irrelevant placements, exclude them and turn off automations you never opted into.
- Exclude branded terms inside the Performance Max account so brand conversions are not counted as Performance Max results.
- When you cannot control CPC, decide whether the achieved CPC is sustainable at your cost-to-LTV ratio — the source argues that if the economics hold, CPC alone is not the metric to monitor.
- Judge launch success weekly: if CPCs remain outside what your margins can sustain even with correct setup, the source's conclusion is that this channel/strategy may simply not be viable for that product and competition level.
- Apply the same discipline to unit economics as for other platforms: the platform delivers conversions at a market CPA, and the question is whether your business can hold that CPA.
Caveat: Reduced control is inherent to Performance Max bidding; you cannot set a manual max CPC.
Caveat: Attribution overlap with other channels means platform-reported ROAS is usually optimistic.
Caveat: Script tools and third-party features change; verify the current interface before implementing.
Caveat: The 'if CPC is sustainable, don't worry about it' framing is the presenter's economics-based opinion; it still requires monitoring CPA against margin.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, google-ads, performance-max, measurement, attribution, placement-exclusions, budget-allocation
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Audience Signals and Conversion Data Are the Real Performance Max Inputs
Use when: Launching a Performance Max campaign from a cold start or improving an underperforming one by changing its inputs.
- Verify account-level conversion tracking is accurate before launch: exactly one primary purchase conversion action, tied to your campaign goal, firing via the Google & YouTube app or Google tag.
- Upload your customer list and, if allowed, in-market audiences that historically work.
- Build custom-intent audiences from high-intent keywords, competitor brand names, specific sites and trigger behaviours relevant to your category.
- Include the same audiences as signals even when running feed-only broad campaigns; Performance Max still needs an explicit definition of who your buyer is and is not.
- Use exclusions to define who not to reach (existing customers, irrelevant audiences) alongside positive signals.
- Expect Performance Max to find the right users eventually, but use strong signals to launch cold from scratch without a long ramp.
Caveat: The source still relies on third-party reporting for new-customer measurement rather than the account-level 'customer acquisition' bidding option, which he never enables.
Caveat: Signal quality depends on available data; a small store may not have enough customer list or conversion volume for full audience-building.

## Use Search Terms and Landing Page Audits to Fix Google Ads Waste
Use when: Running weekly/monthly maintenance on Google search, shopping or Performance Max campaigns.
- Pull the search terms report and sort by conversions and conversion value.
- Remove terms that receive clicks but no conversions, and promote converting broad terms to exact match so budget concentrates on proven queries.
- Check whether your best-converting queries are being served by a generic landing page; if so, build a page congruent with that query and change the keyword's final URL.
- In Performance Max, audit which landing pages placements are sending traffic to and exclude placements that would never convert.
- Remember that the campaign build is only half the job: for shopping campaigns, most ongoing optimization happens in Google Merchant Center, so keep the feed updated or you will see higher cost, lower visibility and reduced click share.
- Re-check audience exclusions (especially existing customers) so spend is reserved for net-new demand.
Caveat: Search-term data requires statistical significance; a few clicks with no conversions is not conclusive proof that a term should be killed.
Caveat: For search, keyword-level final URL changes interact with ad-level URLs; verify which URL the system is actually using in the current interface.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, google-ads, search-terms-report, negative-keywords, landing-page, feeds, measurement

## Performance Max campaign setup with category-specific asset groups
Use when: Launching or restructuring a Performance Max campaign for a store with multiple product categories (e.g. dresses, shoes, hats).
- Create an asset group per major product category rather than dumping all products into one asset group. Use listing group > 'selection of products' and filter by item ID to isolate that category's SKUs.
- Fill brand guidelines (business name, logo, colors, fonts) so ad assets stay visually congruent.
- Max out copy assets: 15 headlines, 5 long headlines, 5 descriptions — shortfall limits Google's combinations. (Agency uses an internal GPT to draft these; third-party tools may change, verify current availability.)
- Supply up to 20 images: product, lifestyle, in-use, high-production; horizontal, square and vertical aspect ratios. Rotate weak images out over time.
- Point the final URL to the matching collection page per asset group so searchers land on the exact category. If you use the brand homepage as final URL, Google can auto-route products — the source says test which approach works for your brand.
- Load search themes (up to 50): your highest-volume, highest-converting terms pulled from Keyword Planner, existing search/shopping campaigns and demand-gen data. Add audience signals: customer lists, website visitors, competitive keywords/sites.
- Set location to 'presence' only, select your language, and set brand exclusions as a first pass (source warns it is not foolproof; brand terms often need manual exclusion after launch).
- Set budget at least $50/day, ideally $100/day, of what you can sustain.
Caveat: Source says brand exclusions in settings are not a complete fix — expect to manually exclude branded search terms later.
Caveat: Source disables tablets and TV screens for PMAX; TV screens only for dedicated demand-gen campaigns.
Caveat: Source keeps only 'images' asset optimization on and disables text and final URL expansion to stop irrelevant landing-page text, sizing charts and support pages being pulled in.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, performance-max, asset-groups, feed-management, campaign-setup, product-category
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Daily PMAX search-term and auction-insight hygiene
Use when: Daily check on a running Performance Max campaign to protect budget and reallocate targeting.
- Open the PMAX campaign > Insights and reports. Review search terms that triggered the ad over the last 7 and 28 days.
- Flag and exclude irrelevant search terms directly inside PMAX to stop wasted spend. The source frames this as building a 'firewall' around the campaign.
- Watch for branded conversions appearing in PMAX search terms — brand is supposed to be excluded; if branded terms show up, exclude them immediately through the additional brand-exclusion process.
- Read cost per conversion and CTR by search term; treat rising costs or falling CTR as a signal that ad assets need refreshing.
- Harvest terms converting in PMAX but not covered by your search campaigns as candidates for dedicated search campaigns.
- Check auction insights (impression share on Search and Shopping, last 28 days) to see who you are competing against.
- Use audience insights to feed what is working back into demand-gen campaigns and to see which audiences respond to which assets.
Caveat: This is described as the source's only required daily PMAX task; everything else is weekly or monthly.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, performance-max, search-terms, brand-exclusions, measurement, optimization
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Weekly PMAX product-level spend and SKU exclusion
Use when: Weekly budget review for a Performance Max campaign with multiple products or categories.
- In the PMAX campaign, open the 'Products' view to see spend and performance at product level.
- Confirm budget flows to best sellers and highest-margin products rather than defaulting to whatever Google picks.
- Identify products that consume spend without converting, and products with weak CTR dragging the asset group down.
- Exclude poor performers: Campaigns > Asset groups > View listing groups > exclude the specific products.
- Keep excluded out-of-stock product pages out of PMAX until inventory returns — source lists removing out-of-stock URLs as part of exclusion hygiene.
- Re-include a SKU only when you have inventory and want to test it again.
Caveat: With a single-product brand the product-level view is trivial; the value appears when multiple products sit inside listing groups.

Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Weekly asset and landing-page exclusions in PMAX
Use when: Weekly creative and traffic-routing review inside a live Performance Max campaign.
- Campaigns > Asset groups > View asset details to see conversion data, clicks, CTR and conversion rate per headline, long headline, description and image.
- Replace assets that get little or no spend or weak conversion performance each week; Google prioritizes high-performing assets, so removing weak ones lifts overall results.
- If automatically created assets or final URL expansion is on, exclude irrelevant URLs: blog posts, about pages, sizing/fitness charts, shipping info, contact and customer-service pages, and other support pages that kill purchase momentum.
- Find which pages are currently being served: Report editor > 'when and where your ad shows' > PMAX campaigns placement; then add those unwanted URLs to exclusions.
- Also check the landing-page report: Report editor > Ads and assets > Landing pages, and list pages with high spend but low conversion rate as first candidates for exclusion or replacement.
- Use analytics to find high-bounce pages and add them to the exclusion list.
Caveat: Source treats asset optimization text and final URL expansion as risky because they pull irrelevant page text; keep only image/layout asset optimization on.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, performance-max, creative-testing, landing-page, exclusions, optimization
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Monthly PMAX search-theme and customer-list refresh
Use when: Monthly optimization cycle for PMAX audience and keyword signals.
- Pull top converting search terms from your search campaigns, shopping campaigns and PMAX itself.
- Open Campaigns > Asset groups > edit signals and replace search themes that are not converting with the proven converting terms.
- Confirm themes align with high-performing queries rather than legacy guesses.
- Export new customer emails and phone numbers from your CRM (Shopify, Klaviyo etc.) for the previous period.
- In Google Ads, go to Audience manager > your data segments > plus icon > Customer list > upload new list.
- Set a monthly reminder to repeat, or automate the upload, so Google can find users similar to your best customers and improve retargeting effectiveness.
Caveat: Customer-list targeting works from first-party data quality — stale or partial lists weaken the audience signal.

## Break-even CPA and ROAS as your scaling baseline
Use when: Deciding whether you can profitably increase Google Ads budget, bids or a new channel's spend.
- Calculate contribution per order before advertising: net order revenue minus COGS, payment fees, variable fulfillment, merchant-paid shipping and expected returns costs. Use consistent tax and refund treatment.
- First-order break-even CPA equals that pre-ad contribution per acquired order; do not subtract COGS twice. Break-even ROAS equals net revenue divided by pre-ad contribution. If $100 net revenue leaves $40 after these costs, CPA is $40 and ROAS is 2.5.
- Set these as non-negotiable baselines for every campaign, including PMAX.
- Recognize this is a CPM arbitrage: platforms charge what they charge for a customer on a given day; if your unit economics cannot sustain the cost per conversion, the fix is better margin, not a campaign setting.
- Track new-customer CPA and ROAS (source calls new-customer ROAS the single most important KPI) alongside conversion rate and marketing efficiency ratio (total revenue ÷ total marketing spend).
Caveat: Source explicitly refuses to give universal good/bad ROAS or CPA numbers — thresholds are entirely business-specific.
Caveat: Break-even ROAS is described as less decision-useful than break-even CPA; compute both but scale on CPA against your margin.
Caveat: Case-study figures elsewhere in the source (e.g. ~$45k spend at ~1.29x ROAS with $44.65 CPA) are that brand's results, not benchmarks.
Caveat: This is contribution break-even before fixed overhead and target profit. Deduct a profit or overhead allowance when setting the actual allowable CPA.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, unit-economics, break-even-cpa, roas, scaling, measurement, google-ads
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx
