## Weekly budget scaling rules with traffic-light KPIs
Use when: Weekly budget and bid decisions across Google Ads campaigns including PMAX.
- Assess KPIs weekly against your break-even CPA and break-even ROAS.
- If ROAS is consistently above break-even and/or CPA trends below break-even CPA, increase budget 10–20% (source says you can go faster but does not recommend it) or raise bids to capture more volume.
- Pause or rebuild anything below break-even — products, asset groups or individual assets.
- If consistently spending 100% of daily budget while hitting KPIs, raise budget by 10–15%. If spending under 80% of daily budget and underperforming, lower tROAS or tCPA to widen reach and generate volume.
- Cut fast, scale slow: pause losing campaigns quickly but also scale winners in controlled increments because Google reacts sensitively to abrupt changes.
- Let bidding changes run 2–4 weeks before evaluating; avoid frequent tweaks.
- Compare maximized conversions versus maximize conversion value with tROAS — conversion value prioritizes higher-value purchases and suits higher AOV products; source starts on maximize conversion value and moves to tROAS for PMAX, but says mileage varies.
- Monitor marketing efficiency ratio across all channels (Meta, TikTok, organic, Klaviyo, Google) because a profitable PMAX can still fail to add incremental lift or cannibalize other channels.
Caveat: 10–20% scale increments and 80%/100% budget-pacing thresholds are the source's heuristics, not derived calculations.
Caveat: Source advises against large budget jumps despite acknowledging faster scaling can work.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, scaling, budget-allocation, bidding, t-roas, measurement
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Device and placement rules for PMAX and demand gen
Use when: Setting device targeting for a Performance Max or demand-gen campaign.
- Turn off tablets for PMAX — the source never runs anything on tablets for any brand.
- Turn off TV screens for PMAX; enable TV screens only for dedicated demand-gen/YouTube campaigns where the TV viewership matters.
- Keep mobile phones on: source describes mobile as the highest-converting, highest-searching and highest-cost device.
- Break the campaign down by device to see how computers compare with mobile. Keep desktop only if its metrics are strong; otherwise turn it off.
- Consider that a large share of US YouTube views happen on TV screens, so excluding TV placements can forfeit a big chunk of reach — a reason to run TV on demand-gen rather than PMAX.
Caveat: Device cost/conversion relationships vary by brand; the source instructs checking your own desktop performance rather than assuming.

## Where YouTube and demand gen sit in the Google Ads funnel
Use when: Auditing an account's campaign mix or deciding where to add YouTube/demand-gen spend.
- Top of funnel: demand gen campaigns run on YouTube Shorts and YouTube in-stream; Google Display is optional and higher risk. These generate demand and educate unaware/problem-aware audiences.
- Middle of funnel: prospecting search, prospecting shopping and Performance Max — these capture demand and are capped by the available search volume and competitor CPC inflation. Do not mistake PMAX/search for top of funnel.
- Bottom of funnel: branded search, branded shopping, homepage/product page, add-to-cart and dynamic remarketing via Merchant Center or a dedicated remarketing campaign.
- Connect the layers: every drop-off point gets dynamic remarketing back to the relevant page; cart abandoners return to the product page.
- Sequence expansion: launch branded and search campaigns first, then add YouTube demand gen to generate additional search volume that your existing search/shopping campaigns capture.
- Treat YouTube as the accelerant that raises brand search volume and improves conversion rates on Meta and Google, not just a standalone channel.
Caveat: The funnel split is the source's framework; actual incremental lift from YouTube is asserted via third-party incrementality studies, not measured in the course itself.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, funnel-design, demand-gen, youtube-ads, performance-max, campaign-structure
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Why YouTube ads scale past search-volume ceilings
Use when: Evaluating whether to open a new acquisition channel because search/shopping volume or margin is maxed out.
- Recognize the ceiling: Google search/shopping can only serve people actively searching, so spend is capped by search volume and rising competitor CPCs reduce profitability.
- Target top-of-funnel viewers who have the problem but are not searching — educate them so they later search for your brand/product and hit your branded search and shopping campaigns.
- Reuse creative that already works on Meta by adapting it for YouTube in-stream and Shorts; this taps customers who do not buy from Facebook/Instagram without adding more Meta spend that might be unprofitable.
- Exploit CPM arbitrage: source claims YouTube CPMs/CPCs are far lower than Meta because fewer advertisers are sophisticated there — verify current rates in your own account rather than assuming.
- Factor in durability: source reports YouTube creative lasting up to a year or two versus Meta creative fatigue, so fewer new assets are needed once a winner is found.
- Value channel diversification both for stability (if one channel turns off) and for enterprise value at exit.
Caveat: The CPM-arbitrage and 'creative lasts a year' claims are the source's observations for their client base, not guarantees.
Caveat: YouTube is not a replacement for bottom-funnel brand control; it works with search/shopping to capture the generated demand.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, youtube-ads, demand-gen, acquisition, creative-strategy, channel-mix
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Choosing the right YouTube placement: Shorts, in-stream or in-feed
Use when: Allocating YouTube demand-gen budget across placements for an ecommerce brand.
- YouTube in-stream (skippable): the placement with the most scale and where the source spends thousands per day per client; best for proven winning creative.
- YouTube Shorts: cheap CPMs and very cheap clicks (source cites 1–2 cent clicks), lots of volume, quick creative testing. Shorts winners usually also win on in-stream after tweaking, so test there first.
- YouTube in-feed: higher production demand — requires a strong thumbnail competing against organic videos; only worth scaling once you have real creative quality or an organic channel.
- Do not run Discover, Gmail or the Display Network for ecommerce YouTube — the source restricts YouTube to in-stream and Shorts (Display optional only at top of funnel if you accept the risk).
- Note that in-feed suits longer, organic-style videos (the source cites buying competitors' products and reviewing them in an ~8-minute sponsored video with a CTA at the end); a 2-minute spot belongs in in-stream.
- Budget the higher-production in-feed efforts after Shorts and in-stream are producing winners.
Caveat: Click-cost and CPM figures are the source's observed ranges at the time of recording; verify current auction rates.
Caveat: In-feed is explicitly described as lower-leverage and harder to get right for most ecommerce brands.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, youtube-ads, placements, demand-gen, creative-testing
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## YouTube in-stream creative structure and first 5 seconds
Use when: Writing or editing YouTube in-stream ad creative for a cold ecommerce audience.
- Treat the first 5 seconds as fixed and non-skippable plus up to ~30 seconds before a view counts — the hook must be the strongest element you have and work both visually and in audio.
- Use a movie-trailer style hook: assume the viewer is about to skip, so the ad must be compelling enough to make them abandon the video they intended to watch.
- Structure after the hook: next ~5 seconds to introduce product or problem, then product demo showing use and effects, then social proof near the end, then a strong direct-response CTA.
- Aim the whole ad at a direct-response outcome — you need high-intent clicks, not passive viewing; source targets above 1% CTR on in-stream.
- Choose one of five creative types that work: high-production talking head, podcast-style two-person hook, founder ads (source calls founder ads a 'cheat code' and even suggests hiring someone to play the founder if dropshipping), story ads (customer- or founder-told) and straight product demos.
- Avoid cheesy AI-generated UGC style with bad captions — source says it no longer works well on YouTube; authenticity and craft matter more here than on Meta.
Caveat: Format timings (5s hook, ~30s to view) reflect the source's era of YouTube in-stream mechanics; verify current ad specs.
Caveat: The '1% CTR' target is the source's own working target, not a platform benchmark.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, youtube-ads, creative-strategy, in-stream, hook-writing, conversion-optimization
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## YouTube as brand-lift and TV-reach play
Use when: Justifying and measuring upper-funnel YouTube spend for a brand that mostly converts later through search.
- Account for TV reach: source claims over 50–60% of US YouTube views happen on TV screens, so mobile-only or desktop-only buying misses roughly half the audience.
- Operate with the expectation that TV viewers rarely convert immediately; they see the ad, search the brand later and convert through a view-through conversion.
- Track view-through conversions as a meaningful signal, not noise, especially for podcast/creator-led creative.
- Leverage perceived legitimacy: TV and YouTube placement is perceived as a higher barrier to entry, which the source says can lift conversion rates across Meta, Google search/shopping and retail (citing third-party incrementality studies).
- Use brand lift studies where available rather than judging YouTube purely on last-click ROAS in-dashboard.
Caveat: The TV-view share figure and incrementality effects are the source's cited claims, not measured in this course — validate with your own lift data.
Caveat: View-through conversions can overstate causal impact; pair with account-level incrementality checks.

## Composite approach: standard shopping alongside PMAX
Use when: Considering advanced Google Ads structures after a PMAX campaign has conversion data.
- Optionally run standard shopping at a low tROAS while PMAX works as a catch-all at a higher tROAS — source says this sometimes works and sometimes does not, so treat it as a test in your account.
- Use PMAX conversion data to decide new search campaigns: if terms convert in PMAX but are not covered by existing search campaigns, build dedicated search campaigns around them for more control over the funnel and experience.
- Note that PMAX consumes a lot of search spend; the Micros PPC script (Google Ads script) reveals this hidden spend and additional PMAX data for deeper optimization.
- For product-aware versus problem-aware keyword choices, start search campaigns on product-aware terms and use PMAX data to extend into other converting terms.
- For multi-location sellers, either run a dedicated Google Ads account per location or duplicate the PMAX campaign and change the location — horizontal scaling.
Caveat: Source explicitly says the standard-shopping + PMAX combination is not a universal play and is used selectively.
Caveat: Micros PPC is a third-party script; verify current availability and that it still works with the current Google Ads interface.

## Demand Gen Campaign Setup for YouTube Cold Traffic
Use when: Launching your first YouTube/Demand Gen cold-traffic campaign in Google Ads and you need the exact settings to configure.
- In Google Ads, click + > New campaign > Sales, and confirm the conversion goal is set to Purchases with a single primary conversion action.
- Choose campaign type Demand Gen; name it so it's identifiable among all your campaigns. Turn OFF the product feed (source states it is never worth running on for this use case).
- Bid strategy: Maximize Conversions with conversion goal = purchase. Do NOT set a target CPA yet.
- Budget: minimum $100/day to start.
- Location: the country you sell in (e.g. United States). Explicitly define language (e.g. English) so you don't get mis-targeted language traffic.
- Devices: turn tablets OFF always. If starting from Meta only, run mobile-only at first — most conversions come from mobile in-stream/Shorts. As you scale, turn on computers and TV screens and test horizontal (16:9) ads.
- Ad schedule: all day. No third-party measurement unless you're running Triple Whale (which handles this automatically).
- Ad group: 'Let me choose' placements, turn OFF everything except YouTube in-stream and YouTube Shorts (turn off in-feed, Discover, Gmail, Display).
- Audiences: run completely broad, no audiences — let the creative, copy and landing page do the targeting. (Source runs $8K/day broad and profitable.)
- Optimized targeting: turn ON when scaling; turn OFF when only testing creative/policy compliance at low budget.
- Final URL: never the homepage. Use a product page, VSSL, listicle, advertorial or quiz funnel.
- Ad copy: you get up to 5 headlines at 40 characters (vs 30 in search), plus 90-character long headlines and 90-character descriptions — use the full character count. CTA: 'Shop Now'. Always turn site links off (they look bad on YouTube).
- Then review and Publish.
Caveat: The source's own settings ($100/day minimum, tablets off, broad targeting) are recommendations from their account experience, not platform-mandated rules.
Caveat: Interface labels may change — verify the current Google Ads UI before instructing a team.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, youtube-ads, demand-gen, campaign-setup, google-ads, cold-traffic, ad-targeting
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Video Upload and Ad Group Structure for YouTube Ads
Use when: Setting up the video/creative layer of a YouTube demand gen campaign and deciding how to organize ad groups.
- Upload your ad videos unlisted to your YouTube channel, then copy the video URL.
- Paste the video URL into the ad's video box. You can add up to 5 videos per ad group.
- Use the 5-slot limit to test 5 different concepts in one ad group and see which wins.
- Once a winner emerges, segment it into its own ad group so you can hook-test on top of the winning control.
- Structure the campaign like a CBO: one campaign containing a 'winners' ad group (clearly performing ads) and a 'testing' ad group (new/untested ads).
- When a testing ad performs well in the dashboard or in Triple Whale, graduate it from testing into the winners ad group.
- Placement selection by length: if the ad is under ~60 seconds, you can speed it up, shift the pitch to keep audio natural, and run it on Shorts. If it's over 60 seconds, turn Shorts off and run in-stream only.
- Asset optimization: turn off the 'get shorter versions' and vertical/square auto-versions — run the creative as-is so Google doesn't cut off content.
Caveat: Source runs 16:9 winners on mobile in-stream and notes it looks fine, but recommends generating a 16:9 version of winners for better CPMs as you scale.
Caveat: Never run in-feed for this cold-traffic setup.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, youtube-ads, creative-testing, ad-groups, video-ads, demand-gen
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## The Six YouTube Ad KPIs and Their Ranges
Use when: Reviewing performance of a running YouTube/Demand Gen cold-traffic campaign and deciding whether to keep, pause or scale an ad.
- View rate (in-stream and Shorts): ~20% is really good for in-stream; ~10% is really good for Shorts. Anything above is a 'banger'.
- Creative watch-depth: enable columns for 25%/50%/75%/100% watched, segmented by in-stream vs Shorts, to see how much of each video people actually watch.
- CTR: above 1% is really good for in-stream (source typically sees 1.3–1.4%); 2% is 'cracked' and a massive scaler. For Shorts, 0.6%–1% is really good; closer to 1% is cracked. This measures strength of the CTA/click into your funnel.
- Conversion rate: look for ~0.05% and up for both Shorts and in-stream (Google dashboard). Below that (e.g. 0.02–0.03) means work is needed on the post-click experience / landing page.
- New customer CPA — the only metric that 'actually matters' in e-commerce. Track religiously in Triple Whale because Google's in-platform numbers mislead. Optimize and scale off campaign-level new customer CPA, not individual ads (ad sequencing means a converting ad may not be the one shown first).
- New customer ROAS: is it above breakeven for your unit economics? A low ROAS can still mean a good CPA depending on AOV.
- View-through conversions: people who watched 30+ seconds, didn't click, but later converted within the view-through window. Treat as a 'cherry on top' invisibility metric — 700 view-through conversions is effectively extra conversions baked into the campaign's total.
Caveat: Ranges are the source's rough estimates from their accounts, not universal benchmarks.
Caveat: New customer CPA, new customer ROAS and view-through benchmarks depend entirely on your own unit economics (COGS, shipping, LTV) and cannot be generalized.
Caveat: View-through conversions exclude people converted through another Google campaign and don't count all conversions — use overall new customer CPA as the primary decision metric.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, measurement, youtube-ads, kpi, conversion-tracking, new-customer-cpa, triple-whale
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Traffic Scaling Rules: When to Pause, Keep or Scale an Ad
Use when: Evaluating individual YouTube ad creatives to decide pause/continue/scale in a cold-traffic campaign.
- Poor metrics (poor view rate, poor CTR, no conversions, out-of-KPI new customer CPA): pause the ad immediately.
- Soft metrics (okay view rate, good CTR, some conversions, KPI-level new customer CPA): keep the ad running a bit longer while searching for a stronger creative.
- Strong metrics (great view rate, great CTR, new customer CPA at KPI): the source says you are 'morally obligated' to spend more money — increase the budget as fast as possible because the ad will break eventually anyway.
- Scale sequence: (1) simply increase budget while still on Maximize Conversions; (2) add more creatives, always trying to beat the control; (3) hook-test the winners (in-stream has a forced 5-second view, so hooks drive view rate); (4) create a 16:9 version of winners (duplicate in Premiere/Cut, blur background and run it) to lower CPMs; (5) test new offers and CTAs to lift CTR; (6) test new conversion mechanisms to lift conversion rate; (7) only at the end, expand into in-feed with a longer, properly produced long-form video/thumbnail.
- The source reports one winning ad had a Shorts CPM around $17 versus roughly $8 for its 16:9 horizontal version — this is an example, not a guaranteed result.
Caveat: Scaling rules assume you already know your breakeven new customer CPA and ROAS from your unit economics — the source explicitly says it can't give a KPI threshold for these.
Caveat: 'Morally obligated to scale' is the presenter's strong opinion, not a universal rule.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, scaling, creative-testing, youtube-ads, kpi, ad-optimization, cpp-benchmark
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Segment Branded vs Non-Branded Campaigns
Use when: Auditing or structuring a Google Ads account, especially for brands with existing organic or Meta-driven branded search demand.
- Exclude all branded terms from the main cold-traffic campaigns (e.g. Pmax and demand gen).
- Build branded search and branded shopping as separate, capped campaigns rather than mixing them with prospecting.
- Dig deep into how people find the store — what search terms they use — and feed that back into Google signals (custom audiences based on cold search terms, upload the customer list as an observation).
- For a Meta-heavy brand, check search impression share on brand campaigns; use absolute target impression share as the bidding strategy if running brand.
- If impression share is very low (the source cites cases around 14% or under 10% of page) despite cheap clicks, the brand campaign isn't achieving its goal (protecting the brand term, returning people to the funnel) — consider turning brand off entirely.
- Keep brand spend capped at roughly 1%–5% of total budget if you do run it, and never let it be the primary scaling lever.
Caveat: Source cites one brand where 95% of spend was on Meta with ~50% overlap before segmenting; after segmentation ~30% overlap remained and 87% of Google purchases came from previously unaware customers. This is a case result, not a promise.
Caveat: Cold traffic does not equal branded conversions — turning brand off entirely is the source's opinion for Meta-heavy direct-response brands.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, branded-search, google-ads, measurement, attribution, cold-traffic, account-structure
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Problem-Aware Creative vs Demographic Targeting on YouTube
Use when: Writing or briefing YouTube ad hooks and creative for a cold-traffic e-commerce product, especially a health/supplement/wellness offer.
- Write hooks around the situation/lifestyle problem the viewer is in, not the demographic. Example: for an arthritis product, don't call out 50-year-olds; talk about not being able to bend over or play with grandkids.
- Aim for a 'that's me' reaction — the viewer is in an entertainment or education state, so use edutainment creatives that name their problem.
- This also supports compliance because you are not linking to a specific condition or making a claim — you are describing lifestyle problems.
- First 5 seconds matter most on in-stream (in-stream forces a 5-second view) — a high-quality, problem-aware hook is what carries it.
- CTA should match your conversion mechanism: 'learn more' for an article/listicle/advertorial; a CTA to an offer-direct product page; a CTA to a VSSL; or a one-minute quiz ('find out which type is for you').
- Make creatives highly produced, look organic and intentional, and fit the feed — avoid lazy AI-generated (e.g. ElevenLabs-style) ads.
- Because YouTube inventory is massive (especially in the US), broad problem-aware creative can pull in a much wider audience than demo-targeted ads.
Caveat: Source's claim that YouTube audiences are more 'sophisticated' with a higher BS detector than Meta audiences is the presenter's opinion.
Caveat: Compliance claims are general guidance — always verify against current Google/YouTube ad policies for your category.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, creative-strategy, hooks, compliance, youtube-ads, problem-aware, copywriting
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Choose Conversion Mechanisms in Order of Proven Performance
Use when: Deciding where to send YouTube cold traffic and which landing page/conversion mechanism to test for a Direct-to-Consumer product.
- Start with a fully decked-out product/sales page — not just a buy button. Disguise the sales process but include bundle options and the option to buy.
- Next, run advertorials: information, value or story advertorials. The source prefers story advertorials because you can make the ad congruent ('I can't explain it here, click to learn more about my story').
- Then try quiz funnels — source says quizzes work well on YouTube because people like interacting; it acts like a personalized consultation and disguises the sales process.
- Use listicles cautiously — the source hasn't seen '5 reasons why' style lists perform as well; prefers dead sales pages and tutorial quizzes first.
- VSSLs (video sales letters): only run at scale once other mechanisms are saturated. The source hasn't seen VSSLs perform as well as other options because viewers already just watched a video and are off-platform.
- Match the ad CTA to the mechanism — the mechanism determines what the CTA says.
Caveat: This is the source's ordered preference based on their account experience, not a universal ranking — test mechanisms against each other for your own product.
Caveat: VSSL advice is explicitly contextual: it works when scaling massively and you need an additional mechanism to test.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, landing-page, conversion-optimization, advertorial, quiz-funnel, vssl, ecommerce
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Set Up a New-Customer Conversion Tag
Use when: Setting up conversion tracking for Google Ads on a store where you want to optimize for new customers rather than all purchasers.
- Install two tags: one traditional purchase tag, and one custom event (via the pixel or Shopify) that triggers only on a customer's first order.
- Set the first-order custom event as the primary conversion action; set the standard purchase as a secondary/observation action.
- Optimize campaigns around the new-customer event so Google bids toward genuine cold acquisition rather than repeat buyers.
- You can build this yourself or use a tool like Blotout; the source builds it in-house for clients.
- This matters because you want to be optimizing around new customers, not all purchasers, especially on cold-traffic Google campaigns.
Caveat: Verify current Shopify/pixel/webhook capabilities and Google Ads conversion-action settings before building — interfaces change.
Caveat: This is the source's recommended 2025 approach, not a platform requirement.

## Google Ads Budget Allocation: 80/20 for Meta-Heavy Brands
Use when: Deciding how to split Google Ads budget across campaign types for a brand whose acquisition is predominantly creative-led cold traffic.
- Focus ~80% of Google budget on demand gen (YouTube in-stream + Shorts on mobile initially), because you already have creatives and funnels and can transfer them over.
- Allocate ~10–15% to search/shopping (prospecting), but only if the product has genuine category search demand.
- Cap brand campaigns at ~1%–5% of budget (or turn them off entirely for Meta-heavy brands).
- Skip shopping/Merchant Center entirely if the brand is gray-hat or high-AOV creative-led and likely to get banned — don't waste effort there.
- Skip search entirely if your product has low search volume (e.g. a niche supplement) — you have too little volume to justify spend.
- Do not use the stock agency setup (branded search, shopping/Pmax, dynamic search ads) that's copy-pasted for every brand — it doesn't account for where your traffic actually comes from.
- Start on mobile until you hit ~$1K/day spend, then expand winning creatives into 16:9 and add desktop/TV placements.
Caveat: The 80/20 split and the 1%/10-15% caps are the source's recommendations, not platform rules — the 80/20 principle itself is presented as a general heuristic.
Caveat: As you scale, the source shifts search share up to ~20-30% for large categories with true demand.

## Demand Gen as the Cold-Traffic Engine for Meta-Heavy Brands
Use when: Choosing Google campaign type for a cold-traffic e-commerce acquisition push.
- Identify where most of your traffic comes from — if you're predominantly Meta/cold-traffic direct response, that determines your channel choice.
- Use Demand Gen (YouTube in-stream + Shorts) as the primary top-of-funnel acquisition campaign because you already have creative assets and funnels that transfer over.
- Run search and shopping only when the product has inherent search demand (e.g. blood flow/pressure supplements, blue/category-specific products) or a popular branded supplement.
- Avoid dynamic search ads unless you have a mass content farm with multiple product categories — the source cites a skincare one-pager with a Funnelish-based funnel that had no business running DSA.
- Do not run traffic straight to a bare product page if customers need education — use advertorials, sales arguments, listicles or pre-sale pages first; product-page-direct only works for product-aware searches or when you have a live Merchant Center.
- Structure the campaign so the creative + conversion mechanism carry the targeting, not detailed audience segmentation.
Caveat: The source's claim that 'the creative plus mechanism is 80% of the outcome, not bidding or campaign type' is their opinion.
Caveat: Search/shopping viability genuinely depends on category search volume — don't force it for low-volume products.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, campaign-strategy, demand-gen, google-ads, cold-traffic, search-ads, shopping-ads
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## PMAX for a Single Hero Product
Use when: Structuring Google Ads for a store built around one hero product/SKU.
- If you have one hero winning product with one good funnel, you can run a single Pmax campaign across Search, Display and Shopping instead of splitting into multiple campaigns.
- Never dump all products into one asset group/campaign just to scale if you have multiple products — instead consider separate bestseller and testing PMAX campaigns.
- For multiple products, test the feed with a testing PMAX (e.g. feed-only on test products) and check COGS per product to confirm each is profitable independently.
- Feed Google the right signals: upload the customer list as an observation, build custom audiences from cold search terms, exclude all branded terms from the main PMAX.
- One clean campaign with high signal density is better than many split campaigns where Google doesn't know which channel to convert on.
- Keep the setup clean — the source says 90% of the game is clean setup, exclusions and feeding Google the right data.
- At sufficient spend you may get a Google rep; use that plus a tool like Microscript to dig into PMAX effectiveness (source notes PMAX is 'not the black box it used to be').
Caveat: Case study results (e.g. $486K revenue on $149K spend, 1.71 new-customer ROAS on PMAX, $27.66 new customer CPA) are the source's examples, not promises.
Caveat: Verify current PMAX controls and rep availability — they change over time.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, google-ads, pmax, campaign-structure, hero-product, cold-traffic, feed-optimization
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Compliance and Landing Page Prep Before Running YouTube Ads
Use when: Preparing a health/supplement/wellness (or otherwise restricted-category) store to launch YouTube/Google ads.
- Audit all ads, product pages and site pages for policy compliance before spending — non-compliant pages will get ads disapproved or the Merchant Center suspended.
- Make the site mobile-optimized — the source says CRO is non-negotiable and focuses 80% of traffic on YouTube mobile, so build and optimize for mobile-first.
- YouTube traffic won't tolerate weak sites or scammy offers — invest in a trustworthy, high-effort, properly branded site and sales page, even if your brand isn't truly premium.
- Write problem-aware copy instead of linking to a specific condition or claim, which keeps you compliant and broad.
- If you can't get Merchant Center done right (proper policies, brand experience, one-of-a-kind brand), skip GMC/shopping entirely and focus on YouTube instead of fighting bans.
- Disguise the sales process with education — advertorials, listicles, pre-sale pages — rather than a bare buy-button page.
Caveat: Compliance requirements vary by product category and change over time — always check current Google/YouTube/Merchant Center policies.
Caveat: Source's guidance is framed around banned/restricted supplement brands; not every brand needs the same caution.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, compliance, youtube-ads, merchant-center, cro, landing-page, health-supplements

## Retain YouTube Cold Traffic With Email Capture and Flows
Use when: Planning the retention and LTV layer behind a cold-traffic YouTube campaign to make acquisition economics work.
- Add an email popup to the landing page to capture cold visitors who don't buy immediately. Source reports a 14.7% popup conversion rate (36K unique YouTube visitors → 5.3K signups in 7 days).
- Have the popup feed a welcome flow — source uses a five-email deep welcome flow that leads with a strong offer (they cite 11% discount) and drives the cold-traffic conversion.
- For customers who purchase, run a post-purchase flow (thank-you + free post-purchase emails) with a replenishment/stock-up trigger — source used a 25-day wait before the replenishment email.
- Because the source tracks new customer CPA as the primary metric, they say they can keep scaling while first-order profitable and rely on LTV to fix the ratio: increasing LTV is one lever if CPA can't be lowered.
- Set up the retention layer as part of the acquisition plan from the start so acquired customers can be contacted for repeat purchase.
Caveat: The 14.7% popup rate and 5.3K signups are case-study numbers from one brand, not benchmarks.
Caveat: Retention flow specifics depend on your product's repurchase cycle; the 25-day window matched that brand's 30-day purchase cadence.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, retention, email-marketing, ltv, youtube-ads, conversion-optimization, replenishment

## Post-Click Landing Page Structure for YouTube Cold Traffic
Use when: Designing or auditing the landing page that YouTube cold traffic is sent to and trying to lift conversion rate beyond ~0.05%.
- Lead with a strong above-the-fold section: benefit bullets, high-quality visuals and multiple paths to buy or get educated, not just a buy button.
- Stack supporting sections in order: benefits, product details, lab results/proof, FAQs, banners, simple steps, differentiation, social proof, timelines/journeys, research and studies, community videos, founder story, a large guarantee, comparison table, more FAQs, customer reviews, additional offers/products, and a closing offer.
- Use the full page as a disguise for the sales process — give people a reason to buy and to educate themselves beyond the ad.
- The source's case study page converted at 2% on YouTube cold traffic (example, not a benchmark) and drove the email popup capture described above.
- If your conversion rate is around 0.02–0.03%, the source attributes this to work needed on the post-click experience / landing page.
Caveat: 2% on cold traffic is the source's case-study figure, not a guaranteed conversion rate.
Caveat: Copying the exact section order without testing is not recommended — the source emphasizes iterating the creative and page around the audience.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, landing-page, cro, conversion-optimization, product-page, social-proof, ecommerce
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Consolidate Performance Max for high signal density
Use when: Setting up or restructuring Google Ads account structure for a store's cold acquisition, deciding whether to split one PMax campaign into many.
- Put the core cold acquisition budget into a single PMax campaign rather than spreading it across multiple campaigns and channels; the source argues this keeps signal density high so Google learns how to convert on the channel.
- Use asset group exclusions and brand/non-brand segmentation within that structure instead of separate campaigns per channel.
- Feed clean data: verify conversion tracking fires correctly on the purchase event and on any qualifying lead events you actually want optimized.
- Push hardest on the product feed — product titles, images, descriptions — because the source calls feed optimization '90% of the game' for PMax performance.
- If you have access to a Google rep (typically tied to spend level), use them for account support, and use a third-party PMax insight tool (the source names Microscript; verify current availability) to inspect asset-group and search-term level performance.
- Exclude brand terms from cold campaigns so cold and returning demand can be judged separately.
Caveat: PMax transparency has improved but is still not fully granular; results depend on spend level and feed quality.
Caveat: The source's claim that a single consolidated campaign is always better reflects their own experience, not a universal rule — test against a segmented structure if you have data.

## Rebuild the PDP as a direct-response cold-traffic page
Use when: A store is scaling into new audiences and its current PDP converts returning customers but stalls cold traffic.
- Audit the current PDP: if it is just product images plus a couple of FAQs, treat it as an educational page optimized for people who already know you.
- Restructure the page into a persuasive flow that segments the cold visitor: what the product is, why it is different, why it is credible, why buy now.
- Add explicit education for the unfamiliar visitor — if they need to understand the category (e.g. 'what is this ingredient'), the page must teach before it sells.
- Insert objection handling answering the top reasons a cold visitor would hesitate to buy from you instead of a competitor.
- Layer in trust builders and proof: founder story, third-party test results, reviews, relevant certifications.
- Add comparison content against competitor alternatives so a shopper who is researching has the comparison done for them.
- Close with a subscriber-first offer to capture the next purchase, not just this one.
- Judge the change on cold-traffic conversion rate specifically, not blended site conversion.
Caveat: The source reports conversion rate on cold traffic roughly doubling overnight for one methylene blue brand — a case result, not a benchmark.
Caveat: Loyal customers convert on almost any page, so blended conversion rate masks whether the rewrite worked for cold traffic.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, product-page, conversion-optimization, cold-traffic, offer-design, objection-handling, social-proof
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Build the full cold-traffic conversion mechanism, not just ads
Use when: Planning a cold acquisition push and deciding which assets must be built or fixed before raising spend.
- Define the chain end to end: YouTube/Google creative → pre-sale page → product page → checkout/order → post-purchase upsell/after-sell.
- Write the ad creative and the landing page together so the promise made in the ad is answered immediately on the page.
- Use the pre-sale page to educate and sell the idea of the brand before the PDP, particularly when the market is unsophisticated about the product.
- Put an after-sell or upsell step after order to lift AOV and pull blended CAC down.
- Assess how sophisticated the market is before writing anything: a market that already understands the product needs differentiation, not basic education; a market that doesn't needs education first.
- Keep the whole system in-house or tightly coordinated, since disjointed vendors obscure which step is leaking.
Caveat: The source is an agency describing its own full-funnel build; the same structure is achievable with in-house or mixed teams if the steps are owned by one accountable plan.
Caveat: Pre-sale pages must comply with the ad platform's landing-page policies for regulated categories.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, funnel-design, landing-page, product-page, aov, acquisition, creative-strategy
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Design an objection-handling block sequence on the PDP
Use when: Merchandising a PDP for a supplement, wellness or other considered-purchase product where cold visitors need convincing.
- Open with a clear statement of what the product is and the outcome it delivers, in plain language for someone who has never heard of the brand.
- Follow with objection handling: price, skepticism about efficacy, safety concerns, subscription/commitment fears, 'why not the cheaper competitor'.
- Add proof elements next — test results, third-party validation, review volume — placed where the skeptic is most likely to be reading.
- Add a comparison section positioning the product against named or implied alternatives, since competitors will enter the market once a category gets attention.
- Add FAQs that answer the questions support actually receives, not generic filler.
- End with a strong subscriber-first offer (subscribe and save, first-order bundle) to capture repeat revenue from the first purchase.
- Keep founder/credibility content visible — the source credits a strong founder image as part of why the brand held up against new entrants.
Caveat: Requires real proof assets; inventing test results or reviews is both non-compliant and destructive.
Caveat: Order matters less than completeness for some audiences — test section order rather than assuming one fixed sequence.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, product-page, conversion-optimization, objection-handling, social-proof, subscriptions, positioning
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Monitor the ad account daily to catch demand spikes
Use when: Running Google Ads for a category that can be featured in podcasts, news or social media and may spike suddenly.
- Log into the ad account daily, not weekly; the source's example spike was visible only to someone checking that morning.
- Watch for the platform spending above the usual daily budget, which can signal rising available traffic (Google may overspend within the 30-day average).
- Check external sources when spend jumps: the source traced a spike to a podcast episode that had run two hours earlier.
- If the spike is genuine demand for your product, raise the budget aggressively rather than incrementally — in the source's case from roughly $2K to $20K per day for the spike window.
- Track search impression share during the spike to see how much of the demand you are capturing (they reported roughly 70% at peak).
- Hold the higher budget after the spike if performance supports it, rather than reverting automatically.
Caveat: Aggressive budget raises assume your break-even CPA and conversion mechanism can absorb the volume without breaking profitability.
Caveat: Competitor non-response is not guaranteed; in a well-funded category rivals may also raise budgets.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, google-ads, budget-management, trend-response, measurement, impression-share, acquisition
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Run 30/60/90/180/365-day contribution math before deciding how much to pay per customer
Use when: Setting target CPA, deciding whether to accept near break-even or loss-making first orders to win market share in a repeat-purchase category.
- Calculate contribution margin per order: price minus COGS minus shipping minus payment fees minus any variable fulfillment cost.
- Build cohort windows at 30, 60, 90, 180 and 365 days and compute cumulative contribution per customer across each window, including repeat purchases, subscription revenue and upsells.
- Define break-even CPA as the point where cumulative contribution equals acquisition cost over your chosen window.
- If acquisition cost stays at or below break-even across the window, you can scale spend aggressively; if it exceeds it, the customer is not worth enough yet.
- Treat the customer's worth as something you can increase: raise AOV, add upsells, improve repurchase and subscription rates rather than only cutting acquisition cost.
- Recheck the model after any pricing, COGS or AOV change before using it to justify a bigger budget.
Caveat: Long-window models assume retention and repurchase rates hold; new competitors or product changes can break that assumption.
Caveat: The source's 'never went below break even' outcome is a case result for one brand, not a guarantee for your category.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, unit-economics, contribution-margin, break-even-cpa, ltv, pricing, retention
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Position 'RoRoaWAS' correctly: low is the goal
Use when: Reviewing ad reporting and reacting to a metric that looks counterintuitively weak or strong.
- Clarify which metric your account and tools are actually showing before acting on it — the source uses a ratio framed around payback window rather than the more common 'higher is better' ROAS.
- Under this framing, a low value means you are getting your money back quickly; the source explicitly says you want low values.
- Do not cut a campaign just because this metric looks low; check whether it reflects fast payback instead.
- Pair the metric with the long-window contribution math so you know the true ceiling on what you can pay per customer.
- Confirm the definition in your own reporting stack — terms like RoRoaWAS are not standardized and depend on how the window is defined.
Caveat: This is the source's own metric framing, borrowed from ecommerce ad reporting conventions; definitions vary, so verify what your tool means by it before applying the rule.
Caveat: A metric alone should not override contribution-margin math.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, measurement, roas, payback-window, unit-economics, reporting
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Use YouTube as the scaling lever once search and shopping plateau
Use when: Google search, shopping and display spend has hit a ceiling and the store needs new cold audience volume.
- Confirm search and shopping are tapped out — the source reported roughly $2–4K/day max on high-search-volume days before adding YouTube.
- Build a YouTube campaign structure that feeds the same conversion mechanism (pre-sale page and PDP) already proven on search.
- Start with a small set of compliant creatives, then let spend concentrate on whichever one clears policy and performs; the source describes a single creative carrying $300–500/day early.
- Expect YouTube to tolerate more frequency than search because inventory is far larger, easing creative fatigue relative to other channels.
- Track new-customer acquisition separately from retargeting so you can attribute YouTube's incremental contribution.
- Set the scaling target in new customers per month rather than only in spend.
Caveat: The source's figures ($6.5K/day target, 10K+ new customers/month aim) are their own goals for one brand, not benchmarks.
Caveat: A second brand mentioned had a break-even around 1.2–1.3 by their framing; break-even levels are store-specific.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, youtube-ads, google-ads, scaling, cold-traffic, creative-fatigue, acquisition
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Plan for creative volume to beat ad platform compliance filters
Use when: Running health, wellness or supplement ads on Google where policy review rejects most creative angles that work on Meta.
- Assume most creative that works on Meta will not clear Google policy in regulated categories — the source reports only one of a batch of Meta ads ran on Google.
- Write and produce compliant first: remove prohibited claims, avoid medical claims, and keep language within the platform's health-category rules before you test.
- Produce volume, not one polished ad; the goal is enough variants to survive review filtering and still leave a testable set.
- Once creative clears policy, test aggressively for conversion and scale potential, concentrating spend on winners.
- When creative is the bottleneck, add production capacity rather than cutting spend — the source says their bottleneck shifted from backend to creative once search, shopping and display were solved.
- Re-verify current platform policy rules before each production cycle, since health ad policies change.
Caveat: Compliance constraints are category and platform specific; some products (the source names methylene blue) are not allowable on most platforms at all.
Caveat: Do not infer that compliant creative is less effective — the source's goal is to clear policy and still convert.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, creative-strategy, compliance, google-ads, youtube-ads, health-supplements, testing
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Set the LTV engine: front-end acquisition campaigns feeding email/SMS and upsells
Use when: Designing the relationship between acquisition campaigns and retention channels to justify higher cold-traffic spend.
- Separate the roles: search, shopping and display campaigns deliver first-touch points; email, SMS and post-purchase upsell flows produce repeat revenue.
- Make sure every acquired customer is retargetable — capture email/SMS consent at purchase or via a subscriber-first offer.
- Build post-purchase upsell and cross-sell flows so the first order is not the only revenue event.
- Use the retention revenue in your contribution math to set how much you can pay for a first order.
- Treat the quality of the backend as the scaling moat: if the customer is not worth enough, improve AOV, repeat purchase and subscription rather than only squeezing CPA.
- Consult or plan product drops so there is something new to sell existing customers when acquisition volume rises.
Caveat: High acquisition volume stresses fulfillment — the source flags that fulfillment will break if you push too many purchases before operations are ready.
Caveat: Retention economics depend on a genuinely repeat-consumable product; one-time-purchase categories cannot support this model the same way.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, retention, email-marketing, sms, upsell, ltv, acquisition, fulfillment
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Differentiate a PDP when competitors enter a validated category
Use when: A store's product category is being talked about publicly and new competitors are launching similar products.
- Anticipate new entrants as soon as your product starts working — the source predicted competitors entering their category well before they did.
- Audit competitor product pages: the source found competitor pages had no education, no founder story, no differentiation and no brand feel.
- Rework the funnel so evidence, clarity and differentiation appear at every step: ad, pre-sale page, PDP and post-purchase.
- Dimensionalize the brand — tell the founder story and make the brand feel like a brand, not a white-label listing.
- Maintain the positioning rather than relying on being first; first-mover status degrades once the category becomes known.
- Keep the conversion mechanism strong enough that attention spikes convert to first orders you own, not to the category generally.
Caveat: Some competitor pages may still convert on price alone; differentiation must be paired with a competitive offer.
Caveat: The source's specific category example (methylene blue and public figures discussing it) is illustrative, not applicable to every product.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, positioning, differentiation, product-page, founder-story, competition, conversion-optimization
Source: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

## Start Google Ads with Search and Shopping, add Performance Max later
Use when: Deciding which Google Ads campaign types to launch first for a store, or judging whether the account is ready for Performance Max.
- Launch with Search (text ads) and Shopping (product carousel showing image, price point and click-through) because they are the most intuitive and easiest to understand, and they map to how people already think about Google ads: someone searches, relevant ads appear.
- Hold off on Performance Max, Demand Gen and Display at the start; Performance Max draws on search, shopping, YouTube, Display, Discover and Gmail placements and relies heavily on Google's automatic targeting, bidding and placement, so it needs a lot of conversion data to work.
- Treat roughly 100 purchases in the ad account as the point where adding a Performance Max campaign can work well (the source says 'more than say 100 purchases, ideally as many as possible'); this is a practitioner heuristic, not a hard rule.
- Use the early Search/Shopping period to learn the platform and build conversion history before handing more control to automation.
- If you already run Performance Max and results are murky, consider whether conversion volume is the issue before blaming the campaign type.
- Verify current campaign-type names and setup screens in the Google Ads interface, since formats and options change.
Caveat: The 100-purchase threshold is the presenter's rule of thumb for their own agency, not a published Google benchmark.
Caveat: Performance Max can be added 'later on' as an addition rather than a replacement; the source does not say to abandon Search or Shopping.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, google-ads, campaign-setup, performance-max, shopping-ads, search-ads, conversion-data
Source: Google Ads For Ecommerce_ 9 Keys To Success.docx

## Concentrate cold-traffic spend on one or a few winning products
Use when: Structuring Google Ads campaigns and budget allocation across a multi-SKU catalog, especially when prospecting to cold audiences.
- Audit the account for cost per purchase and ROAS by product; identify the one product or handful of products that acquire customers far more efficiently than the rest.
- Divert budget away from the long tail of SKUs and into those winners rather than running broad campaigns across the full catalog — the source describes this as one of the fastest early wins when taking over an ecommerce account.
- In hobby or enthusiast niches, expect the beginner/entry-level version of the product to be the cold-traffic hero, with advanced products sold later once the customer is invested.
- Accept that in most ecommerce categories (the source cites apparel as an example) there is nearly always one item or product range that dominates cold-audience acquisition.
- Segregate cold and warm strategy: keep cold traffic tightly focused, and reverse the logic for warm audiences.
- Be prepared to re-engineer supply chain if one product suddenly sells far more than before — the source flags this as a real consequence ecommerce owners should anticipate.
Caveat: The source is explicit that this focus applies to cold audiences only; remarketing can and should open up the full range.
Caveat: Selling mostly one hero product may complicate eventually selling the business, though the source says that is not impossible at scale.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, google-ads, budget-allocation, cold-traffic, product-selection, roas, sku-focus
Source: Google Ads For Ecommerce_ 9 Keys To Success.docx

---

## Open up the full catalog only for warm and remarketing audiences
Use when: Building Google Ads remarketing and dynamic product ad campaigns for site visitors and past customers, or deciding which SKUs to show which audience.
- For warm audiences — especially previous purchasers and recent site visitors — do not apply the cold-traffic 'focus on one hero' rule; instead broaden the product set.
- Run dynamic product ads using a product catalog so that someone who viewed or added a specific item to cart sees that item, rather than the storewide bestseller that may not match their intent.
- Let Google use signals such as prior product views, add-to-cart events and past similar purchases to tailor which product is served to each user.
- Use remarketing, email and SMS together to sell the rest of the range to people already in the ecosystem, since acquisition cost on these audiences is far lower.
- Keep cold prospecting concentrated so the algorithm receives clean conversion signals, then spend the warm budget on breadth and repeat purchase.
Caveat: The source presents this as their standard practice, not a universal law; catalog ad availability and feed requirements should be verified in the current Google Ads interface.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, google-ads, remarketing, dynamic-product-ads, warm-audience, retention, product-catalog
Source: Google Ads For Ecommerce_ 9 Keys To Success.docx

## Know AOV, margin and LTV before setting an allowable CAC
Use when: Setting target CPA/ROAS for Google Ads, deciding whether a campaign can be profitable, or diagnosing why acquisition costs feel unaffordable.
- Establish average order value first; the source says an AOV over $100 makes profitable advertising much easier, and if you are below that, get as close to $100 as possible.
- If your AOV sits around $40, look for structural ways to lift it — bundling multiple items, buy-one-for-you buy-one-as-a-gift offers, or adding complementary products — rather than accepting the ceiling.
- Calculate gross profit margin on the order, not just the sale price: an AOV of $120 at a 10% gross margin yields only about $12 of gross profit per order, which is easily exceeded by acquisition cost.
- Identify which individual products carry better margins and direct more advertising budget toward them.
- Estimate customer lifetime value (total spend over the customer relationship) and use it to set the maximum allowable cost per purchase.
Caveat: The '$100 AOV' and '10% margin' figures are illustrative examples from the presenter, not benchmarks for any specific category.
Caveat: Margin and LTV figures must come from your own P&L and cohort data; the source gives no method for calculating LTV.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, unit-economics, aov, gross-margin, ltv, cac, google-ads
Source: Google Ads For Ecommerce_ 9 Keys To Success.docx

---

## Raise allowable acquisition cost by improving LTV rather than shaving CPA
Use when: Setting CPC/CPA ceilings, deciding whether to run ads at a temporarily unprofitable ROAS, or prioritising between conversion-rate tweaks and retention improvements.
- Model the arithmetic: if first-purchase value is $100 and average lifetime value rises to $400, the maximum acceptable cost per purchase can rise from roughly $30 to roughly $120 — a 4x increase in affordable acquisition cost (the source's own worked example).
- Prioritise LTV levers — repeat purchases, subscriptions, consumable ecosystems, post-purchase email and SMS — over chasing a 15–20% reduction in cost per purchase, which the source describes as the focus of many businesses but not of the biggest, most successful companies.
- Consider the Starbucks illustration the source gives: a roughly $5.65 average order value alongside a very large lifetime value means the business can justify spending far more than a few dollars to acquire one customer; the source explicitly says not every business will match that, but the logic still applies.
- Accept a lower ROAS when LTV justifies it: the source describes scaling even at a 1.5 ROAS after doubling LTV, or going down to around 1.2, because the LTV work has made those numbers affordable.
- Recognise that scale compounds — more customers means a larger remarketing pool, email list and SMS list, and more participants for seasonal promotions like Black Friday or Christmas.
Caveat: All numeric examples (four to five times LTV, $30 to $120 CPA, 1.5 and 1.2 ROAS) are the presenter's illustrative figures, not benchmarks.
Caveat: Deliberately advertising at a loss depends on reliable LTV measurement and cash flow to fund the payback period; the source warns that the free-gift style of aggressive front-end spend must be done intelligently with cash flow in mind.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, ltv, cac, roas, retention, subscriptions, scaling
Source: Google Ads For Ecommerce_ 9 Keys To Success.docx

---

## Use a free-plus-shipping or generous front-end offer to acquire at scale
Use when: Designing a new-customer acquisition offer or entry-point product for cold Google Ads traffic.
- Choose a giveaway product that creates demand for your paid range rather than satisfying the need outright — the source's example is a free football to a family whose child is starting to play: the ball arrives, and boots, apparel and garden goals follow naturally.
- Charge only the cost of shipping/postage so the offer is genuinely low-risk for the buyer while still covering fulfilment costs.
- Check that the giveaway suits a market-entry moment — the source frames it as best for introducing people to a new type of product or a new category they haven't bought before.
- Model cash flow carefully: front-loading cost of goods and shipping ahead of repeat revenue only works if the business can fund the gap and the entry product genuinely leads to follow-on purchases.
- Expect the goodwill and the customer relationship to produce the return later, through the same ecosystem you would use for remarketing, email and SMS.
Caveat: The source insists this must be done intelligently and with attention to cash flow; it is not a blanket recommendation.
Caveat: It only works where the free item predictably leads to additional purchases — a giveaway that closes the need will not pay back.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, offer-design, acquisition, reciprocity, front-end-offer, cash-flow, google-ads
Source: Google Ads For Ecommerce_ 9 Keys To Success.docx

## Discount tactically instead of defaulting to blanket sales
Use when: Planning seasonal promotions, Google Ads offer messaging, or a discount-led acquisition campaign.
- Analyse which products carry high enough margin to be discounted without destroying gross profit, and discount those rather than the whole catalog.
- Consider giving an inexpensive free item with the purchase of a high-margin product instead of cutting the price of the main item.
- Gate discounts behind an AOV threshold — for example 'spend over X and get 20% off' — mirroring the free-shipping threshold mechanic that exists to raise AOV.
- If you position as premium or luxury, avoid straight discounts altogether; the source compares it to a fine-dining restaurant, where you would not expect a discount on the menu but would expect free extras such as wine advice or valet parking. Offer complimentary add-ons instead.
- If your entire business model is being the cheapest or bulk provider, the source says to lean into that as your competitive advantage and discount accordingly.
- Recognise that discounting volume without gross profit is not a win, even if units move.
Caveat: The source is a fan of running sales and discounts and is not arguing against them — only against doing them without margin analysis.
Caveat: The threshold mechanic is presented as a general AOV technique; the specific percentage and threshold must be set from your own economics.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, pricing, discount-strategy, aov, bundles, margin-protection, promotions
Source: Google Ads For Ecommerce_ 9 Keys To Success.docx

## Mine customer reviews to write ad copy and find product fixes
Use when: Writing Google Ads copy and creative for an ecommerce product, or looking for product/fulfilment improvements.
- Read reviews closely and identify repeated themes in five-star feedback — the source notes that owners often assume they know why people buy, but reviews frequently surface benefits they never considered important.
- Amplify the recurring five-star themes directly in ad copy and creative, since ecommerce generates far more reviews than service businesses and the sample is large.
- Use negative reviews as product feedback: the source's example is recurring packaging complaints, which can be fixed outside of marketing.
- If you have no reviews yet, read competitor reviews: mirror what buyers praise about comparable products, and highlight any competitor weakness your product solves — for example a long installation time or slow delivery that you can guarantee against (the source uses a 24- or 48-hour guarantee as an illustration).
- Make sure any claim you pull from reviews is true and verifiable for your own product before putting it in an ad.
Caveat: The 24/48-hour delivery guarantee is the presenter's illustrative example of a competitive claim, not a promised result.
Caveat: Review mining tells you what buyers say, not why non-buyers don't convert; pair it with other research.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, customer-research, reviews, ad-copy, creative-strategy, product-improvement, positioning
Source: Google Ads For Ecommerce_ 9 Keys To Success.docx

## Fix the campaign before increasing budget — ROAS falls as spend rises
Use when: Deciding whether to raise Google Ads budget on an underperforming campaign, or planning a scaling sequence for a store.
- If a campaign isn't profitable at the current budget, treat the problem as campaign quality — offer, ad copy, creative and targeting — not under-spending; the source states plainly that raising budget in this situation nearly always makes ROAS worse.
- Accept the structure of the auction: at low spend Google reaches the keenest prospects; as spend rises it extends to progressively less interested audiences who need more convincing, so ROAS declines to some degree.
- Get the campaign comfortably profitable at the current spend before scaling, then scale with the expectation that ROAS will fall — the source says the drop can be minor rather than dramatic, but it will happen.
- Evaluate the trade-off in total profit, not ratio: the source prefers a 4x ROAS at $100,000/month over a 6x ROAS at $10,000/month because absolute profit and customer volume are larger.
- Expect the ROAS floor you can accept to shift upward as LTV work matures — the source describes scaling at 1.5, or even down to 1.2, after doubling LTV.
Caveat: This is the presenter's stated view, framed as correcting a common misconception among newer advertisers; it assumes you have reliable profit and LTV data.
Caveat: The source warns that scaling incorrectly will wreck results and references a separate scaling strategy it does not detail here.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, google-ads, scaling, roas, budget-management, profitability, experiment-design
Source: Google Ads For Ecommerce_ 9 Keys To Success.docx

- Implement a dedicated attribution/tracking tool (the source names Hyros, which they use for their own ads) so that lead and purchase sources are visible across Google Ads and organic results.
- Use the cross-channel view to see exactly where a lead or sale came from before shifting budget between Google and other channels.
- Note that the source's example use case is tracking which source produced a booked call for their agency; the ecommerce application is the equivalent — attributing purchases rather than calls, and reconciling platform-reported conversions against a single source of truth.
- Verify current integrations and pricing of any attribution tool directly, as interfaces and features change.

## Build founder visibility and tell the product origin story
Use when: Developing brand positioning and ad creative for an ecommerce store, or deciding whether to invest in founder-led content.
- Consider building a personal brand as a founder or owner — the source says that among their ecommerce clients, the ones whose results 'fly' typically have a celebrity or heavily involved, well-followed person associated with the company.
- Understand the mechanism: personal brand is trust at scale, and trust matters most when a prospect is comparing your product with a competitor's; buyers assume a trusted founder has built the product carefully and cares about the category.
- Weigh the barrier to entry as an advantage: building a personal brand takes time and resources, which the source argues deters competitors and produces a durable edge.
- If a full personal brand is not viable, at minimum tell your origin story — the source's example is a mother who made a moisturiser for her child's eczema; that story is what made a friend of the presenter buy and then retell it to others.
- Use the story in ad creative and copy, since it gives prospects a reason to choose and a reason to repeat the story to others.
Caveat: The source acknowledges downsides: an attached personal brand makes an ecommerce business harder to sell later, though not impossible at large scale.
Caveat: The claimed performance gap (a 2x versus 6x ROAS between otherwise similar businesses) is the presenter's anecdotal observation, not a controlled benchmark.

## Why your ad creative—not your targeting—selects the buyer
Use when: Deciding how to allocate budget between targeting settings and creative production, or when an agency proposes rebuilding interest and lookalike ad sets.
- Accept the source's frame: as of the 2023–2026 rebuild, Meta selects the audience, not your manually entered interests. The practical implication is that creative is the lever you control for audience selection.
- Understand the mechanism to reason about your account: instead of a static 'pets' label, Meta plots each user as a vector in a very high-dimensional space and nudges that vector with every organic and paid interaction, so users cluster by behavior rather than by declared interest.
- When you run broad targeting, treat early spend as a probe: Meta spreads impressions across the space, observes who engages and buys, then concentrates delivery on the clusters that converted.
- Because of that mechanism, ask what your creative visually and verbally signals, since the algorithm reads the ad to find the matching cluster. Distinct concepts reach distinct clusters; near-identical ads reach the same one.
- Deprecate dependence on interest and lookalike targeting in your structure. The source states interests/lookalikes were deprecated in July 2025 and says broad targeting outperforms interest targeting on large data sets over long periods.
- Keep the controls the source says you still hold: exclusions, minimum age, locations (never worldwide by default), and languages.
Caveat: The 'broad always beats interests' claim is the presenter's position, tied to large data sets and long time horizons, not a guaranteed result for small budgets or narrow catalogs.
Caveat: Age bands and gender are only treated as suggestions, not controls, per the source.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, broad-targeting, creative-strategy, meta-ads, audience-targeting, exclusions, campaign-setup
Source: How The Meta Ads Algorithm Works in 2026.docx

## The three-stage Meta delivery pipeline: retrieval, ranking, auction
Use when: Diagnosing why ads get no delivery or poor performance, or deciding whether a change targets creative, structure, or bid.
- Map your problem to the stage it belongs to. Retrieval is where Meta scans the full ad inventory and shortlists a few thousand candidates relevant to the user. If your ads are never retrieved, creative signal and account structure are the suspects.
- Ranking is where shortlisted ads are scored for relevance and personal fit, using the user's historical paid and organic interactions. Creative diversity and offer clarity drive this stage.
- The auction is the final stage, where hundreds of ads bid for the placement. Bid and economics live here.
- When Meta ships an update, identify which stage it touches (retrieval, ranking, or auction dynamics) so you adapt the corresponding part of your account instead of rewriting everything.
- Useful update history for orientation: Lattice (2023) consolidated ranking, a November 2024 sequence-learning update optimized across ad sequences (supporting one ad per ad set structures), Andromeda (December 2024) changed retrieval via creative understanding, GEM added multimodal reading of video/audio and grouping by format, and an adaptive ranking model allocates compute per impression.
- Do not expect platform updates to lift your ROAS; the source's expectation is that your ROAS holds roughly flat while Meta raises CPMs to capture the efficiency gains.
Caveat: The 200-millisecond figure and 3% conversion / 5% CTR platform-lift claims come from Meta and the presenter flags platform number claims as things to treat carefully.
Caveat: Update names and dates are historical context; verify current behavior against Meta's own documentation, which the presenter says he is sourcing.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, meta-ads, algorithm-mechanics, ad-delivery, auction-dynamics, andromeda, measurement
Source: How The Meta Ads Algorithm Works in 2026.docx

## Trigger creative fatigue deliberately, then refresh before ROAS tapers
Use when: Planning creative refresh cadence, or explaining declining ROAS and rising frequency on a narrowly targeted persona-based ad.
- Recognize the mechanism: a highly specific ad (for example, a callout to business owners doing $10M+/year) causes Meta to converge on that narrow cluster and saturate it.
- Expect the source's reported pattern: saturation can arrive around $10,000 in spend on such a narrow concept, after which there is no one new in the cluster to reach.
- When saturation hits, Meta either keeps showing the ad to the same users (frequency climbs) or expands outward to adjacent clusters who are no longer your ideal customer profile, which is why ROAS tapers as the algorithm bridges out.
- Pre-empt this by maintaining a pipeline of diverse concepts rather than repeatedly iterating one persona. Iterations are fine inside the account, but reaching net-new audiences requires diversity in concepting.
- Define concepts as the intersection of an angle, an offer, and a persona. Changing format may also register as a different ad with Meta even when angle, offer, and persona stay constant.
- Monitor frequency and cluster-level spend as your refresh triggers rather than waiting for ROAS to visibly decay.
Caveat: The ~$10K saturation point is an illustrative example from the presenter's experience, not a benchmark to plan budgets against.
Caveat: This describes behavior the presenter attributes to the algorithm; treat it as a model for decision-making, not a documented rule.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, creative-strategy, meta-ads, creative-fatigue, audience-saturation, frequency, scaling
Source: How The Meta Ads Algorithm Works in 2026.docx

## Use exclusions to stop budget leaking to your warm customer cluster
Use when: Setting up a new broad-targeting campaign or auditing whether reported conversion efficiency is inflated by existing customers.
- Understand the risk: because vector clusters can correspond to warm existing customers, Meta is incentivized to push your ads there since conversion likelihood is high. This can mask poor new-customer acquisition.
- Build exclusion audiences for existing customers and apply them to your acquisition campaigns, so delivery is forced toward net-new clusters rather than the warm core.
- Treat exclusions as the single most important targeting control you still own, since interests, lookalikes, and other manual targeting have been deprecated or reduced to suggestions.
- Pair exclusions with the other retained controls: minimum age (a real control, unlike age bands, which are only suggestions), locations (don't default to worldwide), and languages.
- When reviewing performance, separate existing-customer conversions from new-customer conversions so you can tell whether the algorithm is prospecting or harvesting.
- If you also run retargeting, keep it deliberate and separated from acquisition so the two aren't bidding for the same warm cluster unintentionally.
Caveat: The source presents this as a growing risk under vector-based delivery; the magnitude depends on your customer file quality and how well your exclusions are matched.
Caveat: Exclusions reduce reachable audience, which is intentional but means your addressable pool shrinks as your customer base grows.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, exclusions, broad-targeting, meta-ads, audience-targeting, acquisition, customer-retention
Source: How The Meta Ads Algorithm Works in 2026.docx

## Bid equation: relevance multipliers beat raising bids
Use when: Considering whether to raise bids to win more auctions, or diagnosing why a competitor wins placements at a lower apparent cost.
- Internalize the formula: winning the auction equals bid times estimated action rate, plus ad quality.
- Note that estimated action rate is expected CTR times expected conversion rate, so both click and post-click behavior feed the multiplier.
- Use the practical consequence: two advertisers showing the same product to the same person can win at very different bids, so a $1 bid can lose to a $0.50 bid if the cheaper advertiser's relevance and quality are superior.
- Therefore treat 'be more relevant' as the primary cost-reduction lever rather than increasing bids, which just buys placement at worse unit economics.
- Do not chase ad quality directly. The source says quality score is not visible and changes in every auction, and attempts to optimize it directly are likened to star signs. Do the fundamentals and accept that it is immeasurable.
- Treat estimated action rate and ad quality as diagnostic (rearview) metrics, not live levers you can tune inside the auction.
- The presenter's strongest claim: economics are the real bid—higher sustainable bid from better AOV, LTV, and gross margin wins more auctions and scales further than platform tactics. The source asserts you cannot out-tactic bad economics.
Caveat: The claim that better economics dominate creatives, structure, and measurement is the presenter's opinion; it is directionally useful but not a universal law.
Caveat: Quality score optimization advice is explicitly called unreliable by the source because the metric is not measurable by advertisers.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, auction-dynamics, meta-ads, unit-economics, bidding-strategy, ad-quality, scaling
Source: How The Meta Ads Algorithm Works in 2026.docx
