## Google-specific audit checks: search terms, feed, currency
Use when: You are auditing Google Ads and Google Merchant Center ahead of a seasonal peak or a restructure.
- Open each cold campaign, go to search terms, and verify branded terms are not pulling through into cold campaigns.
- Check the Google Merchant Center feed: optimize titles, fill in all relevant feed variables, and eliminate warnings and errors.
- If selling across multiple countries, use a multi-currency feed — the source warns that running everything through a single currency triggers auto-conversion and adds tax as it presents in Shopping, hurting performance.
- Then investigate the halo effect: Google often sits bottom-of-funnel, so check whether cold search-term demand is genuinely converting cold traffic.
- If ROAS on non-brand campaigns does not correlate with acquisition MER after these checks, the source usually proposes an incrementality test for Google — but only when they suspect a halo effect or need rigorous validation.
Caveat: The source notes Google can be a strong new-customer channel — one of their own brands was Google-only and reached a seven-figure run rate around 2019–2020 — so Google is not inherently bottom-of-funnel.
Caveat: Feed and interface details change; verify current GMC and Google Ads UI.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, google-ads, merchant-center, shopping, search-terms, feed-optimization, incrementality
Source: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

## Creative volume rule: one new ad per $1,000 of monthly spend
Use when: You are deciding whether creative volume is the bottleneck or setting a production target for your creative team or agency.
- Divide monthly ad spend by $1,000 to get a baseline monthly new-ad target (source example: $100k/month implies ~100 new ads per month).
- Treat this as a rough rule of thumb, not a linear law — the source says at $1–3M/month you likely do not need 3,000 assets, and there are diminishing returns to raw creative volume at large scale.
- If you need a more precise target, use one of two models: (a) a churn model — monthly churn rate of winners implies a replacement rate; combine with hit rate to back into volume; or (b) average winner spend and revenue generation — if an average winner generates $20k, use that and your win rate to back-propagate to volume.
- If your actual output is far below the rule-of-thumb target, treat creative volume as a likely bottleneck.
Caveat: $1,000/ad is explicitly a simplification; the source's real models are described as complicated.
Caveat: Churn-model inputs (winner churn, hit rate, average winner revenue) are business-specific and must come from your own account.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, creative-strategy, creative-velocity, production-planning, budget-allocation, scaling
Source: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

## Separate volume, diversity, and quality as the creative bottleneck
Use when: You are diagnosing why creative performance has plateaued and need to pick the right fix.
- First check volume against your spend-based target (see the $1,000/new-ad card); if output is far off, that is the bottleneck.
- If volume is fine, check diversity — specifically concept diversification, not format diversification (see concept-diversity card).
- If both volume and diversity are adequate, assess quality by reading the actual scripts and content, judging angles, personas, scripting, talent, and offer. This is the hardest to systematize and requires direct-response marketing judgment; the source recommends looking at the ads directly and rescripting/reshooting what is weak.
- Assign exactly one bottleneck at a time — the source emphasizes you only have one creative bottleneck at any moment; pick it and fix it before moving on.
Caveat: Quality has no SOP in the source — it requires domain judgment and reviewing actual creative.
Caveat: You may end up with a different bottleneck than the source would call it if your spend model differs.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, creative-strategy, diagnosis, creative-velocity, ad-copywriting, quality-control
Source: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

## Diversify concepts, not just formats
Use when: You are planning creative strategy for a scaling account or diagnosing why a single winning ad fatigues.
- Define concepts as a combination of angle, offer, and persona — not format (video vs static vs UGC). The source says people over-index on format diversity and under-index on concept diversity.
- Illustration: a creatine brand spending $200k/month may be launching 200 ads/month but if all spend sits behind one concept (e.g., men 25–45, gym-performance angle, single bundle offer), it is not diverse — it is one concept being fatigued into the ground.
- Set concept targets by spend band: sub-$100k/month, 1–3 concepts is fine; $100k–$500k/month, aim for around 2 winning concepts with 2–6 in testing; $500k+/month, aim for 3+ concepts and 4–5 core working funnels, unless you are targeting the US/worldwide where two scalable concepts can carry a lot of spend.
- Sector-specific interpretation: in fashion, diverse concepts typically mean different products/categories; in CPG, typically different reframes of the same product.
- If your concept coverage is far below the band for your spend, treat diversity as the creative bottleneck.
Caveat: Concept-count targets are source heuristics, not verified benchmarks, and depend on market size and breadth.
Caveat: Some format diversity is still needed (e.g., not running only statics); the point is to not over-index on format.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, creative-strategy, concept-diversification, ad-creative, scaling, fatigue-management, brand-vs-cpg
Source: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

## Don't over-allocate to dynamic product ads
Use when: You are rebalancing spend inside a Meta account where DPAs are consuming the majority of budget.
- Check what percentage of account spend is in dynamic product ads.
- If a large share (source flags accounts sitting near 70% of spend in DPAs), rebalance — DPAs are bottom of funnel and, in the source's view, not incremental.
- Acknowledge DPAs can spend on cold and perform 'okay' there, but do not treat that as justification for the dominant share.
- Move reallocated budget into diversified cold campaigns with concept-level creative.
Caveat: '70%' and 'not incremental' are the source's observations/opinions, not measured facts across all accounts.
Caveat: DPA performance varies by category and catalog size; validate with your own incrementality read.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, meta-ads, retargeting, budget-allocation, creative-strategy, incrementality, dynamic-product-ads
Source: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

## Analyze winners to replicate the source of success
Use when: You have recently found a winning creative and are deciding whether to iterate on it or chase entirely new ideas.
- Do not abandon a winner to search for whatever comes next — the source says some accounts find a winner and never replicate on it.
- Decompose the winner across variables: persona, angle, offer, format, script structure, influencer/talent, and any other material difference.
- Identify which variable drove the result (the source asks explicitly: was it the persona, the angle, the format, the scripting, the influencer or the talent?).
- Brief the creative team to produce variations that hold the winning variable constant and vary the rest, to validate and extend the win.
- Feed this back into the creative roadmap so winners inform the next production cycle.
Caveat: Attribution of a win to a single variable is inherently uncertain; treat it as a hypothesis to test in the next round.
Caveat: Winners decay over time — this is about reinforcement, not indefinite reuse.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, creative-strategy, iteration, ad-testing, ad-copywriting, talent-selection, roadmap
Source: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

---

## Run creative production as a system with a feedback loop
Use when: You are setting up or reviewing your creative roadmap and production cadence against a scale target.
- Ask whether creative is shot reactively when ads are needed, or produced continuously against a roadmap.
- If ad hoc, build a consistent production system that puts a high volume of assets into the account on an ongoing basis.
- Include a feedback loop: performance data from live creative should feed back into the briefing and production process.
- Set expected volume using the spend-based rule or a churn/average-winner model, and check whether production capacity genuinely matches it.
- Align internal creative team skills or agency selection to the required volume and quality standard; the source notes this may require upskilling the team or changing creative agencies.
Caveat: Source does not prescribe a specific production tool or headcount — the requirement is output against volume and quality targets.
Caveat: Volume targets should be revisited as spend scales, per the diminishing-returns caveat.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, creative-strategy, production-planning, creative-velocity, roadmap, agency-management, systems
Source: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

---

## Drill down from business metrics to the ad that's the bottleneck
Use when: You have identified a top-level problem (e.g., rising CAC) and need to find where in the account it lives.
- Start at the top with business numbers: Shopify revenue, new customer revenue, and CAC.
- Identify the level of the problem (e.g., CAC issue), then go into Meta and Google and determine which platform.
- Within the failing platform, go into campaigns, then adsets, then ads, until you reach the element holding back performance.
- Confirm the diagnosis with data-integrity checks (platform ROAS versus acquisition MER) before making structural decisions.
- Sequence the fixes: generally data integrity first, then account structure, then creative — the source notes creative often has the highest impact but the longest fix time.
Caveat: Order of fixes is a source heuristic, not a universal law; the appropriate sequence can vary with business context.
Caveat: If your metrics are not trustworthy, do not attempt to diagnose deeper levels until the data-integrity layer is fixed.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, diagnosis, measurement, ad-account-structure, creative-strategy, prioritization, root-cause-analysis
Source: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

---

## Fix data integrity before creative or account structure
Use when: You are sequencing a paid-media turnaround and deciding what to fix first.
- Check whether a large gap exists between acquisition MER and platform-attributed ROAS.
- If the gap is large and unresolved by attribution-setting changes, make data integrity the number-one bottleneck — the source's rationale is that you cannot do valid creative analysis or account structuring on metrics that are not causally tied to business outcomes.
- Complete the data-integrity work first (attribution settings, breakdown-based reporting, fixed P&L and first-time P&L).
- Then fix account structure, which the source describes as a relatively fast, high-leverage fix (consolidating campaigns, removing bleed into existing customers, fixing settings errors).
- Then move into creative, which the source treats as high-impact but slow to fix because it requires structural changes to production capability.
Caveat: This ordering is a source opinion based on their client portfolio, not an empirical sequence validated across all businesses.
Caveat: Some businesses with accurate data may benefit from starting on creative instead.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, prioritization, measurement, data-integrity, ad-account-structure, creative-strategy, turnaround
Source: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

---

## Ad account audit order: data → structure → creative
Use when: Diagnosing a declining or flat paid acquisition program (Meta/Google) and deciding which fix to tackle first this quarter.
- Start with data integrity: verify tracking, pixel/events, attribution windows and reporting so decisions rest on trustworthy numbers. The source treats this as the highest commercial-impact item and the foundation for everything downstream.
- Second, review account structure: campaign/ad set organization, budget allocation, consolidation vs fragmentation — the source places this as the number-two priority by commercial impact.
- Third, move to creative: only once the data and structure are sound does creative testing become a reliable lever.
- Note the source's distinction: by commercial impact the ranking is data, account structure, creative — but by time-to-implement the practical order is often data first, then account structure, then creative.
- Apply the sequence as a recovery roadmap when a brand is going sideways or declining, rather than jumping straight to new creative.
Caveat: This ordering is the presenter's framework/opinion, not a universal law; some accounts with obviously broken creative may warrant a different entry point.
Caveat: The source describes its audit process at a high level in this section and does not detail the specific checks inside each phase.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, measurement, acquisition, account-structure, audit, attribution, creative-strategy
Source: How We Audit 8 and 9 Figure Ad Accounts (Full Process).docx

---

## Write ads as salesmanship in print
Use when: Writing or reviewing any acquisition creative — Meta/TikTok ad, product page hero, landing page, or email subject line — and you need a single test to cut indecision.
- Before finalizing a creative, ask: 'Would this help a salesman sell the goods if I met the buyer in person?' If the line only exists to be clever or short, cut it.
- Do not shorten copy just because people 'read very little.' Hopkins's point: you would never hand a real prospect to a salesman and cap him at 10 words. Length is not the constraint — relevance is.
- Because advertising 'may appeal to thousands while the salesman will talk to one,' a mediocre ad damages every prospect at once, whereas a mediocre salesman only wastes one conversation. Apply the higher bar to the ad.
- Rewrite any line that would embarrass a salesperson saying it face-to-face — especially boasts, brand commands, and 'avoid imitations' style warnings, which Hopkins says indicate a motive buyers cannot sympathize with.
- Check the final creative against one question: does every sentence increase good impression and speak to the prospect's desire, not the advertiser's pride?
Caveat: This is Hopkins's framework from early-1900s direct-response advertising; the 'salesman' test is a reasoning tool, not a measured conversion benchmark.
Caveat: Longer copy is not automatically better — the test is relevance and sales-helpfulness, not word count.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, ad-copy, landing-page, conversion-optimization, direct-response, positioning
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Sell service, not your brand
Use when: Drafting ad copy or landing page hero sections where the instinct is to lead with the brand name, product features, or company achievements.
- Identify every self-referential line in the creative — company history, plant size, awards, 'we're the best' claims — and tag each as a boast to be removed or reframed.
- Rewrite each as the customer benefit that follows from it. The size of your plant, for example, becomes a reason the buyer gets faster shipping or lower risk.
- Make the salesperson's plea match Hopkins's model: 'I was selling service... the advantage to myself was covered up in my efforts to please him.' The buyer should feel you are solving their problem, not asking a favor.
- Apply the same to creative in competitive categories: Hopkins says you cannot enter a well-occupied field on a plain 'buy my brand' appeal, because it is repugnant. Offer exceptional service to induce switching from a favorite brand.
- Re-audit existing top-of-funnel ads monthly. Hopkins's observation is that most advertisers merely 'cry a name' and their evident desire is selfish advantage — such advertising may pay somewhat but never as well as apparent unselfishness.
Caveat: Hopkins presents this as a general principle ('argue for your own advantage and people will resist to the limit'), not a tested conversion lift.
Caveat: Service framing still needs a real differentiator or specific promise; empty service language without substance is just another kind of vacancy.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, offer-design, positioning, ad-copy, conversion-optimization, direct-response
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Advertise to one person, not the masses
Use when: Setting up email capture, retargeting sequences, PDP recommendations, or paid traffic flows where all visitors currently get the same generic response.
- Segment the entry point by expressed intent. Hopkins's example: a woman writing about a sewing machine should receive the sewing-machine catalog with every style and price, not the full company catalog sent to all inquiries alike.
- Add social proof local to the prospect. Hopkins sent names of every buyer in the inquirer's town and asked her to go see the machine and talk to owners. For ecommerce, substitute nearby reviews, UGC, or a demo they can inspect in person.
- Treat 'people in the mass' as a mistake. Hopkins: 'We must get down to individuals. We must treat people in advertising as we treat them in person.'
- Apply this to retargeting and email: an ad creative that speaks to the searched category won't work for a cold, broad audience — match the creative to the individual's demonstrated desire.
- Build the flow so a person who showed one specific intent gets one specific, complete answer (product, price, proof) rather than being routed to everything you sell.
Caveat: Hopkins describes this principle from letter-inquiry handling, not digital funnels; the metaphor is the transferable part, not the mechanics.
Caveat: Personalizing by intent requires enough traffic or data per segment; below that, use one clear offer rather than leaking budget across thin segments.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, personalization, landing-page, email-marketing, retargeting, customer-research, conversion-optimization
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Tell the pains you take (the Schlitz story)
Use when: Writing a product page, brand story section, or ad angle for a commodity-like product where you believe 'everyone does this, so it's not a differentiator.'
- Do first-hand research at the source of production — visit the facility, interview the operators, ask why every step exists. Hopkins saw plate-glass rooms, white wood-pulp filters, pipes cleaned twice daily, bottles cleaned four times by machinery, 4,000-ft artisan wells, six-month aging, and a mother yeast developed by 1,200 experiments.
- Capture each step's purpose, not just its existence. For ecommerce, that could be inspection steps, material sourcing, QA thresholds, or fulfillment processes.
- Resist the founder's reflex that it's just ordinary. Hopkins's clients said 'the processes we use are just the same as others' — his answer: 'Others have never told this story... It will startle everyone in print.'
- Write the process into the PDP or ad as a purity/quality narrative with concrete numbers and specifics, giving your claim a visible meaning instead of merely repeating 'pure' or 'premium'.
- Test this against your current PDP claims: 'the maker is too close to his product. He sees in his methods only the ordinary.' The steps you find boring are exactly what a buyer has never seen explained.
Caveat: Schlitz allegedly went from fifth to neck-and-neck with first after the campaign — a case-study result attributed to the source, not a promised outcome.
Caveat: The technique works only if the claimed process is true and verifiable; inventing hidden steps is not the method, and it can be easily exposed.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, product-page, positioning, brand-story, differentiation, creative-strategy
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Sell painkillers, not prevention
Use when: Choosing the angle for health, wellness, supplement, dental, financial, or maintenance-focused products where the default pitch is risk prevention.
- Write both angles for the same product: the prevention angle ('use this so your teeth don't decay') and the reward angle ('use this to become more attractive, happier, more cheerful').
- Hopkins's Pepso dent decision: he resolved to advertise the toothpaste as a creator of beauty rather than a preventative. Apply the same shift to skincare, supplements, supplements-for-prevention, or device warranties.
- Never picture the afflicted in creative. Hopkins says he never referred to disasters and every illustration he used showed attractive people. Shoot and select creators accordingly.
- Frame recurring-purchase products around the positive identity the customer attains, not the loss they avoid, because that is what drives the buying psychology.
- Use the appeal audit across the whole campaign: Hopkins says every campaign depends on its psychology and success is determined by right or wrong appeal — so pick one dominant psychological appeal and make all ad variants consistent with it before testing.
Caveat: Hopkins made a reported million dollars on Pepso dent from this psychological choice — a dramatic historical case, not a benchmark for modern conversion rates.
Caveat: Reward positioning must still be honest and compliant; beauty/outcome claims in regulated categories (supplements, health) may need legal review.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, ad-copy, positioning, creative-strategy, consumer-psychology, retention
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Sample the right way: require an effort
Use when: Designing lead magnets, free-trial offers, sample distribution, or PR-box mailers — deciding whether to send product free or require an opt-in.
- Do not propend samples on people who didn't ask. Hopkins: 'I have never found that it paid to give samples to people who do not request it... Products handed out without asking lose respect.'
- Gate the sample behind a small action — filling out a request form, giving an email, completing a quiz. 'It is different when you force people to make an effort.'
- Sequence it: 'We must arouse interest in our product before it has value to anybody.' Use the ad or PDP to create desire first, then offer the demo/sample as the response.
- Use the demonstration principle the sample represents. Hopkins sold about 1 in 10 women when merely talking about his mother's silver polish, but nearly all when he could get inside the house and demonstrate it — 'a good product is its own best salesman.'
- For ecommerce, replicate the demonstration with sampling programs, money-back guarantees, or in-home trials that require an explicit claim, then let the product do the selling.
Caveat: Hopkins calls promiscuous sampling a 'very bad plan' from his direct-selling era; the transferable rule is that perceived value depends on an effort threshold, not on refusing all free sampling.
Caveat: Gating raises friction — measure both claim rate and downstream conversion/repeat purchase rather than assuming fewer, better leads pay off.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, offer-design, lead-magnet, product-sampling, conversion-optimization, customer-research
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Give your brand a human personality
Use when: Building brand identity, creator-led content, founder-led marketing, or repositioning a faceless ecommerce brand in categories where competitors are all 'soulless corporations.'
- Decide whether the founder, a named expert, or a recurring persona will front the brand. Hopkins used a persona called Professor Anderson with an actual person behind it and said he did this wherever possible.
- Make the person the face and voice of the advertising — not a stock model or a logo — because 'personalities appeal while soulless corporations do not. Make a man famous, and you make his creation famous.'
- Have the person talk about the product's accomplishments and its making, since 'all of us love to study men and their accomplishments.' For ecommerce, this can be founder storytelling on the PDP, creator-style ad creative, or an expert answering objections on video.
- Keep the persona consistent across channels so the human becomes a recognizable asset, consistent with the 'stick to what works' rule for campaigns.
- Apply it especially where the founder is uniquely qualified: the person who built the product knows every in and out and is the best advocate for why customers should buy.
Caveat: The Professor Anderson example is historical; the transferable claim is that personality aids persuasion, not that every brand needs a fictional persona.
Caveat: Invented authority personas can breach modern ad-platform policies and consumer trust if they misrepresent expertise — prefer a real named person.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, brand-personality, founder-led-marketing, creative-strategy, positioning, retention
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Test, never assume your own taste predicts demand
Use when: Deciding what products, creatives, or angles to launch or kill when you have a personal gut reaction for or against them.
- Separate your taste from the market's. Hopkins: 'We must never judge humanity by ourselves. The things we want, the things we like may appeal to a small minority.'
- He explicitly says product selection goes wrong when operators reject products as 'stupid' that then sell hugely because the audience is billions of people, not the operator.
- Write down your prediction before launching, then compare against actual performance — the practice mirrors Hopkins making mistakes in a small way and learning from each (he says he made no mistake twice).
- Run small, cheap tests first rather than betting the campaign on a personal conviction, so the market rather than the operator adjudicates.
- Record what worked and re-use it; Hopkins links this habit to developing enduring advertising principles, in contrast to repeatedly changing your mind based on your own impression of the creative.
Caveat: Hopkins's argument is specifically against relying on personal preference and for empirical testing; it is not a formula for how many tests or what sample size to run.
Caveat: Testing does not mean ignoring strategy or brand constraints — it means the audience, not the founder, is the judge of appeal.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, experiment-design, product-selection, customer-research, creative-strategy, measurement
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Stay close to the buyer and the money
Use when: Doing customer research for ad angles, or negotiating roles, contracts, or agency compensation tied to advertising and sales performance.
- Study real sellers up close. Hopkins spent hours under torchlight listening to pitchmen and canvassers and said: 'Study salesmen, canvassers, and fakers if you want to know how to sell goods.' For ecommerce, this means watching sales calls, reading support tickets and chat logs, and interviewing repeat buyers — not just reading dashboards.
- Watch for reactions, not just stated preferences: when you're close to the buyer, 'you can hear, you can see what they reject, you can see what appeal lights up their eyes.'
- Document the specific phrases and objections that recur and test them as ad angles, since direct-response salespeople are the closest real-world laboratory for appeals that work.
- On compensation, apply Hopkins's 'stay close to the money' principle: he moved from the expense side of a business to the sales-generating side, then negotiated a share of the sales he brought in (e.g., asking for a portion of the million dollars in toothpaste sales he generated).
- Evidence value created and ask for a share of measured incremental value rather than flat fees disconnected from results.
Caveat: 'Stay close to the money' is a career/business principle from Hopkins's autobiography, not a prescribed commission structure; deal terms vary by role and market.
Caveat: 'Fakers' in Hopkins's era includes deceptive pitchmen — study the mechanics of persuasion, not tactics that mislead buyers.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, customer-research, creative-strategy, offer-design, pricing, direct-response
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Stick with the ad that works (moving parade)
Use when: Deciding whether to refresh or replace a profitable creative, offer, or PDP hero because it 'feels stale' internally.
- Before changing a working ad, distinguish internal boredom from market fatigue. 'The advertising becomes monotonous to the men who read every ad… they always come to want something new,' but customers have not read every ad.
- Use the framing: you are not advertising to a standing army, you are advertising to a moving parade — most of your audience is seeing the message for the first time, which is why repetition across a changing audience keeps working.
- Set a decision rule for refreshing: change when measured performance degrades, not on a fixed internal schedule or subjective creative boredom.
- If you must change, keep the winning core (appeal, claim, offer) intact and swap the execution shell (imagery, format, channel), so you preserve what won millions and only vary the wrapper.
- Record which principles have endured for you the way Hopkins kept his — this turns one-off wins into reusable rules rather than restarting from scratch each cycle.
Caveat: This is Hopkins's stated preference for continuity, echoed later by David Ogilvy; some modern platforms show genuine creative fatigue, so treat 'never change' as the source's bias, not an absolute — reconcile with your own retention curves.
Caveat: A moving parade still implies reach and frequency are being bought repeatedly; if you only ever reach the same small audience, repeated exposure can fatigue.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, creative-strategy, campaign-management, retention, measurement, advertising-frequency
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Judge advertising by salesmanship and the customer's mind
Use when: Choosing an appeal/angle before writing a campaign, or diagnosing why a campaign isn't converting despite decent execution.
- State the appeal in one sentence before writing: prevention, status/beauty, convenience, effort saved, time saved, etc. Hopkins says 'every advertising campaign depends on its psychology. Success or failure is determined by the right or wrong appeal.'
- Check the appeal against what humans actually do: people 'do little to prevent' trouble but pursue rewards, happiness, beauty, and cheer — so test one dominant positive-outcome appeal before loading multiple appeals into one ad.
- Apply the salesmanship standard to every executional question (length, tone, claims): 'Ask yourself, would this help a salesman sell the goods?' rather than following generic copywriting rules.
- Because advertising is 'multiplied salesmanship,' the same mediocre message reaches your whole audience, so errors cost more than in person — raise the bar on the main promise before polishing anything else.
- Use customer perspective as the final filter: no manufacturer should conduct his own advertising because he is too close to the factory and tells what he takes pride in rather than what the customer wants to know.
Caveat: The 'right or wrong appeal' is a directional principle, not a guarantee; categories and audiences differ, and regulated categories constrain appeal choices.
Caveat: Hopkins's own framework favors positive-outcome appeals; some products genuinely sell on risk-avoidance (insurance, security), so treat it as a starting hypothesis to test, not law.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, positioning, creative-strategy, consumer-psychology, conversion-optimization, customer-research
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Prove the product, don't just talk about it
Use when: Designing acquisition creative, PDP media, or landing page proof sections that currently rely on claims instead of showing the product working.
- Identify what a live demonstration would look like: the silver-polish example is the literal product applied to the buyer's own problem in front of them. For ecommerce, this means demo video, before/after, side-by-side, or a trial the customer physically experiences.
- Prefer showing to arguing. Hopkins: 'No argument in the world can ever compare with one dramatic demonstration.' Replace persuasive copy with a visual proof asset where possible.
- Get the product into the buyer's hands when feasible, since 'a good product is its own best salesman.' This is the rationale behind trials, guarantees, and in-home tests.
- Choose demo formats that face the particular objection the buyer has — show cleaning power, fit, durability, or result timeline — rather than a generic brand film.
- Keep demo creative central on the PDP and in paid ads, not buried; if the product genuinely wins on demonstration, make it the lead, not a supporting detail.
Caveat: The one-in-ten versus 'nearly all' figures are Hopkins's door-to-door experience, not an ecommerce benchmark.
Caveat: Demos must be accurate to real product performance; an exaggerated demo creates post-purchase returns and review damage.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, product-page, creative-strategy, conversion-optimization, ugc, product-demo
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Capitalizing on insights: put your money where your copy is
Use when: Structuring performance-based deals, agency compensation, affiliate arrangements, or deciding how to bet on a product angle you believe will outperform.
- Apply the principle that 'the big salaries are paid to the salesmen... and to the men in the factory who reduce costs,' i.e., value accrues near revenue and profit creation — position your work and compensation close to that lever.
- If you believe your creative will materially lift a brand's sales, negotiate a share of measured incremental value or performance-based terms rather than purely time-based fees.
- Hopkins's Pepso dent example: he bought shares for $13,000 at the start of the project; the position paid him $200,000 in dividends and later sold for $500,000. Use this as an illustration of aligning upside with the results of your own work, not a promised return.
- Build measurement into the deal up front — agree on what constitutes incremental sales attributable to advertising before the campaign begins.
- For an operator running their own store, the analogous move is to reinvest in the channels and product angles with proven incremental lift instead of spreading budget evenly.
Caveat: The Pepso dent numbers are a historical case study, not a benchmark; many campaigns don't produce that outcome and share-of-upside deals require trusted attribution.
Caveat: Tying compensation to performance only works when sales lift can be reliably attributed — otherwise you are negotiating over an unmeasurable number.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, pricing, measurement, offer-design, attribution, campaign-management
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Do the work in volume with focus
Use when: Building a sustainable creative testing cadence or deciding how much output an in-house or agency ecommerce marketing function should produce.
- Increase the volume of finished work — ads written, creatives shipped, tests run — rather than endlessly perfecting one asset, because volume is what generates both mistakes and successes to learn from.
- Treat mistakes as the tuition: Hopkins says he learned from each and 'made no mistake twice,' turning errors into an operating record of enduring principles.
- Pair volume with a learning log so insights from tests persist beyond the individual campaign and inform the next one.
- Hopkins worked nights and Sundays (rarely an evening free for 16 years) and calls business a game he plays; the transferable mechanic is sustained focused repetitions in one domain, not the literal hours and not a recommendation to burn out.
- Direct the volume at one thing you can go deep in — Hopkins says those with singular focus derive insights others simply won't have; for ecommerce, pick the domain (e.g., landing pages or paid creative) and do many deliberate reps.
Caveat: Hopkins himself writes 'I am not advising others to follow my example' on the extreme hours; treat the durable lesson as focused volume, not the workaholism.
Caveat: Volume without measurement or learning produces churn, not improvement — you still need to record what worked.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, experiment-design, creative-strategy, measurement, operations, campaign-management
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Reframe advertising questions around the buyer's desires
Use when: Resolving copy, offer, or page-layout debates inside a team where opinions conflict and no test data yet exists.
- Identify the prospect's expressed desire first: for the sewing machine inquirer it was a sewing machine; for your store it may be a specific use case, budget, or occasion. 'Consider the person who stands before you with certain expressed desires.'
- Answer the ad question in that person's terms: 'However big your business, get down to the units, for those units are all that make size.'
- Cut lines that serve the brand's interests instead of the prospect's. Hopkins says 'argue anything for your own advantage and people will resist to the limit... seem unselfishly to consider your customer's desires and they will naturally flock to you.'
- Test the creative against the standard 'Say only what you think a good salesman should say if that prospect stood before him' — this resolves disputes without waiting for an A/B test when budget or traffic is limited.
- Use this as a fast internal filter before running the more expensive statistical test on the remaining, genuinely ambiguous options.
Caveat: This is a judgment framework, not a substitute for measurement; where traffic allows, still validate against conversion data.
Caveat: What the prospect 'wants to know' is inferred, not given — validate assumptions with support tickets, reviews, and sales conversations.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, conversion-optimization, positioning, landing-page, ad-copy, customer-research
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Don't let success in one area convince you you can run any
Use when: Deciding whether to expand your store into an unrelated product category, new market, or a different business, especially when an existing product line is performing well.
- Inventory the specific competencies your current success depends on — sourcing, creative, fulfilment, audience — and ask which of these actually transfer to the proposed expansion.
- Treat the planned move as a new business, not an extension of a proven one: Hopkins says 'it is curious how we all desire to excel in something outside of our own province. This leads many men astray.'
- If expanding categories or markets, allocate a small test budget and staff it with people who do have domain experience, rather than assuming the core team's proven playbook carries over.
- Watch for the moment confidence substitutes for evidence — the pattern Hopkins names is that one success makes people feel qualified to run anything.
- Keep the proven core investment protected while the new venture is unproven, since losses in the new area can drain cash generated by the successful one.
Caveat: This is a cautionary pattern, not a rule against diversification; adjacent expansions that share competencies may transfer well.
Caveat: The claim is Hopkins's observation about businesses of his era; modern operators should still evaluate with their own data.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, product-selection, operations, capital-allocation, expansion, measurement
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Earn the role by demonstrating the work, not just applying
Use when: Pitching a major retailer partnership, applying for an in-house leadership role, or winning a large client when you have no direct relationship and the competition is strong.
- Prepare proof of skill from third parties: Hopkins had dozens of people send letters vouching for his copywriting ability — for ecommerce, gather retailer logos, GMV case studies, or client statements.
- Create a public body of work that the decision-maker will encounter: Hopkins wrote a daily newspaper column on advertising sharing everything he learned, so the hiring decision-maker saw his expertise repeatedly.
- Do all the standard moves too — apply, call, try to meet — but treat those as the baseline, not the winning move, since the testimonials and column are what differentiated him.
- Aim the pitch at the decision-maker's actual need, echoing Lasker's recruiting speech: acknowledge the best available copy still isn't good enough, then ask for exactly what's needed (e.g., 'give me three ads that will start the campaign').
- Make the ask concrete and tied to a result, as Lasker did when offering any car on the street charged to him in exchange for three campaign-starting ads — pair a clear deliverable with a clear reward.
Caveat: The job win is an anecdote from Hopkins's career, not a hiring guaranteed by this method.
Caveat: The newspaper-column tactic relied on local print reach; adapt the 'public proof of work' to channels your target buyer actually sees.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, partnerships, personal-branding, positioning, direct-response, creative-strategy
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Write every ad as one-to-one salesmanship
Use when: Drafting or reviewing any paid ad, product page or email where the prospect has already clicked or shown interest.
- Assume your reader already raised their hand — the headline or creative image earned the click, so treat the following copy as a live conversation with a warm prospect rather than a broadcast to a crowd.
- For each line, ask: 'Would I say this to a buyer standing in front of me right now?' If it is something you'd only say to a mass audience, rewrite it.
- Do not cap length artificially by a word count — as the source argues, confining a salesman to a set number of words would be an unthinkable handicap. Let the copy run as long as it stays interesting and useful to that one person.
- Do what a good salesman does with a half-sold prospect: give enough specific information to prompt action, without boasting or showing off.
- End with the equivalent of the natural close the salesman would reach — a service framed offer, not 'give me your money'.
Caveat: The 'no length limit' view is Claude Hopkins' position; short-form ad formats and platform character limits may still force brevity, so adapt rather than abandon the principle.
Caveat: Treat this as a copy-review heuristic, not a testable claim — you still need your own measured results.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, ad-copy, creative-strategy, conversion-optimization, customer-research, headline
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Long copy works when it stays interesting
Use when: Deciding whether a product page, landing page or advertorial should be short or long-form for an interested audience.
- Accept Hopkins' maxim 'the more you tell, the more you sell' — some of his most successful ads reportedly ran to around 15,000 words, framed as interesting information about a product the reader already showed interest in via the headline.
- Make the copy interesting, not merely long: the source's logic is that people give time to what interests them if you make it interesting.
- Only extend after the headline has confirmed interest; long copy shown to someone who never opted in is wasted.
- Use this as a testable hypothesis on your own store: run a longer, information-rich variant against a short variant and measure purchase conversion, not just click-through.
Caveat: The 15,000-word and other Hopkins figures describe a print-era direct response context; they are examples of what worked then, not benchmarks for modern feeds.
Caveat: Do not confuse 'more you tell' with padding — Hopkins frames it as story and useful information, not repetition of features.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, ad-copy, product-page, landing-page, conversion-optimization, experiment-design
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Frame ads around service, not buying requests
Use when: Writing the offer framing and call to action for an ad, landing page or door-opener promotion.
- Assume the reader is selfish in the ordinary sense — they care nothing about your brand, interest or profit, and only seek service for themselves.
- Avoid the appeal Hopkins calls unpopular: 'Buy my brand, give me the trade you give others, let me have the money.'
- Build the ad around offered service: wanted information, cited advantages to users, a genuine benefit the reader gets whether or not they buy.
- Model the door-to-door hairbrush case: 2,000 salespeople were sent to say 'I was sent here to give you a brush; take your choice from these samples.' The housewife, picking one brush, saw several she wanted and felt anxious to reciprocate the gift — producing the order without any direct ask.
- Apply the same structure to your offer: let the prospect choose, experience or receive value first, so the purchase becomes the natural result.
Caveat: Hopkins notes these seemingly altruistic ads are based on knowledge of human nature — they are designed, not accidental charity; do not mistake this for simply being nice.
Caveat: The hairbrush example is historical anecdote, not a tested result for your category.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, offer-design, ad-copy, positioning, conversion-optimization, creative-strategy
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Spend most of your copy time on the headline
Use when: Allocating copywriting time across a headline, subhead and body for an ad, landing page or PDP above-the-fold block.
- Follow Hopkins: the purpose of a headline is to pick out the people you could interest, like saying 'Hey there, Bill Jones' to one person in a crowd — headlines must not be misleading.
- Recognize that most readers scan headlines and only some proceed to body copy (the source cites Ogilvy's estimate that roughly 80–90% read the headline versus the body).
- Invest accordingly: Hopkins says he spent far more time on headlines than on the writing itself, often hours on a single headline and discarding scores before choosing.
- Ask whether the promise — the actual benefit the customer gets from your product — is stated in the headline. The source's archetype: '1,000 songs in your pocket' puts the main appeal directly in the headline.
- Because return depends on attracting the right sort of readers, cut any headline that pulls the wrong audience even if it pulls volume.
Caveat: The 80–90% headline-versus-body figure is attributed here to Ogilvy, not established in the source text as a measurement; treat as a heuristic.
Caveat: Hopkins reports headline changes sometimes multiplying returns five- to tenfold, and Ogilvy later reportedly saw 19-to-1 differences — these are historical observations, not guaranteed lift ranges.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, headline, ad-copy, creative-strategy, conversion-optimization, landing-page
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Use specificity to make claims land
Use when: Rewriting generic benefit claims on ads, PDPs or landing pages into defensible, specific statements.
- Identify every claim of the type 'best in the world', 'lowest prices', 'high quality' — Hopkins says these are simply claiming the expected and have no impression whatsoever.
- Replace each with a definitive statement carrying an actual figure or tested fact; Hopkins notes actual figures are not genuinely discounted, while specific facts carry full weight.
- Study his examples: a clothing seller claimed 'my net profit is 3%' instead of 'lowest prices in America'; a razor maker advertised a '78-second shave', indicating actual test results, versus the generic 'quick shaves'.
- Make sure any figure you deploy is true and verifiable for your own product — the technique derives its power from credibility, and a false specific damages it.
Caveat: Hopkins' examples come from a pre-regulatory print era; modern advertising rules on comparative and substantiated claims apply, so verify every figure you publish.
Caveat: Specificity multiplies the weight of an argument you already have — it cannot rescue an irrelevant or unwanted offer.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, ad-copy, offer-design, positioning, conversion-optimization, product-page
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Exploit price perception and exclusivity psychology
Use when: Framing price, tiered access, membership or VIP offers in ads and on site merchandising.
- Use the painting example: announced without a price, most passers-by ignored it; once told it cost $750,000, people returned and a crowd formed around it — price itself created attention and perceived value.
- Consider deliberately signalling premium pricing rather than hiding it, if the product's positioning supports it, since people judge things largely by price.
- Apply the tribal principle: offers limited to a defined class — veterans, lodge members, executives — outperform general offers, because those entitled to a group advantage will go a long way not to lose it.
- Translate into ecommerce specifics: members-only drops, founders' pricing, a named customer segment ('for working chefs') on the landing page, or early access restricted to an email list.
- Recognize Hopkins' broader point: an identical offer presented in different ways can bring multiplied returns, so the framing — not just the discount — is the lever.
Caveat: The $750,000 figure is Hopkins' historical illustration, not a tested conversion result for your category.
Caveat: Do not fabricate exclusivity or fake a group the customer cannot plausibly belong to; the principle rests on the buyer's belief in genuine entitlement.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, pricing, offer-design, positioning, retention, psychology
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Rewrite the same offer in different framings
Use when: Planning the next round of ad, landing page or email creative variants when the offer and price must stay fixed.
- Hold the offer constant — same product, same price, same discount — and change one framing element at a time: the headline, the group it is addressed to, the price presentation, or the degree of specificity.
- Draw your variant ideas from the source's demonstrated framing levers: headline appeal, group-restricted versus general offer, price emphasis, and concise numbers instead of generalities.
- Accept Hopkins' claim that, once you find a working ad, the best way to get new customers is the way you got the previous ones — repeat and iterate on what works rather than abandoning it for novelty.
- Set up the comparison so you measure purchase conversion for the same audience, since different framings attract different readers and raw volume can mislead.
Caveat: Keeping the same ad and re-running it versus rewriting it is a strategic call — Hopkins advocates repetition, but modern platform fatigue effects are outside his evidence.
Caveat: Framing changes can pull a different audience, so compare conversion within comparable traffic, not across mismatched segments.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, ad-copy, creative-strategy, experiment-design, conversion-optimization, positioning
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Research deeply to find the keystone fact
Use when: Preparing the creative brief or angle list for a new product launch or a stalled ad account.
- Before writing, gather full information on the subject, as Hopkins insists an ad writer must: read widely, including technical, dry or obscure material that was never written for marketers.
- Accept that you may read volumes and find few usable facts — but one fact can be the keystone of the campaign. The source cites a toothpaste writer who read volumes of scientific matter and found in one volume the idea that 'helped make millions'.
- He also cites the Rolls-Royce case, where a line found in an obscure engineering document became the basis for one of the most successful campaigns of all time.
- For your store, hunt in the same terrain: supplier specs, factory documentation, warranties, ingredient sheets, support tickets, review language — places competitors have not mined for ad copy.
- Treat research volume as the job: the source describes campaigns preceded by very large volumes of data and months of research, with the finished ad looking simple on purpose.
Caveat: The 'millions' and campaign-success outcomes are historical case examples, not reproducible promises.
Caveat: The source's maxim 'genius is the art of taking pains' is Hopkins' view of effort, not a guarantee that effort alone produces a winner.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, customer-research, creative-strategy, research, ad-copy, product-page
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Keep an enduring human-psychology checklist
Use when: Building a standing checklist or briefing template your team uses before shipping any ad or page.
- Adopt Hopkins' premise that human nature is perpetual — the same today as in Caesar's time — so the psychological principles you learn will never need to be unlearned.
- Include curiosity on the checklist: he calls it one of the strongest human incentives and says it should be employed whenever possible, which in ecommerce terms means intriguing headlines and open loops rather than full disclosure upfront.
- Include price perception: people judge things largely by price, so decide deliberately what your price signals.
- Include belonging: group-limited offers beat general ones because people will work to keep an advantage tied to their group.
- Include self-interest: readers act to please themselves, never to help your profit — test every draft against that filter.
- Run the draft through the checklist and flag any claim that only serves the brand.
Caveat: The claim that psychological principles are fixed and enduring is Hopkins' assertion; it should not be read as evidence that any specific tactic works on every platform today.
Caveat: Individual execution still requires testing — the checklist generates candidates, not proven winners for your store.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, psychology, ad-copy, creative-strategy, customer-research, conversion-optimization
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Reconcile headline impact with measured conversion
Use when: Setting expectations and measurement discipline before running a headline or creative test on your store.
- Note the source's claims: the identical ad run with various headlines differs tremendously in returns, and a headline change is said to multiply returns five to ten times; Ogilvy is cited as having seen differences up to 19 to 1.
- Treat these as historical observations from print direct response, not as forecast ranges for your account — they justify investing in headlines and testing them.
- Design your test so the headline is the isolated variable: same offer, same audience, same placement and creative where possible, differing only in headline.
- Measure the metric that matches the goal — purchase conversion for a sales headline, qualified click-through if the headline's job is audience selection.
- Remember Hopkins' framing that headline return depends on attracting the right sort of readers, so a lower-volume headline may be the winner if it brings better-qualified buyers.
Caveat: Do not present the five-to-ten-times or 19-to-1 figures as expected lifts for a client or stakeholder; they are source-cited historical anecdotes.
Caveat: Small-sample tests on niche stores may need longer runs or larger creative differences to show reliable effects.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, headline, measurement, experiment-design, conversion-optimization, ad-copy
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Choose headlines that reveal interest, not conceal it
Use when: Selecting among headline options for an ad, email subject line or landing page hero.
- Apply the source's stated purpose: to pick out the people you could interest, the way a newspaper headline lets readers choose what they wish to read.
- Keep it truthful — Hopkins stresses that headlines must not be misleading, because attracting the wrong readers wastes the entire ad spend.
- Account for hurry: people want to be amused or benefited, so the headline has to deliver one of those immediately.
- Recognize that a profitable product may interest a reader more than anything else, but they will never know unless the headline tells them — so the headline must surface the specific interest rather than a vague tease.
- Use the 'empty church' framing: you cannot educate or inspire a prospect who never clicked, so the hook must earn attention before any persuasion, teaching or product explanation begins.
Caveat: The idea that you must entertain before you educate is the presenter's interpretation of Hopkins; treat it as editorial guidance, not Hopkins' own tested conclusion.
Caveat: Do not let entertainment slide into misleading curiosity — Hopkins explicitly warns against headlines that conceal the interest they should reveal.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, headline, ad-copy, creative-strategy, landing-page, conversion-optimization
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Match copy length and detail to the interested reader
Use when: Deciding how much detail to include on a PDP, landing page or long-form ad for a considered purchase.
- Separate the two audiences: the uninterested scanner who never clicks and the interested prospect who arrived by clicking the headline or image.
- For the interested prospect, follow the source's instruction to consider them as prospects standing before you seeking information, and give them enough to get action.
- Do not apply mass-market brevity rules — the source argues that telling a salesman to use a certain number of words with a live prospect would be an unthinkable handicap.
- Include the specific facts and service-oriented detail the prospect needs (Hopkins' razor example: a definitive '78-second shave' rather than 'quick shaves').
- Review whether each added paragraph helps a half-sold buyer decide; cut content that only serves the brand or repeats the headline.
Caveat: Length guidance is contingent on the prospect's existing interest — long copy shown to cold traffic or before the click is a different case the source does not address.
Caveat: Platform formats (short video, display, character-limited ads) constrain this approach; apply it where the medium allows depth.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, product-page, landing-page, ad-copy, conversion-optimization, offer-design
Source: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx

---

## Run static-first creative volume instead of VSLs on Meta
Use when: Deciding how to allocate your creative budget and team time between video and static ad formats for a Meta campaign.
- Accept the source's premise: Andromeda behaves like a 'hungry panda' that needs an absurd volume of fresh creatives before ads fatigue, and producing that volume in video is expensive and slow.
- Recognize Facebook can only serve so many video ads per user session, so the algorithm biases toward statics it can show more of per session; the presenter calls this the main reason his cheap native statics beat a VSL that took 2.5 months to produce.
- Book one hour every week to produce fresh creatives from your winning offer/product; treat this as the core scaling activity, not a side task.
- If you still want video, use proof-of-concept content that already works organically rather than polished productions built from scratch.
- Test the format call yourself rather than assuming: the source's claim that statics 'all day of the week' beat video is the presenter's opinion based on his own account.
Caveat: The claim that Meta structurally biases toward statics is the presenter's interpretation, not a confirmed platform mechanic.
Caveat: His account reportedly runs 17 VSLs simultaneously, so his static preference comes from a context of very high existing video volume.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, creative-strategy, static-ads, meta-ads, scaling, video-ads
Source: Learn 97% of Meta Ads in Under 19 Minutes.docx

---

## Use identity triggers in ad copy instead of backend interest targeting
Use when: Preparing ad copy and targeting for a Meta campaign where you want to reach a specific customer segment without manual interest stacking.
- Find your best winning ad and identify the 20% of clients that represent 80% of revenue; note the niches they operate in.
- Duplicate the winning ad and swap in one of those niches as a keyword: e.g. change '462 leads per week on autopilot' to '462 dental leads,' then repeat with 'lawyer leads,' 'property investment leads,' etc.
- Launch the variants and review CTR; the source claims performance improves markedly and that new audience pockets open up that a generic ad would never reach.
- Explain the mechanism as the presenter does: it is not a magic word but a category/identity word that feeds the algorithm a signal about who to look for, because the creative now functions as the targeting.
- Apply the same idea to demographics: write copy variations for a 25-year-old woman versus a 30-year-old woman so the ad itself carries the targeting context.
Caveat: This is one presenter's observed tactic, not a guarantee; validate CTR and cost per lead against your own control ad.
Caveat: Do not paste niche keywords that misrepresent your offer just to chase a segment.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, targeting, meta-ads, creative-strategy, audience-research, broad-targeting
Source: Learn 97% of Meta Ads in Under 19 Minutes.docx

---

## Clone your winning ad into hundreds of AI-generated variations
Use when: Scaling a proven Meta ad that risks fatiguing, when you need more creative supply from one winning format.
- Do not turn off all non-winning ads and ride a single winner to death; the presenter calls that amateur hour because fatigue kills your only asset.
- Give the winning ad to an LLM (he names Claude or his own tool Kong; verify current interfaces) with the premise: 'write to 100 people and none of them could tell this was written by a different person.'
- Prompt it to rewrite for specific segments, e.g. 'now write this for 25-year-old women' and 'for a 30-year-old woman'; the copy should read almost the same but with details relevant to that person.
- Sequence the work: body copy first, then headlines, then the creative itself.
- Place all variations into a Campaign Budget Optimization (CBO) campaign and let Meta's AI shift spend toward the best performers.
Caveat: The source says CBO cloning has not always been perfect; many ads in the campaign may receive no spend.
Caveat: LLM output must still fit your offer and compliance requirements; a variant that reads differently to a real buyer defeats the premise.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, creative-strategy, meta-ads, cbо, llm-workflow, scaling
Source: Learn 97% of Meta Ads in Under 19 Minutes.docx

---

## Rescue ignored ads with a zombie campaign
Use when: After running a CBO clone campaign, when several creatives you believe in recorded zero or near-zero spend.
- Collect all ads in the CBO campaign that received no spend but that you have high conviction are genuinely good ads.
- Place those dead ads into a separate, isolated ad set — the 'zombie campaign' — and launch it.
- The isolated structure forces delivery on ads the algorithm ignored in the primary campaign, letting you extract additional winners.
- The source reports typically juicing out another 20% of ads that turn out to be winners; treat that as one operator's example, not a benchmark.
- Feed any newly proven winners back into your main scaling structure.
Caveat: This is the presenter's tactic and reported result; your extraction rate will vary with account, budget and creative quality.
Caveat: Only run this for ads you genuinely believe in — it will not turn a weak creative into a winner.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, meta-ads, campaign-structure, cbо, scaling, creative-testing
Source: Learn 97% of Meta Ads in Under 19 Minutes.docx

---

## Make ads that do not look like ads
Use when: Developing acquisition creative for a Meta or TikTok campaign where polished ad-looking assets are underperforming.
- Reject the instinct to make ads 'pop off the feed' and hijack attention; the presenter notes people hate ads and install ad blockers by the hundreds of millions.
- Find what content natively performs in your niche. His example: a 46-minute minimally edited YouTube video with millions of organic views is simply run as a paid ad, because it is already proven.
- If you lack organic hits, create a burner account: set up fresh TikTok and Instagram accounts, follow all influencers and pages in your niche, and like their content so the platform surfaces the niche's most popular content on your feed.
- Use whatever rises to the top of that burner feed as the template for the ads you produce and run.
- The source claims this will outperform your current best-performing ad, which is his assertion, not a guaranteed result.
Caveat: The performance claim is the presenter's opinion based on his accounts; validate with your own holdout or split test.
Caveat: Native-looking creative still must comply with platform ad policies and your claims substantiation.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, creative-strategy, meta-ads, tiktok, native-content, ugc
Source: Learn 97% of Meta Ads in Under 19 Minutes.docx

---

## Test broad targeting against interest stacking with identical creative
Use when: Reviewing Meta targeting strategy when deciding whether to keep layered interest targeting or move to broad audiences.
- Duplicate your best winning creative that currently has interest stacking applied.
- Create a version with no interest targeting — just pick a country such as Australia, the US or the UK — and let it run alongside the stacked version.
- After 7 days, compare CPAs between the interest-stacked ad and the broad ad.
- Treat the underlying principle as the presenter states it: the creative is the targeting now, so more context in the creative lets Meta find the right people, and you should not try to beat Meta's engineers at targeting.
- If broad wins, reinvest the time you spent on backend targeting into producing more creative.
Caveat: The 7-day window is the source's suggested comparison period; small sample sizes can mislead, so check spend and conversion volume before concluding.
Caveat: Broad targeting relies on strong creative context; running broad with a thin, generic ad may not replicate the result.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, meta-ads, targeting, broad-targeting, experiment-design, measurement
Source: Learn 97% of Meta Ads in Under 19 Minutes.docx

---

## Write long-form copy to widen Meta's context window
Use when: Writing ad copy for a broad-targeting Meta campaign where the creative must carry the audience definition.
- Stop relying on short-form, very basic ad copy; the presenter argues this shrinks the context window Meta has about who you want.
- Write long-form copy that explicitly describes the person you are targeting — their situation, role, and the niche keyword signals from your identity triggers.
- Understand the causal chain the source asserts: limited context window for your creative means a limited pool of people Meta can target with it; more context expands the reachable audience.
- Pair this with broad targeting settings so the algorithm does the placement work while the copy does the qualification.
- Judge results on cost per acquisition, not on how polished the copy looks.
Caveat: Long copy is not automatically better; it only helps if it contains genuine, accurate targeting context.
Caveat: This is one operator's framing of how the algorithm uses creative context; validate against your own account data.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, meta-ads, copywriting, broad-targeting, context, targeting
Source: Learn 97% of Meta Ads in Under 19 Minutes.docx

---

## Match your best ad headline to the landing page headline
Use when: Optimizing a landing page or PDP after ads are driving clicks but conversion rate and CPA are poor.
- Compare where effort goes: the source says most advertisers put 90% into ads and only 10% into landing pages, which causes high bounce when the page does not match what was clicked.
- Find your best-performing headline by testing 20, 30 or 40 headline variants within an ad, since Meta exposes headlines to roughly a thousand times the people who click through, giving far more statistically significant data than the landing page.
- Take the winner and mirror it on the landing page headline, subheadline and copy lead-in.
- The presenter reports a minimum 15–20% conversion-rate increase from this alone; treat that as his observed result, not a benchmark.
- Run a standing rule of at least three split tests at any time, mining insights from top ads and applying them to the page.
- Immediate action: open your top 3 ads and put their headlines side by side with the page headline; fix any mismatch within 24 hours.
Caveat: 15–20% is the presenter's personal reported lift, not a guaranteed outcome.
Caveat: Message match helps conversion rate but only for traffic that was already qualified by the ad; it will not fix a weak offer.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, conversion-optimization, landing-page, meta-ads, message-match, experiment-design
Source: Learn 97% of Meta Ads in Under 19 Minutes.docx

---

## Retarget non-buyers with a different offer, not the same one louder
Use when: Building retargeting campaigns for a store or service business with multiple products, to recapture non-converting traffic.
- Accept the premise that the number one reason people do not buy is that the offer or product was not right for them, so re-serving the same ad is futile.
- Identify what each visitor clicked on — e.g. they came in for protein powder because that is the product they engaged with.
- Retarget that audience with a different offer, e.g. creatine. The source describes protein powder at a 2–3x return and the non-buyer retargeting to creatine at around 6x, and says to trust the tactic rather than expect it to make intuitive sense.
- Also use a free high-value content offer as the top-of-funnel; outbound calling every person who downloads it tells you their pains, fears, hopes, dreams and why they did not buy.
- Build retargeting first as an objection-handling ad from those non-buyer reasons, then proof/testimonial carousels, then a CBO of best-performing ads for other products retargeted to the same audience.
Caveat: The 2–3x vs 6x figures are the presenter's illustrated example, not a promised result.
Caveat: Outbound calling every lead is appropriate for his service-style business; ecommerce stores without a call operation should adapt the objection-gathering step to surveys or post-purchase feedback.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, retention, retargeting, offer-design, meta-ads, customer-research
Source: Learn 97% of Meta Ads in Under 19 Minutes.docx

---

## Scale against blended ROAS and net free cash flow, not platform ROAS
Use when: Deciding whether to increase Meta ad budget when the presenter's peers hesitate because reported ROAS or cost per lead has worsened.
- Do not optimize to platform-level ROAS percentages; the presenter reframes the goal as blended ROAS across the whole business, and more importantly net free cash flow.
- Distinguish break-even ROAS, a revenue-to-spend ratio, from allowable CPA, a currency amount per acquisition. Calculate both from the store cost model.
- Test budget increases against allowable acquisition cost, available cash, inventory and a predefined loss limit; the source aggressive scaling stance is a hypothesis, not an instruction to spend without a ceiling.
- Accept compression: the source gives the example that ROAS may fall from 15x to 5x or 10x to 5x, but the point is the absolute net cash generated by spending $100,000 versus $1,000 per month.
- When someone reports ROAS dropping from 15 to 11 or cost per lead rising to $50, ask the reframing question: did you make more money in a 30-day period?
- Block three hours a month to personally review the numbers rather than relying only on an analyst or media buyer.
Caveat: Blended and net free cash flow require accurate, complete accounting; if COGS, fulfillment and refunds are excluded, a break-even ROAS is wrong.
Caveat: Scaling to break-even assumes you can tolerate thin or zero profit per acquisition to buy market share; the presenter's opinion on this may not fit a cash-constrained store.
Caveat: The 40x example is anecdotal.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, unit-economics, roas, scaling, measurement, budgeting
Source: Learn 97% of Meta Ads in Under 19 Minutes.docx

## The Three-Question Copy Test (Visualize / Falsify / Distinct)
Use when: You are writing or reviewing a product title, ad headline, PDP hero line, email subject or landing page hook and need a fast filter before shipping.
- Ask question one: 'Can I visualize it?' Close your eyes and try to picture the words. If nothing concrete appears, the line will not be remembered — cut or rewrite it.
- Ask question two: 'Can I falsify it?' If the claim can only be judged as mush (e.g. 'great quality', 'better way'), it reads as filler. Aim for claims that are plainly true-or-false and can be proven.
- Ask question three: 'Can nobody else say this?' If a rival store could paste your line onto their page unchanged, it is not positioning. Push until the line is bespoke to your product's facts.
- Score: the source treats three 'no' answers as a signal you have written rubbish, and three 'yes' answers as a signal you are onto something. Review the copy line by line, not the whole ad.
- Pair the test with the 'One Mississippi, Two Mississippi' speed check: show the creative to another person and if they don't 'get it' within about two seconds of reading, it is too slow for a feed or billboard context.
- Keep scores as a personal screen, not a published benchmark — the source gives no data on conversion lift from passing the test.
Caveat: A line can be visually concrete and falsifiable yet still irrelevant to purchase motivation; the test screens memorability and ownability, not demand.
Caveat: Source's claim that 'if everyone gets it, you may be doing something wrong' is an opinion. Confusing the out-crowd can also simply lose sales — decide per audience.
Caveat: The two-second read threshold is a presenter's heuristic, not a measured conversion rule.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, copywriting, positioning, creative-strategy, ad-creative, product-page, messaging
Source: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

---

## Abstract-to-Concrete Zoom-In Exercise
Use when: Your product benefits read as adjectives ('effective', 'convenient', 'premium') and you need concrete claims for ads, PDP bullets or category positioning.
- Take a sheet of paper and draw a vertical line down the middle. Write 'abstract' at the top of the left column and 'concrete' at the bottom of the right.
- Write your current vague phrase in the left column (e.g. 'regain fitness', 'pretty people in big cities').
- Ask repeatedly, 'What do I actually mean here?' and rewrite the phrase lower and lower in the right column, converting intangible words into objects, people, places or actions a reader can picture.
- Worked example from the source: 'regain fitness' becomes 'getting people up off the couch to run 5K' — the source notes this is effectively the Couch to 5K naming logic.
- Second worked example: 'worn by pretty people in big cities and old people elsewhere' becomes 'worn by supermodels in London and dads in Ohio' — two picturable people in a funny juxtaposition.
- Use the resulting concrete phrasing directly as product name, headline or PDP bullet candidates, then run the three-question copy test on each.
- Sharpen concrete words further where possible: source critique of a Tesla line suggested preferring 'tougher than an F-150' over 'better truck than an F-150' for shorter, more picturable, more ownable phrasing.
Caveat: Drilling down takes real work and multiple rewrites; the source notes 'you can't just like' produce facts — research is required.
Caveat: Concrete wording can be less searchable or less category-obvious; you may need one concrete emotional line plus one plain functional line on the same PDP.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, copywriting, messaging, product-page, ad-creative, positioning
Source: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

## 'You Can't Talk, Only Point' — Replace Adjectives With Proof
Use when: Your product page or ad is adjective-heavy ('high-quality', 'innovative') and you need provable claims, proof points or image directions.
- Set the constraint: describe the product using only statements that are objectively true or false — no 'good-looking', 'trustworthy', 'premium'.
- Convert each adjective into a pointed fact. Source dating-app example: replace 'intelligent' with 'reads on the tube'; replace 'good-looking' with 'looks like Ryan Gosling, 6 foot 2'.
- For a store context: replace 'durable' with a pointed artifact — a test result, a materials spec, a photo of the seam, a 50-year price chart, or the number of units returned.
- Ask for each claim: which object, image or graph can I physically point at that makes this true? If none exists, the claim is wallpaper and should be cut or researched.
- The source's gold example: instead of saying gold 'never goes out of fashion', point at the 50-year gold price chart, a castle, a family's gold stash, or Warren Buffett's portfolio allocation — then research which pointed fact actually motivates the buyer.
- Translate pointed facts into visual and copy direction on the same PDP or ad unit so text and image reinforce each other.
Caveat: Pointing at facts takes research effort; the source explicitly says it 'takes work — that's why it's better', so budget time before publishing.
Caveat: Some pointed facts are true but unpersuasive ('350 million Americans'); choose facts that carry a story or tension.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, copywriting, proof, product-page, ad-creative, messaging
Source: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx
