## Swipe competitor hooks and re-voice them for your product
Use when: You have product and offer ready but are stuck on ad angles, or you want to test multiple opening hooks for the same PDP/offer without reshooting.
- Build a swipe file: use a platform that lets you filter top-performing TikTok (or cross-platform) videos to find proven hooks — the source used Foreplay, which is a paid tool with other options available.
- Pick a hook whose format is transferable to your category (e.g. 'My For You page convinced me to buy something again, but this one is actually worth the hype' works for almost any physical product).
- Download that video and upload it into your AI video tool as the reference.
- Give the tool a short instruction naming your product: the source's example was simply 'Can you talk about my product Premier Supplements?' — the AI preserved the hook and swapped the product.
- Generate and review: in the source's run, the output reproduced the hook and inserted the presenter's product, at a lower credit cost (~0.4 credits) than a from-scratch render.
- Repeat with multiple hooks against the same product to build a hook-test set for your campaign's creative split test.
- Use this as a hook-testing machine, not a final asset: run the variations as separate ads so platform data tells you which hook wins.
Caveat: The source demonstrates hook copying on a made-up brand; results are illustrative, not a performance promise.
Caveat: Reproducing another brand's script verbatim risks IP/brand issues — use the hook structure with your own claims and verify your product claims are compliant.
Caveat: AI may paraphrase or drop parts of the reference; check the output for accurate product claims.

## Choose the right AI video model for your ad by constraint
Use when: You are generating product or UGC-style ad videos and need to decide which generation model to spend credits on for a given spot length or placement.
- If realism and 'does this look like a real person using the product' are the priority, the source prefers Sora 2 / Sora 2 Pro and reports using it for most ad outputs, using a product image plus a short description.
- If you need an exact duration (every second between ~3s and 15s), use Kling 3.0 — this matters when your spot must hit a defined length for a placement or a multi-scene edit.
- If you need high resolution (up to 4K), V0 3.1 offers that, but the source reports its cinematic, artistic style often doesn't match UGC-ad aesthetics and uses it least for ads.
- For Sora 2, plan around fixed length options (4, 8, or 12 seconds) and 1080p; if your ad concept requires other lengths, either use Kling or extend the clip.
- When prompting, attach a product image so the model renders the actual item, and give a plain-language ad brief (source example prompt: 'make me a UGC ad for a company that sells office chairs').
- Allow for post-editing: the source notes Sora 2 sometimes cuts off the video at an odd angle, requiring trimming after generation.
Caveat: Model availability, resolution and duration limits change quickly — verify current options in the tool before building a production plan.

## Motion control and presets to skip
Use when: You want a scroll-stopping format (person reactivating a product, showing a device in motion) without a shoot, or you are deciding which AI presets are worth spending credits on.
- For motion transfer, upload (1) a reference video containing the motion you want, and (2) a still image of the person you want performing it. The tool transfers the motion onto your image.
- Source example workflow: a clip of a woman dancing was used as the motion reference, and an AI-generated image of a man in an office was the subject; the output made the man perform the same motion.
- Adapt the format to commerce: instead of dancing, capture the motion of holding up a product, demonstrating a device, or reacting to unboxing — the motion source can be any clip.
- This is a lower-priority format: the source says they rarely use it, so treat it as a novelty format to test, not a core creative.
- Avoid the 'unboxing POV' preset for product unboxing ads — the source reports the hands (e.g. crumpling paper) look visibly wrong and it isn't worth the credits.
- Instead, prompt Sora 2 to 'make a video of this being unboxed' when you need unboxing content, and treat that output as the testable version.
Caveat: Motion transfer adds a step and may produce artifacts on hands and props — inspect closely before setting spend.
Caveat: Preset quality changes with model updates; the unboxing-POV warning is a snapshot of the presenter's testing, so re-evaluate periodically.

## Pick the TikTok ad objective that matches your goal (and why Sales is the default)
Use when: You are setting up a new TikTok Ads Manager campaign for a product and need to decide what to optimize the account toward before spending budget.
- Treat the objective list as a funnel: Awareness/Reach sits at the top (max reach, no optimization toward a page view or sale), Consideration (Traffic, Video Views, Community Interactions) sits in the middle, and Conversion (App Promotion, Lead Generation, Sales) sits at the bottom.
- Choose Sales for most ecommerce campaigns, because the goal is a purchase and the algorithm optimizes delivery toward the conversion you've selected.
- Only use Reach when the explicit goal is spreading awareness (e.g. a launch) and you accept poor ROAS on that spend.
- Consider Community Interactions only for growing a profile's engagement/followers, not for driving a product purchase.
- Confirm your TikTok pixel is installed and firing before you optimize toward a purchase — you cannot optimize for a conversion event the pixel isn't reporting.
- Inside Sales, you also choose a destination (TikTok Shop vs Website — manual, Smart+, or search). Expect different available options across objectives: the source notes features like creative split testing are not available for every objective, and placements and billing events can differ per objective.
- Start with the manual website campaign rather than the recommended Smart+ campaign, and treat Smart+ as a parallel test later: the source reports mixed results between the two in their testing.
Caveat: If the pixel isn't set up, the purchase optimization will not function; fix the pixel first.
Caveat: Objective availability, Smart+ recommendations, and per-objective feature sets are TikTok product specifics that change — verify in the current Ads Manager.
Caveat: The 'always use Sales' stance is the presenter's opinion for ecommerce; campaigns with pure awareness goals are a legitimate exception.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, tiktok-ads, campaign-structure, pixel, conversion-optimization, campaign-setup
Source: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

## Manual vs Smart+ campaign and the product catalog setting
Use when: You are configuring a new TikTok Sales campaign and deciding whether to use Smart+, whether to show a product catalog under the video, and how to name campaigns.
- Start with the manual campaign instead of the TikTok-recommended Smart+; the source reports mixed results between them and prefers manual first, then testing Smart+ alongside it.
- Turn the campaign catalog OFF for a first campaign. It pulls images from your product catalog and displays products under the video, which can surface products you didn't intend to promote and add visual clutter. The source keeps it unchecked so only the video and the one product you want are shown.
- Name the campaign by audience purpose — the source uses 'Prospecting' to mark cold-audience campaigns — so you can read performance at a glance.
- Only check the Special Categories box if you are advertising housing, employment, or credit; otherwise leave it.
- Leave Create Split Test unchecked for now unless you have a specific structured test planned.
- Decide campaign budget optimization (CBO) here: leaving it off lets you budget at the ad-group level so each audience gets a predictable share (e.g. $25 each across four ad groups), which is what the source recommends for new accounts.
Caveat: The source expects mixed manual-vs-Smart+ results, so don't assume one is universally superior.
Caveat: The catalog setting may be useful for some use cases (e.g. shops with many SKUs); the recommendation to turn it off is specifically for getting-started campaigns.

## Campaign budget optimization: off for testing, on for scaling
Use when: You are deciding between campaign-level and ad-group-level budget allocation for a TikTok campaign, particularly when comparing broad vs interest audiences.
- Understand the mechanism: with CBO on, you set one budget at the campaign level and TikTok distributes it across ad groups however it favors — e.g. $80/$10/$5/$5 out of four groups — with no control from you.
- With CBO off, set budget at the ad-group level (the source's term: ad group budget optimization) so each ad group receives an even, predictable amount (e.g. $25 each) and audience tests stay clean.
- For new accounts, keep CBO off so you can see which audiences perform and manually move budget toward winners.
- Once you've identified winners, switch to CBO for scaling — the source uses it to direct money toward proven ad groups.
- If CBO is on, the campaign asks for a daily budget; if off, the daily budget field appears at the ad-group level. Set it there.
- Keep the structure shallow: the source generally does not recommend more than four ad groups inside a campaign.
Caveat: The >4-ad-group guidance is a practical heuristic from the presenter's experience, not a platform rule.
Caveat: Switching CBO on re-allocates spend in ways you don't control, so don't use it while you still need clean per-audience comparisons.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, tiktok-ads, campaign-structure, budgeting, campaign-setup, scaling
Source: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

## Budget recommendations for TikTok: CPA multiples vs TikTok's 10x rule
Use when: You are deciding how much daily budget to put behind a new TikTok conversion campaign for a product.
- Know the platform constraint: TikTok requires a $20/day minimum. Attempting less is rejected in the interface.
- Know the platform's recommendation so you can judge it: TikTok suggests 10x your current CPA (e.g. $10 CPA -> $100/day; $40 CPA -> $400/day).
- The source does not like the 10x rule for most advertisers. Instead, budget at 2x your current cost per acquisition: a $10 CPA implies a $20/day budget; a $20 CPA on other platforms implies ~$40/day here.
- If you don't know your CPA, start around $50/day as a test budget.
- If budget forces you to $20/day, proceed but expect a long learning phase.
- Understand the learning phase: performance fluctuates while the system finds the best users, and volatility typically settles after 25 campaign results or seven days. Aim to accumulate the 25 results inside the seven-day window if budget allows.
- Set the start time, keep campaigns running continuously rather than scheduling short flights, keep day-parting on all day, and leave the optional target CPA and attribution windows untouched on a new account.
Caveat: The 25-results/7-day learning phase is TikTok's described mechanism; the source's 2x-CPA budget is their own alternative to TikTok's 10x advice, not a platform rule.
Caveat: The 10x recommendation makes 2x-CPA budgets hard for high-CPA products — expect slower learning if you underfund.
Caveat: Leave target CPA blank until you have real data; setting it without data can constrain delivery.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, tiktok-ads, budgeting, campaign-setup, measurement, cpa

## TikTok cost expectations and the one lever that moves them
Use when: You are setting CPA and ROAS targets for a TikTok ad plan or diagnosing why your costs are above/below plan.
- Use these as rough planning ranges rather than promises: CPM roughly $3–$10 per thousand impressions; CPC roughly $0.17–$1.00; cost per view roughly $0.01–$0.07.
- Expect CPA to vary widely depending on product price, category and many other factors — don't apply a single benchmark across categories.
- Understand the cost drivers the source lists: creative quality of the ad (good UGC-style ads get cheaper CPMs), audience targeting (broader is cheaper), industry competition (beauty supplements are more expensive), and seasonality (Q4 holiday costs rise).
- Treat creative quality as the biggest lever: the source says the better the ad, the cheaper your views, and reports seeing this repeatedly across accounts.
- Apply this to decisions: if CPMs are high, test a new hook (see the hook-repurposing workflow) before expanding targeting or raising budget.
- Plan seasonal buys ahead of Q4 — raise budget expectations rather than assuming the same CPA holds.
Caveat: These ranges are presented as typical, not guaranteed; the source notes having seen both lower and much higher costs, especially on poor ads.
Caveat: CPM/CPC/CPV bands vary by country, currency and account history — treat them as directional.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, tiktok-ads, measurement, cpm, cpa, creative-strategy, budgeting
Source: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

## Audience targeting: start broad, layer interest testing later
Use when: You are configuring TikTok ad-group targeting (demographics, interests, spending power, devices) for a product campaign.
- Start with broad targeting — TikTok itself states broad is best for most advertisers, and the source agrees: with a strong ad, the algorithm finds the right people. The source reports testing this multiple times and finding broad works well.
- For a $20/day budget, use one campaign (Prospecting) with one broad ad group containing three ad creatives. Once a winner emerges, move it to a new campaign and scale.
- For a larger budget, duplicate the ad group and keep identical settings except the audience: one broad vs one interest/behavior, running the same three ads in each, so you can compare audiences on equal footing.
- Keep the same ads in both ad groups: the source duplicated the ad group with its ads so the only variable is targeting.
- For interest targeting, search by category keyword (e.g. 'swimsuit') and add 3–5 relevant interests, purchase intentions, video interactions, creator interactions or hashtags. Ignore 'audience narrow' warnings if the reach figure is healthy — the source's example showed ~7 million people while still flagged as narrow.
- Leave spending power on 'All' unless you sell luxury. The source tested narrowing to high spenders and found it limits delivery without improving results.
- Leave household income on 'All' — the source doubts the platform knows true household income well. Leave devices on all, and leave placements automatic, then check placement data later; TikTok placement is generally the strongest performer.
Caveat: Broad vs interest is presented as a budget-dependent test, not a universal rule — the source also admits a personal bias toward granular targeting that the algorithm tends to beat.
Caveat: Interest targeting significantly narrows reach; only worth it if you have the budget to run proper ($20/day per ad group) comparisons.
Caveat: Demographic filters like spending power are the presenter's tested opinion, not platform-verified performance data.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, tiktok-ads, targeting, campaign-structure, audience-research, campaign-setup
Source: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

## Build one ad group, then duplicate it for multiple audiences
Use when: You are structuring a TikTok campaign that needs separate broad and interest (or demographic) ad groups using the same creative set.
- Create one ad group and build all the ads (3–5 creative) inside it first — if you plan to run 3–5 ads, creating them before duplication saves you recreating them in each copy.
- Create the ad group with a temporary name, then name it after targeting is set (e.g. 'broad USA' with language, age, gender adjustments as needed).
- Publish, then go to the ad-group level in the campaign view and use Duplicate -> duplicate the ad group into the existing campaign.
- In the duplicate, change only the audience: add interest/behavior targeting (e.g. swimsuit-related interests), then rename to something like 'interest USA' so broad vs interest is unambiguous in reporting.
- Keep all other settings identical between the two ad groups so the audience is the only variable.
- To add more creatives later, duplicate the ad inside the ad group and use the update button on the copy to swap in a different video or TikTok post.
- Keep at most ~4 ad groups per campaign as a working guideline.
Caveat: Duplicating before all creatives are built forces you to update each copy manually — build ads first.
Caveat: Parallel ad groups each need their own minimum daily budget (~$20/day in the source's examples), so this structure multiplies spend.

- Uncheck the option that places your ad in the TikTok ad library — the source stresses keeping this unchecked so your ads do not appear in the library.
- Publish all, then duplicate the ad if you want additional creative variations inside the ad group.

## Keyword research for TikTok search ads with the Keyword Planner
Use when: You want to run TikTok search ads (users typing queries inside TikTok) for a product and need a keyword list with realistic CPC and volume expectations.
- In TikTok Ads Manager, go to Tools -> Keyword Planner (verify current menu location, as platform UI changes).
- Enter your product or category (e.g. 'swimsuits'), set the target area (e.g. United States), and run Discover.
- Read the output columns: keyword, average monthly searches, three-month change, year-over-year change, competition level, and estimated low/high CPC.
- Filter by low competition first and add any relevant terms — the source finds cheaper average clicks on low-competition terms, though volume is smaller and many results may be irrelevant or in other languages.
- Then re-run with all competition levels, sort by monthly search volume, and add the relevant high-volume terms.
- Aim for roughly 20–50 keywords. Source example: this produced ~52,000 total monthly search volume, which they judged enough to build a campaign on.
- Save the plan with a specific name (e.g. 'swimsuits') — saving is required so you can pull the list into the campaign later.
- Use this research to sanity-check whether search ads are worth running for the product at all: if volume is negligible, skip the campaign.
Caveat: Keyword Planner data is directional; the source notes some results were irrelevant (other languages, unrelated terms) and had to be filtered manually.
Caveat: The 20–50 keyword / 52k volume example is the presenter's working heuristic, not a validated threshold.
Caveat: Tool location and columns can change; check the current interface.

## Build a TikTok search campaign and pick match types
Use when: You are launching a TikTok search ad campaign targeting people actively searching for your product terms.
- Create a new campaign with the Sales objective and select the search campaign type (instead of manual or Smart+). Reference your saved keyword plan.
- Reuse your pixel and conversion settings: website destination, conversion event = purchase. Leave target CPA blank if you don't know it.
- Load your keywords from the saved keyword plan. If you skip pre-research, you can search inside the campaign, but the source finds the in-campaign view gives fewer options — do the research beforehand.
- Understand the three match types: broad maximizes reach by matching relevant searches; phrase shows ads on searches with the same meaning as your keyword; exact shows ads only for searches containing your exact phrase in order and limits reach most.
- The source's default: start with phrase match as the middle ground — you'll appear for related terms like 'modest swimwear' but not wildly unrelated queries.
- If you must only appear for specific terms (e.g. black swimsuit or red swimsuit), use exact match and separate ad groups per keyword theme, accepting reduced reach.
- Turn automated keywords OFF at launch so you know exactly what your ads show up for; the source treats it as an optional later test.
- Set daily budget (minimum $20), start/end times, US + 18+ demographics as appropriate, and note placements are limited to TikTok search results for this campaign type. Allow user comments. Build the ad with a destination URL and a video or spark post, then publish.
Caveat: Exact match will meaningfully cut reach; only use when a term is high-volume and highly relevant.
Caveat: Automated keywords can be tested later, but at launch the source prefers full control over query matching.
Caveat: Search campaign placement is constrained to search results — this is not a feed placement.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, tiktok-ads, search-ads, keyword-research, campaign-setup, match-types
Source: The BEST TikTok Ads Course For Beginners in 2026.docx

## Mine the search term report and add negative keywords
Use when: You have a TikTok search campaign running and need to protect spend from irrelevant queries that don't match product intent.
- Click into the search campaign, go to the ad group level, and open View Data.
- Open the Search tab to see the search term report — the actual queries your ads were shown against.
- Review the list closely, as the source recommends doing this after a couple of days of running, to confirm you're showing up for terms that match your brand and product.
- Where you see irrelevant queries, use the report's option to add them as negative keywords so your ad no longer appears for them.
- Repeat this review periodically — it is described as very important when running search campaigns, because broad/phrase matching will pull in tangents over time.
- If you have keyword-specific product angles (e.g. black swimsuit vs red swimsuit), use this data to decide whether to split them into separate ad groups with their own creative.
Caveat: Search term reports need volume before they're informative; the source suggests checking after a couple of days, not immediately at launch.
Caveat: Match type changes (e.g. switching broad to phrase) affect the quality of the terms you'll later need to exclude.

## Spark ads: requirements and the organic-first six-step workflow
Use when: You want to amplify organic TikTok content (your own or a creator's) as a paid ad rather than treating paid and organic as separate tracks.
- Confirm the prerequisites: a TikTok Ads account (set up in the course), a TikTok profile if the Spark ad runs from your own account, and the profile linked to the ads account. If using influencers, obtain an ad authorization code from them (optional but required for creator posts).
- Step 1 — create three or more videos yourself or have influencers create them.
- Step 2 — post them to your TikTok account, or have influencers post to theirs.
- Step 3 — wait five to seven days for the post to reach its full organic potential; roughly a week is the typical life cycle of a new TikTok post, and you can usually tell within the first two days whether it's starting to get organic traction.
- Step 4 onward — do not step in immediately: the source's rationale is that you don't want to spend ad budget amplifying a post that can still earn free organic impressions.
- After the organic window, run the winning posts as Spark ads to scale the reach that already proved itself.
- Two ways to run them: boost one of your own existing posts, or boost a creator's post using their authorization code.
Caveat: The 5–7 day wait is the presenter's tested workflow, not a platform requirement; faster campaigns can still boost earlier.
Caveat: You must have the profile-to-ad-account link and, for creators, an authorization code — without them the Spark ad can't be created.
Caveat: This is a lead-in to paid amplification and the source covers the full Spark ad build in a later module; verify current linking and authorization steps in Ads Manager.

## Test TikTok creative organically before spending ad budget
Use when: You are planning TikTok acquisition creative for a store and deciding which videos deserve paid spend versus which should be left to run free.
- Produce three or more videos at a time, either in-house or by briefing influencers, so you always have a batch to compare rather than judging a single creative.
- Post them to your own TikTok account, or have the influencers post to theirs, so organic performance data accumulates.
- Wait five to seven days before deciding. The presenter's reasoning is that new TikTok posts typically see organic traffic concentrated in the first couple of days and roughly a week-long life cycle — you don't want to pay to reach people who would have seen it free.
- After the wait, judge each video on the results it produced: sales attributed to that post, follows, and engagement. The presenter's own example shows three influencer videos at 2.3M, 15K and 8M organic views — pick the clear performer to amplify. In a second example the differentiator was engagement, not raw views.
- Run the one or two winners as Spark Ads, then repeat the cycle with a new batch. The loop scales: post 20 videos and take the top 10-30% as ads instead of three.
- Expect the creative selection to be the main lever — in the presenter's account, 400+ SKUs and multiple videos existed, but only the organic winners were worth paying to distribute.
Caveat: The 5-7 day wait and the 'first two days' signal are the presenter's observations about typical TikTok behavior, not guaranteed benchmarks; verify against your own account's data.
Caveat: View counts and engagement are proxies — the presenter also references sales and follows as selection criteria, so prefer whichever metric maps to your objective.

## Run an influencer's video as a Spark Ad using an ad authorization code
Use when: An influencer posted a video with your product and you want to amplify it with paid spend as a Spark Ad from their handle.

- Tell them to set the authorization duration to 365 days (the presenter's recommendation) so you can run the ad as long as possible.
- Once authorized and saved, they generate an ad authorization code, tap manage code and copy it, then send you the code.

- Set the destination URL so traffic goes to the page you want, even though the ad runs from the influencer's profile.

## Why Spark Ads engagement accrues to the organic post
Use when: You are deciding whether to run creator content as a Spark Ad versus a standalone ad creative, and want to understand the compounding effect on the original post.
- Recognize that engagement generated by the paid ad — likes and comments — also shows on the organic post, so the ad and the organic asset reinforce each other.
- Plan creative selection around posts that already show strong engagement, since paid amplification adds to rather than replaces that interaction profile.
- Because the ad runs from the creator's handle, evaluate whether their profile credibility and audience fit the product before committing budget.
- Use the editable destination URL to route paid traffic to the page you control, separating 'who it appears from' (creator) from 'where it lands' (your store).
- Budget the creator relationship around long authorization windows (the presenter suggests 365 days) so the compounding engagement keeps benefiting a single asset.
- Treat Spark Ads as one asset with two distribution layers — organic reach first, paid amplification second — rather than two separate creative lines to manage.
Caveat: The presenter's example mixes co-marketing with a partner profile, so results depend on the creator's existing audience and posting cadence. None of the view or engagement figures in the source are benchmarks.

## Sync your Shopify catalog into TikTok Shop
Use when: You are launching a TikTok Shop and want product listings, pricing and stock to flow from your existing ecommerce catalog rather than manual entry.

- Inside Shopify, click set up on the 'start selling on TikTok' option, then connect to your Seller Center shop account.

- Check listing quality and drive each listing from 'fair' to the highest status, using TikTok's improve-listing-quality checklist for anything below 'good'.

## Structure open and target affiliate collaborations with commission tiers
Use when: You want to recruit TikTok creators to post tagged videos for your products without paying upfront for content that doesn't sell.
- Set up an open collaboration where the creator earns a commission (the presenter uses 20% as an example) only when they actually drive a sale — you pay nothing extra otherwise.
- Decide whether the offer includes free products or a request flow, and whether samples are free or refundable.
- Control sample requests: they arrive as requests you approve or reject, so a creator can't simply pull samples.
- Set thresholds so only qualified creators can request samples — for example a minimum follower count (the presenter cites 10,000) or a minimum revenue driven (e.g. $100, $1,000, $10,000).
- For target collaborations, send a batch invitation with a name, validity dates, contact details, a message, and the specific products.
- Assign each handpicked creator a custom commission rate and optionally a flat fee; you can vary rates per creator (e.g. 24% vs 25%).
- Add a separate shop ads commission rate that pays the creator when their content is amplified as a paid ad. The presenter recommends setting it lower than the standard rate (he cites around 5%) because you're adding ad spend on top.
Caveat: Commission percentages and thresholds in the source are illustrative, not universal rules — set them from your own margin.
Caveat: When reviewing sample requests, the source shows creators with attributes like post rate and 30-day GMV; those are creator-specific data points, not proof of future performance.

## Set up a GMV Max campaign that sells inside TikTok
Use when: You have a TikTok Shop with tagged creator videos and want paid distribution that drives direct in-app purchases.
- Enter via the campaigns flow: sales objective → TikTok Shop destination → continue to GMV Max, or use the GMV Max tab directly.
- Select the shop from the dropdown when creating a campaign. If it doesn't appear, link the Shop to your Business Center first.
- Choose promote products or promote live. For a new account, the presenter recommends not promoting all products — start with your top sellers.
- Note the constraint: you can only run one GMV Max campaign per product, so a single campaign covering many products limits future flexibility. The presenter's default is to take the top 20% of products (using historical order data to rank) into one campaign. If you have no sales history, you must estimate the top products yourself.
- Set product ROI. TikTok suggests a target (the source shows 1.2, which the presenter notes is often below break-even for ecommerce). The presenter takes TikTok's recommendation and adds 1.0 to it (1.2 → 2.2), then watches impressions over the next few days and lowers it if nothing is delivering. Setting ROI too high can stop ads from showing at all.
- Set the daily budget at roughly double your target cost per acquisition (the example: $30 target CPA → $60/day). TikTok will always push for more spend than you set.
- Adjust special promotion days: left at defaults, TikTok can raise budget by 50% and multiply it up to 10x, which turned a $60 budget into a $360 maximum in the example. The presenter narrows it to 50% with a 1x limit, keeping the setting on for genuine holiday demand.
- For ad creative, the presenter recommends leaving auto-select on so TikTok rapidly tests incoming tagged videos, pauses underperformers and amplifies better-ROI ones. You can instead manage specific authorized posts, affiliate posts, custom posts or uploaded videos.
Caveat: The 'add 1.0 to TikTok's recommended ROI' and 'double target CPA' rules are the presenter's heuristics, not verified benchmarks.
Caveat: The one-campaign-per-product limit is a structural constraint that shapes how you group products.
Caveat: Auto-select means TikTok chooses creative; you trade control for automated testing.

## Monitor GMV Max creative performance and boost winning ads
Use when: Your GMV Max campaign is live and you need to see which tagged videos are actually running and where to add incremental spend.
- Open the campaign analytics and find the product list with availability, then use view creative to see the videos attached to each product and their statuses.
- Interpret statuses: in queue (ready to be tested for conversion potential), learning phase, delivering, and not delivering (tested and no longer producing results, so TikTok pauses it automatically). All of this happens without manual intervention.
- When a video is delivering strong return, apply a creative boost by clicking that ad and requesting a daily boost of at least $10/day, with an optional end date.
- Account for the boost stacking on top of campaign spend — a $60/day campaign plus a $10 boost becomes a $70/day maximum.
- Use the creatives view to see how many creators are producing videos and each creator's gross revenue contribution, so you can identify which creators and individual ads deserve their own dedicated campaign.
- Take repeatedly winning videos and run them in their own GMV Max campaign where the one-campaign-per-product rule permits.
Caveat: Creative boost minimum is $10/day and is additional to campaign budget — do not treat it as a reallocation.

## Build retargeting audiences from website, engagement and shop activity
Use when: You want to run TikTok remarketing to store visitors, content engagers or shop visitors and need to define the right audience rules.
- Make sure your TikTok pixel is installed and linked to the ad account before building audiences.
- In Ads Manager, go to tools → audience manager → create audiences, and choose custom audience.
- For website traffic audiences, define the action (page view, add to cart, initiate checkout, purchase) and select the pixel source. You can add a URL-contains rule so only a specific page type qualifies — for example the presenter references targeting pages containing 'product' to reach product-page visitors.
- Add an exclusion for purchasers: exclude users who completed a purchase in the last 30 days from a site-visitor audience, so you don't pay to re-reach customers you already converted.
- Keep auto-refresh on so the audience is refreshed periodically (the presenter references a 30-day refresh).
- Leave off the option to expand the audience with machine-learning-identified users — the presenter prefers knowing he is actually remarketing, arguing that adding lookalike-style expansion defeats the purpose and is no different from broad targeting.
- Expect a delay before the audience is usable — initially it shows as unavailable and typically takes around 24 hours to match.
- Build lookalike audiences from a strong source, ideally a purchasers-based custom audience, choosing a narrow/balanced/broad option (the presenter usually picks balanced) and setting the target location.
Caveat: Auto-refresh interval and the 24-hour match time are the source's observations; platform behavior may vary.
Caveat: The choice to leave off audience expansion is the presenter's opinion and a trade-off, not a universal best practice — expanding may increase reach.

## Run TikTok retargeting campaigns with budget-tiered audience structure

## Performance-Based Shopping Structure by ROAS Tiers
Use when: Setting up or restructuring Standard Shopping campaigns for a store where product-level profit margins are within about 10% of each other.
- Confirm this structure applies: the source recommends it when profit margins are similar across products (within roughly 10% at product level). If margins vary widely, use the gross-profit-margin structure instead.
- Tier 1 — high-ROAS products: allocate more budget to scale winners.
- Tier 2 — low-ROAS products currently getting spend but converting poorly: reduce bids to improve efficiency.
- Tier 3 — low-spend products with insufficient data: give them more opportunity to accumulate data and prove themselves.
- Tier 4 — 'zombie' products with zero spend that have never been tested: isolate into their own campaign with a dedicated budget to revive potential hidden gems.
- Build these as separate campaigns so each tier has its own budget and bidding control rather than relying on a single algorithm-managed pool.
- Feed the tier assignments from your historical ROAS and spend data, and revisit the tiers as new data arrives.
Caveat: Tier classification depends on having enough historical spend/conversion data; new products may sit in Tier 3 by default.
Caveat: The four-tier labels and the ~10% margin-similarity threshold are the source's heuristics, not universal rules.

## Gross Profit Margin Shopping Structure When Margins Vary
Use when: Structuring Standard Shopping campaigns for a catalog where product-level margins vary significantly (the source cites roughly 30% to 70% as an example range).
- Segment products into margin tiers — the source typically uses three to five tiers depending on catalog size and conversion volume. A simple version uses high, mid, and low margin.
- Build a separate campaign per margin tier so you can assign distinct ROAS targets.
- For high-margin products, set a lower ROAS target so you can bid more aggressively and capture more volume — even at lower ROAS you remain profitable because the margin is high.
- For low-margin products, set a higher ROAS target to stay conservative, since there is less room for error and less profit per sale.
- Remember the underlying insight: PMax does not know your product margins and treats every product the same, so this margin-aware structure is something only you can impose.
- Review margin tiers periodically as supplier costs or pricing change, since the structure's value depends on accurate margin data.
Caveat: The 30-70% margin range is an illustrative example, not a benchmark.
Caveat: Three-to-five tiers is a starting heuristic; too few products or conversions per tier weakens the approach.

## Separate Brand and Non-Brand Search Campaigns
Use when: Restructuring Google Search campaigns to reveal true incremental acquisition and avoid PMax's tendency to over-index on branded traffic.
- Create separate campaigns for brand queries (searches for your company/brand name) and non-brand queries. PMax does not separate these by default, which the source says leads it to over-rely on branded traffic.
- Recognize that brand traffic is less incremental: those searchers already know you and likely first arrived via another channel, so a brand click-to-purchase is often a sale you would have gotten anyway.
- Set a much higher ROAS target for the brand campaign because brand converts more easily and is less incremental; set a lower ROAS target for non-brand because those sales are more incremental.
- Use the separated reporting to view brand ROAS and non-brand ROAS as distinct numbers, then control the brand vs non-brand budget split — shift budget to non-brand if you are over-indexed on brand.
- Build a dedicated strategy to grow non-brand keyword presence, which the source identifies as where real business growth comes from.
- Note that the source still sees value in bidding on brand in Google, but with much higher ROAS expectations.
Caveat: Brand and non-brand ROAS targets will differ substantially; the source does not provide universal numbers.
Caveat: The claim that branded sales are usually non-incremental is the presenter's view and may vary by business.

## The PMax ROAS-Floor Hack: Keep PMax as a De-Prioritized Safety Net
Use when: After building Standard Shopping, Search, and Demand Gen campaigns, deciding what to do with the existing Performance Max campaign.
- Do not pause or delete PMax — keep it active but de-prioritized.
- Set PMax's ROAS target significantly higher than your new manual campaigns. The source's example: if manual campaigns run around 300-400% average ROAS target, set PMax to 600% or even 700%.
- Understand the mechanism: lower ROAS targets in manual campaigns translate to higher CPC bids, so Google prioritizes those campaigns and they win more auctions, getting the lion's share of impressions and clicks.
- Let PMax act as the catch-all: it picks up search queries your Search campaigns did not cover or audiences your Demand Gen campaigns missed.
- Monitor that PMax is genuinely de-prioritized rather than still dominant, and adjust the target gap if it keeps taking meaningful volume.
- Treat the 300-400 vs 600-700 numbers as an illustrative starting ratio, not a required setting.
Caveat: This is the source's described hack, not a documented platform feature or guarantee.
Caveat: ROAS targets must be meaningful in your own account's economics; the example numbers may be inappropriate for low-margin catalogs.
Caveat: Behavior of platform bidding and target semantics can change; verify current mechanics before relying on the effect.

## Set Different ROAS Targets for Incremental vs Non-Incremental Traffic
Use when: Setting campaign-level ROAS targets or evaluating whether reported Google Ads ROAS represents genuine new-customer growth for an ecommerce store.

- Set aggressive (higher) ROAS targets on high-intent branded traffic.
- Set lower ROAS targets on non-brand acquisition to allow more aggressive bidding for incremental growth.
- Interpret blended or PMax-reported ROAS with caution: the source warns that strong ROAS can hide an over-reliance on retargeting and branded traffic that was already in the funnel.
- Judge success by whether non-brand/incremental volume grows, not only by the headline ROAS figure.
- Keep brand and non-brand reporting separated wherever possible so you can apply and monitor the distinct targets.

## The Rule of One: Anchor Each Ad and Landing Page to a Single Big Idea
Use when: Deciding the core message for a paid social ad, landing page, advertorial, or PDP before briefing creative or writing copy.
- Before writing, select one big idea to be the 'tip of the spear' for the ad or page. Everything else is subordinate to it.
- Apply Masterson's three tests to the candidate idea: it must be easy to understand, easy to believe, and interesting or unique. If it fails any test, keep hunting.
- Strip out competing selling points. Masterson calls stacked, unrelated claims 'tossed salad copy' — throwing many selling points in hoping one sticks, which dilutes conversion power.
- Make all sub-bullets, arguments, facts, and stories serve only to reinforce the single concept. A 'six morning strategies' list works only if all six are sub-points of one core benefit; if each is unrelated, it is a tossed salad.
- Review your best-converting ads and check whether they share simplicity, directness, and clarity — use them as evidence for how narrow your message should be.
- Recognize the hard part is choosing the one idea, not writing the copy. The writing gets simpler once the single idea is fixed.
Caveat: The 91-of-100 claim comes from Masterson's review of top historical offers and is the source's evidence, not a guaranteed outcome at your scale.
Caveat: The presenter's opinion that the best-converting ads are 'the ones that do best are the simplest' is a personal observation, not a universal rule.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, creative-strategy, messaging-and-positioning, offer-design, landing-page, paid-social, unique-selling-proposition
Source: The Copy Rule I Learned From The Best Copywriter I Know.docx

## Audit Ad and Page Copy for 'Tossed Salad' Clutter
Use when: Reviewing an underperforming ad, landing page, or advertorial that has accumulated multiple selling points over iterations.
- Read the creative or page and list every distinct selling point, claim, and benefit that appears.
- Flag any point that is not a sub-point of the same core idea — those are the tossed-salad elements.
- Identify which single point is easiest to understand, easiest to believe, and most unique. That becomes the candidate big idea.
- Rewrite remaining sub-bullets, stories, facts, and arguments so each one reinforces that one concept rather than introducing a new angle.
- If a strong sub-point cannot be made to reinforce the core idea, cut it; do not keep it 'just in case'.
- Re-read the final message and check that a stranger could state its one argument back in a sentence.
Caveat: Cutting compelling-but-off-topic points is uncomfortable; the source frames that discomfort as the forcing function that improves selection.
Caveat: This is a messaging framework, not a testing protocol — validate any rewrite with your own ad or page tests.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, creative-strategy, messaging-and-positioning, conversion-optimization, landing-page, paid-social
Source: The Copy Rule I Learned From The Best Copywriter I Know.docx

## Use the Rule of One to Force a Single USP
Use when: Defining or revising the unique selling proposition for a product launch, brand campaign, or product page.
- Gather every plausible selling proposition you have for the product or offer.
- Apply Masterson's three criteria as a filter: easy to understand, easy to believe, counterintuitive or unique.
- Select one proposition as the anchor. The source is explicit that you want one core selling proposition, not 19.
- Position that proposition as the central claim of the ad, landing page, and any supporting advertorial.
- Check that the proposition is believable — a counterintuitive claim that is not credible will not move buyers.
- Use the selected USP to decide which supporting proof, testimonials, and facts belong on the page, and which to drop.
Caveat: The source presents this as Masterson's framework rather than a tested rule; results depend on product and audience.
Caveat: Uniqueness that isn't believable fails the framework's own test — don't chase novelty alone.

## Build Three Custom Audiences, Then Lookalikes Instead of Direct Retargeting
Use when: You have a Shopify store with pixel traffic, video views or customer data and want to build TikTok audiences for prospecting campaigns.
- In Tools > Audience Manager, click Create Audience > Custom Audience.
- Build three seed audiences: (1) web traffic page views in the last 180 days, (2) engagement audience of people who completed your videos in the last 30 days (100% watch), and (3) an uploaded customer CSV.
- Name them clearly, such as '180 days web visitors', '30 days video views' and 'customer file'.
- Do not target these seeds directly; instead click Create Lookalike Audience and select each custom audience as the source.
- Set the lookalike location to the country you are targeting and generally use the 'balanced' setting for large markets like the U.S.; use broad for small markets such as Finland to keep the pool large enough to spend.
- In the ad group, add the lookalike audience under Include Audience to tell TikTok to find more people similar to your seed.
- Verify current audience manager options, as retention windows and lookalike settings are interface-dependent.
Caveat: Retention windows and lookalike expansion options are platform-specific and can change; the 180-day and 30-day windows are the presenter's recommendations.
Caveat: If seed audiences are very small, lookalikes may be ineffective.

## Keep Interest Targeting to Two or Three Broad Parent Categories
Use when: You are setting interest targeting for a TikTok conversion ad group and are tempted to stack many detailed interests.
- Select no more than two to three broad, related interests, such as 'fashion and accessories' for an apparel store.
- Choose parent categories rather than drilling into many sub-interests, so TikTok's algorithm can identify buyers.
- Use the source's example as orientation: a fashion brand started with over 15 detailed interests and saw cost per result above $100 consistently; after stripping down to one broad fashion category, the source reports CPA dropped to 34–41 (currency unit not specified).
- Treat this as a case study, not a promise; your category, price point and creative quality affect results.
- Pair with behavioral targeting sparingly; the source generally uses only one behavior setting such as iOS 8 and above.

## Use a Four-Week Targeting Ladder to Refine Audiences Without Overspending
Use when: You are launching or scaling a TikTok campaign and want a structured sequence for audience refinement instead of guessing all targeting at once.
- Week 1: run broad targeting with only location and basic age range.
- Week 2: add one basic interest category that matches the product niche.
- Week 3: introduce lookalike audiences built from your custom audience seeds (see the custom/lookalike card).
- Week 4: stack winning audiences that performed in earlier weeks, combining lookalikes and proven interests.
- Keep budget at the ad group level so each week's tests remain independently readable.
- Use the weekly data to decide whether to keep, refine or kill audience configurations rather than making all changes at once.
Caveat: The ladder is the presenter's current recommendation; the optimal pace depends on spend volume and how quickly your ad groups accumulate enough impressions.
Caveat: Do not stack audiences before you have enough spend to learn from each testing layer.

- Test the same creatives against different audiences, because the source reports some creatives bomb with cold traffic but perform well with warm traffic.
- Use the winning hooks, angles and CTAs to build the next round of variations rather than changing everything at once.

## Structure a 3:2:1 Test: Three Creatives, Two Audiences, One Objective
Use when: You are launching a first paid test for a store and need a concrete test plan with budget, duration and audience options.
- Set the objective to a single clear conversion goal, such as web conversions or complete payment.
- Allocate at least $50 per ad group per day for three to four days, giving a total test budget around $300–400.
- Creative one: pain-solution video with the pain point as hook, a demo of the solution and a clear CTA.
- Creative two: tutorial-style video with a how-to format, feature highlights and an educational angle.
- Creative three: UGC testimonial with real results, before-and-after and an authentic feel.
- Audience one: broad interest-based targeting using one or two relevant interests, no age restriction or demographic narrowing.
- Audience two: lookalike audience based on purchases, narrowed to top markets such as the U.S. or U.K., with no extra restrictions.
- Use distinct styles so the test has clear winners and losers rather than marginal differences.
Caveat: The 3:2:1 structure and $300–400 budget are the presenter's recommended test; smaller stores may need to run shorter or lower-budget tests.
Caveat: The source says this framework generated over eight figures in sales for their clients; treat as a case example, not a guarantee.

## Check Core TikTok Metrics in the First 24–72 Hours
Use when: You have launched a TikTok ad group and need a fast, structured read on whether to fix, kill or scale it.
- Within the first 24 hours, check that CTR is above 1%, watch time is above 25% and CPM is under $15.
- After three days, look for CPC under $2, add-to-cart cost below $10 and purchase cost under $30.
- If CTR is below 1% within 24 hours, treat it as a creative problem and produce a stronger hook or transitions.
- If CPM is above $20, treat it as an audience problem and adjust targeting.
- If watch time is below 20%, treat the hook as insufficient and create variations of the first three seconds.
- Kill the bottom 50% of ads after three days and double down on the winners with new variations.
- Do not optimize any ad before spending at least $50 or reaching 1,000 impressions, because the data is not yet meaningful.
- Verify current metric benchmarks, as the presenter's thresholds are TikTok-specific snapshots and may vary by market and product.
Caveat: These thresholds (CTR >1%, watch time >25%, CPM <$15, CPC <$2, ATC <$10, purchase <$30) are the presenter's current heuristics, not universal benchmarks.
Caveat: The $50 or 1,000-impression minimum is the source's stated floor for statistical significance; it does not guarantee a reliable read.

## Use the Diagnostic Checklist to Separate Creative Problems from Audience Problems
Use when: A TikTok ad group is underperforming and you need to decide whether to change the creative or the targeting before spending more.
- If CTR is low (below 1% in the first 24 hours), replace the creative with a stronger hook and better transitions rather than changing audiences first.
- If CPM is high (above $20), adjust audience targeting and broaden or refine the audience setup; do not assume the creative is the sole cause.
- If watch time is low (below 20%), remake the first three seconds specifically rather than overhauling the whole video.
- Continue to check each metric independently within the first 24–72 hours, since multiple issues can coexist.
- After three days, if the ad group is still weak, kill the bottom 50% and reinvest into winners instead of repeatedly patching failing creative.
- Verify current platform reporting, as metric windows and definitions can change.
Caveat: The thresholds are the presenter's stated TikTok benchmarks; different categories and markets may perform differently.
Caveat: A low CTR can also result from poor product-market fit or a mismatched landing page, which the diagnostic does not cover.

## Use Native Video Formats and the Five Highest-Converting Hook Patterns

## Follow the 0–35 Second Ad Structure and Technical Specs
Use when: You are scripting and producing a TikTok ad for a store and want a concrete structure and export settings.
- Structure the first 0–3 seconds as the hook.
- Use 3–15 seconds for the core promise or problem.
- Use 15–30 seconds for proof and demonstration.
- Use the final 30–35 seconds for the call to action.
- Layer pattern interrupts every two seconds, text overlays for silent viewers and multiple micro-CTAs throughout the video.
- Use emotional triggers such as before/after, transformations or validations.
- Export at 9:16 aspect ratio (1080 x 1920), keep the file under 500 MB, and aim for a video length of 15–30 seconds; the source says their sweet spot is around 32 seconds.
- Keep cuts every two to three seconds, use trending sounds from TikTok's library where appropriate, keep background music at most 80% volume and voiceover at -3 dB, and add captions for accessibility.
Caveat: The 'sweet spot' length of 32 seconds is the presenter's finding, not a universal rule.
Caveat: Technical specs such as 1080 x 1920, codec and file size may change; confirm current TikTok upload requirements.
Caveat: Trending sounds for ads may have commercial-use restrictions; the source later notes using commercial music in CapCut for ads.

## Build a High-Retention Ad with an Undeniable Hook and Rhythmic Editing
Use when: You are editing a TikTok ad for a store and want to increase watch time and rewatch rate through pacing and payoff structure.
- Open with a hook that implies a clear 'what's in it for me', such as revealing an underrated resource or tool.
- Keep the hook short—around two seconds—and deliver on its promise quickly so viewers feel rewarded.
- Cut clips at varied lengths (some 3 seconds, some half a second) to create rhythm and avoid monotony.
- Vary the audio and visual cadence: alternate speaking and silence, zoom in and out, and accelerate clips to create fast-to-slow pacing.
- End by delivering the promised payoff, such as showing the actual tool or result.
- If retention is the priority, test ads without a spoken call to action; the source says CTAs can damage retention and rewatch rate, and TikTok automatically adds a clickable button.
- Verify current features, as automatic ad buttons and retention metrics are platform-dependent.
- Note: the 30M views, 2.3M likes and 7% CTR are specific results from the source's client, not a guarantee.
Caveat: The recommendation to omit a verbal CTA is the presenter's opinion based on retention metrics; it may not apply to every product or campaign objective.
Caveat: Retention is one factor among many; conversion still depends on offer, landing page and product fit.

## Edit UGC-Style TikTok Ads in CapCut with the Agency Formula
Use when: You are producing TikTok ad creative in-house and need a repeatable editing workflow with specific settings.
- Film clips with natural window light, a clean background, phone held vertically, in 3–5 second segments and from multiple angles.
- In CapCut, create a project, drag in raw clips and click Adapt to convert everything to 9:16 vertical format.
- Apply the 4K filter across the entire timeline as the base effect for UGC-style ads.
- Trim the first clip to a maximum of three seconds and make it the strongest hook.
- Add text over the hook clip using a readable font such as Gilroy Semi Bold or your brand font; adjust tracking tighter, position the text just above eye level and add a subtle stroke or outline if visibility is poor.
- Apply a typewriter text animation to the hook text as a small pattern interrupt.
- Add background music from CapCut's commercial music section—not TikTok sounds—to keep usage commercially safe; lower music to 70% if using a voiceover.
- Export at 1080p, H.264, MP4, 60 fps and recommended bit rate. Always preview on a phone before uploading.
- Structure the ad as hook, problem, solution, call to action and ensure text and pacing reflect that sequence.
Caveat: CapCut's interface, filter names and export settings may change; verify the current app version.
Caveat: The source recommends CapCut because it is free and TikTok-owned, but other editors can produce equivalent results.
Caveat: Commercial music availability and licensing terms can change.

## Meta CPM inflation and the efficiency trade-off
Use when: Planning annual ad budget, forecasting CPM/CPA inflation, or explaining to a founder why yesterday's winning creative stopped being profitable.
- Understand Meta's core objective: maximizing revenue per user per minute. It grows this by adding ad inventory (more ads per feed, more surfaces) and by raising CPMs.
- Accept that CPM inflation of roughly 20–30% year over year is the norm (the source measured this across 150M+ in spend; factor out natural dollar inflation).
- Recognize Meta cannot simply make advertisers unprofitable, so alongside CPM increases it must improve conversion efficiency and ROI for advertisers.
- Practical implication: a creative or offer that broke even 12 months ago may now be unprofitable. Bake CPM inflation into your target CPA and margin assumptions when setting bids and budgets.
- Because Meta constantly rolls out updates (Andromeda, Gemini, smaller ones), treat every update as an attempt to raise ad-serving efficiency so it can charge more — expect to keep improving creative and landing pages, not just structure.
- Verify current platform features and inflation figures in your own account before forecasting.
Caveat: The 20–30% figure is the presenter's observation from their aggregated data and is cyclical with Black Friday; it is not a universal benchmark.
Caveat: Some advertisers can still be profitable on Meta during CPM inflation, but the margin of safety narrows.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, meta-ads, CPM, budget-planning, forecasting, creative-strategy
Source: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

## Last-click reality vs. Meta's multi-touch optimization
Use when: Deciding which ads to kill or scale, or reconciling an ad's reported ROAS with actually getting spend.
- Know that the platform shows last-click attribution, giving full credit to the final ad a user clicked before buying.
- Meta itself optimizes across multi-touch sequences, spreading credit across the chain of impressions and clicks that led to the purchase.
- Consequence: an ad that looks like a loser on last-click may still be genuinely contributing, and Meta may keep spending on it because it sees earlier or later value in the sequence.
- Because bidding and optimization are inherited at the adset level (cost caps are set at adset, never ad level), evaluate creative performance and make budget decisions at the adset level, not the ad level.
- When you see one ad soaking up credit while others look weak, ask whether they are part of a sequence before cutting them.
- For incrementality you care about, use 7-day-click or incremental attribution views before reallocating budget — the source found an ad showing 7x ROAS that was actually 1.9x incremental.
Caveat: The source's 7x vs 1.9x example is a single case, not a promised ratio.
Caveat: Check current attribution and reporting options in the platform, since interfaces change.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, meta-ads, attribution, measurement, conversion-optimization, budget-planning
Source: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

## Trust the algorithm's breakdown spend distribution
Use when: Tempted to launch a dedicated campaign for a placement or demographic that shows higher ROAS in a breakdown report.
- When a breakdown shows one segment (e.g., Stories at 4x ROAS) beating another (Feed at 3x) yet getting less spend, don't assume Meta is misallocating.
- Understand the breakdown effect: Meta is testing increments. It has already tried pushing more spend into the higher-base-return segment and hit zero incremental returns; the lower base-return segment still returns more on each additional dollar.
- Metaphor: if an ad at $300/day gains nothing at $320 but another at $200/day earns more at $250, Meta routes spend to the second even though its base ROAS is lower.
- Practical rule: unless you are a very experienced media buyer, do not implement changes based on complex breakdowns or ad-level ROAS. Beginners who over-segment breakdowns usually make commercially misaligned decisions and get worse performance.
- Focus instead on the things with real leverage: creative, landing pages, and the structure of adsets.
Caveat: There are genuine cases where spend distribution is wrong, but identifying them requires expertise the source says most advertisers lack.
Caveat: Breakdown data is blended and does not capture incremental impact.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, meta-ads, measurement, budget-planning, media-buying
Source: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

## Creative-as-targeting and why broad targeting works
Use when: Setting up a new cold campaign or considering interest/lookalike tests instead of broad targeting.
- Shift from the old model (pick interests/lookalikes, then load creative) to the current model: load creative, leave targeting broad, and let Meta's retrieval system read the creative and serve it to relevant users.
- Understand why interests are flawed: they record interaction (a like, comment, click) not intent. Someone posting 'I hate dogs' gets labeled interested in dogs.
- Meta's modeling now behaves like a high-dimensional vector space (the source illustrates ~10,000 dimensions). Real-time interactions move each user through the space, and users cluster naturally; your ads are spread broadly and Meta finds the hotspots where people buy.
- Fact: with broad targeting, Meta targets the whole space, finds buying hotspots, and as you scale the target area expands into colder people — which is why ads fatigue during scaling.
- Replace interest-targeting tests with landing-page tests and CRO experiments, which the source says produce larger conversion-rate inflections.
- Don't burn test budget on interest or lookalike audiences; the source asserts interests are flawed and lookalikes don't work.
Caveat: Personal opinion attributed to the source: interest targeting 'shouldn't be in your account.' Some advertisers report niche cases where interests still help — validate in your own account.
Caveat: Broad targeting requires strong creative; weak creative will simply fatigue faster as you scale.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, meta-ads, targeting, creative-strategy, audience-research, conversion-optimization
Source: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

## Consolidation beats segmentation: the campaign-level data silo
Use when: Restructuring a Meta account that has many campaigns, or deciding whether to add a new campaign or adset for a new angle or product.
- Know the architecture: conversion data is siloed most strongly at the campaign level, shared more at the adset level, and inherited downward. Every added campaign chunks your conversion signal.
- Example: 100 conversions/month split across four campaigns means each gets ~25 — less signal, worse optimization via small sample size bias.
- Expect an efficiency boost when you push through roughly 100–200 conversions per month because Meta finally has enough signal to understand who to target.
- Therefore consolidate up at the campaign level. At the adset level, segmentation swings efficiency only around 5–10% — you can segment or consolidate more freely there.
- Do not stack multiple creatives into a single flexible ad: you lose insight into which creative is working, so you can't make more of the winner.
- Exception: keep campaigns separate where unit economics differ, personas don't overlap, or regions need independent budget control.
Caveat: The 5–10% adset swing and 100–200 conversion threshold are source heuristics, not universal constants.
Caveat: Total consolidation into one campaign/one adset is a bad idea for ~90% of brands per the source; only a minority can get away with it.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, meta-ads, account-structure, measurement, budget-planning, conversion-optimization
Source: The Only Video You Need On Meta Ads In 2026.docx

## Five diagnostic questions for account structure
Use when: Designing or restructuring a store's Meta account to match the business's products, margins and goals.
- Ask how many product categories you have — more categories (with differing goals) generally require more segmentation.
- Ask how wide the margin spread is — if margins vary substantially by category, you may need campaigns that prevent low-margin items from soaking up spend.
- Ask whether you have multiple personas that genuinely don't overlap — non-overlapping personas belong in the structure; slightly tweaked versions of the same person don't.
- Ask how many regions you sell in — multiple regions usually require campaign-level segmentation to control spend distribution and sell-through, especially if you hold inventory or have per-region revenue targets.
- Ask what your creative throughput is — 10 ads/month allows little segmentation; 2,000 ads/month needs a methodical pipeline from testing into scaling structures.
- Apply two non-negotiables: data integrity (the structure must produce readable, actionable data) and commercial alignment (the structure must reflect margins, goals, and categories that need spend).
Caveat: There is no universal perfect structure; the answer depends on each business's specifics.
Caveat: Structures that aren't readable are not actionable and force costly restructures.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, meta-ads, account-structure, merchandising, budget-planning, measurement

## Generic sub-$50k/month Meta structure
Use when: Launching or cleaning up a Meta account spending under roughly $50k/month with limited creative volume.
- Run one dedicated testing campaign (CBO or ABO) with adsets built around concepts. A concept = Persona + Angle + Offer, and creatives are made under that combination.
- Place 3–5 creatives per adset as a starting point; you can go higher if you genuinely have the creative volume, but most sub-$50k accounts don't.
- When you make more creatives for a concept: if the adset is underperforming, add them to that same adset to try to revive it.
- If the adset is hitting KPI, don't touch it — launch the new creatives in a new adset for the same concept. 'Never touch something that's working.'
- Expect this to produce multiple adsets for one winning concept over time; that's fine and expected.
- Exclude existing customers from the cold/testing campaign so retargeting purchases don't skew results.
- Verify current campaign settings and audience-exclusion options in the platform before launching.
Caveat: This generic structure is not tailored to any business; use the five diagnostic questions for a custom build.
Caveat: The source states a hard rule — don't change a performing adset — which is an opinion based on media-buying experience, not a measured law.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, meta-ads, account-structure, creative-strategy, experiment-design, small-business

## Budgeting the retargeting support layer
Use when: Setting or auditing retargeting/DPA spend for existing customers or engaged audiences.
- Define retargeting (DPAs, existing-customer ads) as a support layer, not a growth driver. Cap it rather than letting it scale with the account.
- Calculate the retargeting budget with the formula: Total Audience Size × Desired Frequency × CPM.
- Set a frequency ceiling: the source keeps existing-customer retargeting under a frequency of 7 on a 30-day rolling window.
- For a small CPG-style account, the retargeting campaign may be as small as roughly $20/day — enough to capture incrementality without over-spending.
- Exclude existing customers from cold campaigns so retargeting revenue doesn't overattribute into cold and push frequency up artificially.
- In fashion, where existing-customer targeting is more incremental, split the retargeting campaign into two adsets (new arrivals and DPA) so DPA doesn't absorb all spend.
Caveat: The formula's frequency and CPM inputs must come from your own account and audience estimates.
Caveat: The $20/day and frequency-7 figures are source examples, not universal targets.

## Calculating daily testing budgets by back-propagation
Use when: Setting the daily spend for a specific creative or landing-page test and deciding how long to run it.
- Decide the target number of conversions you want the test to observe (enough for a meaningful read).
- Multiply target conversions by expected CPA to get total test cost.
- Divide by test duration in days (the source's example uses 7 days) to get the daily testing budget.
- Example structure: 20 conversions × $30 CPA = $600 total; over 7 days that's ~$86/day.
- Use this to back-propagate from business goals to the platform budget rather than picking a round number.
- Keep the test budget separate from scaling spend so you can evaluate the outcome against a known conversion threshold.
Caveat: All inputs are account-specific; the 7-day example is illustrative, not a required duration.
Caveat: Conversion counts this small produce noisy reads, so treat the result as directional.

## Choosing ABO vs CBO by conversion volume and signal
Use when: Deciding campaign budget type for a store, especially with high AOV, low order volume, or risky product ranges.
- Default to CBO (Advantage campaign budget) when conversion volume is healthy: the algorithm distributes spend more efficiently than you will and can operate on an 80/20 pattern where 20% of ads get 80% of spend.
- Switch toward ABO (adset-level budgets) when conversion volume is very low, e.g. a $10k AOV brand doing ~5 orders/day. With so little signal Meta optimizes upstream on CPC/CTR/hold rate, and those metrics have almost no correlation with revenue except at extremes.
- Recognize the drawbacks of full CBO: no control over testing, no spend for new creatives, and dependence on one fatigue-prone winner.
- Contrast with ABO: you control where spend is forced, which de-risks and enables testing, but a novice can burn money by forcing spend into weak adsets.
- Rule of thumb from the source: an inexperienced in-house buyer should lean CBO; an experienced buyer can run mid-structure with controlled spend.
- Audit case: a $20–30M furniture brand's consolidated CBO put 57% of spend into a DPA adset showing 7x ROAS but only 1.9x on incremental or 7-day-click — DPA overspend on cold audiences is common.
Caveat: The furniture 7x vs 1.9x example is a single audit, not a universal pattern.
Caveat: CPC/revenue correlation claim is the source's assertion; verify in your own data.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, meta-ads, budget-planning, account-structure, media-buying, conversion-optimization

## Segment accounts by unit economics and audience
Use when: Deciding whether to separate products, categories or audiences into their own campaigns despite the consolidation rule.
- Watch for margin spread: if category A carries 70% margin and category B 60%, or if distressed ('grade C') inventory must be discounted, consolidation can funnel spend into compressed-margin items and hurt contribution margin and branding.
- Watch for non-overlapping personas: for a menswear/womenswear brand, put men's and women's ads in one adset and the adset gets confused — check via the gender breakdown whether women's ads are serving to men. Women buying for partners is directional and real, but the reverse is rarely efficient.
- Watch for high AOV/low volume: a $10k AOV brand at ~5 orders/day lacks the signal for CBO to optimize on purchases, so its structure must differ from a typical account.
- When you do segment, keep campaigns aligned to how the business thinks about products, margins and goals (commercial alignment).
- Where possible, push category segmentation down to adsets rather than multiplying campaigns, to limit data chunking.
Caveat: Segmentation carries a data-splitting cost; only segment for a concrete commercial reason.
Caveat: The gender-mismatch audit pattern is a screening heuristic, not proof of poor performance in every category.

## Worked example: CPG brand structure with one persona and two markets
Use when: Designing structure for a simple consumable product with high repeat rate and few personas.
- Use one consolidated cold campaign per country (one for US, one for AU) — do not manufacture extra personas at this revenue level.
- Run creative testing at the adset level based on concepts, with most spend flowing to the one concept/persona currently performing.
- Exclude existing customers from both cold campaigns — in CPG, returning-customer revenue will overattribute into cold and inflate frequency through self-retargeting.
- Add a small existing-customer/retargeting campaign at very low spend (roughly $20/day at this size) to capture incremental revenue while holding frequency under 7 over 30 days.
- Keep it simple: one advantage-plus-cold campaign per market plus a small retargeting layer.
- Treat repeat-purchase behavior as the reason to exclude customers, not a reason to scale retargeting.
Caveat: This is a source example for specific parameters (one product, one persona, 70% GM, $5M); changing any parameter may change the structure.

## Worked example: fashion brand with SKUs, personas and regions
Use when: Designing structure for a multi-category, multi-region store with discounting and seasonal differences.
- Create category campaigns (e.g., pants, tops, dresses) because purchase orders, revenue goals and sell-through differ per category and unsold stock goes to sale and erodes margin.
- Consolidate AU and NZ into one campaign: NZ typically maxes out at 7–10% of total spend and orders fulfill from an Australian warehouse.
- For the UK, decide based on inventory: if UK stock is held in Australia, you can consolidate regions and sell through stock anywhere; if you make UK seasonal purchase orders (northern vs southern hemisphere seasons), keep the UK separate.
- If you keep separate regions, move category segmentation down to adsets inside one AU campaign and one UK campaign to avoid doubling to six campaigns — this also handles separate UK subdomains/URLs.
- Add a DPA retargeting campaign to engaged audiences (e.g., 90-day site visitors).
- Add an existing-customer retargeting campaign with two separate adsets — new arrivals and DPA — so DPA doesn't absorb all spend and you can keep showing new arrivals to repeat buyers.
- Exclude existing customers from cold campaigns.
Caveat: Region consolidation is contingent on where inventory physically sits and whether regions have independent targets.
Caveat: Fashion existing-customer targeting is described as more incremental than other categories, which justifies the extra spend.

## Page caps, whitelisting and regional pages
Use when: Scaling weekly creative output and being blocked from launching more ads on a single page.
- Know the cap: Meta allows roughly 300–500 live ads per page, which high-volume accounts hit quickly.
- Option 1 — duplicate pages: create multiple brand pages with minor differences (e.g., a different logo color) and run ads across them. Example cited: Gruns with ~15 Gunrs pages.
- Option 2 — partnership ads: run ads through a real influencer/creator's page; often requires paying the creator if they have leverage.
- Option 3 — whitelisting: create a third-party-style page (e.g., 'Fiber Health Magazine') and run the same or advertorial-adjusted ads through it; the third-party framing reduces the 'being sold to' feel.
- Option 4 — regional pages: if you run separate country campaigns (UK, AU, US) and hit the cap, create per-country pages so each region gets its own cap.
- The source would do all of these simultaneously and isn't concerned about consolidating onto a single page.
Caveat: The exact cap changes over time — verify the current limit in Meta's interface.
Caveat: Some advertisers have brand-team concerns about consolidating onto one page; the source notes some do.

Tags: ad-copy-deployment, meta-ads, creative-strategy, partnership-ads, scaling, account-structure

## What media buying still controls (and what's dead)
Use when: Allocating media-buyer time across an account, or deciding which levers to pull for efficiency.
- Stop daily bid tweaks with cost/bid caps — the source calls this low-leverage; even if it yields ~5%, the same hours spent on better creative can double or triple the account.
- Stop daily budget pacing for small accounts; it churns campaigns and decisions are made on tiny samples. Both were viable around 2019–2020 but not now.
- Focus on account structure and architecture aligned with commercial objectives.
- Focus on concept-level segmentation at the adset level (Persona + Angle + Offer).
- Focus on controlling percent/dollar allocation to existing customers over time.
- Replace interest-targeting tests with landing-page tests and CRO experiments on the site, which the source says move conversion rates more.
- Recognize media buying still matters at high spend ($100k+/month), where the source estimates 10–20% efficiency lift from good buying; at ~$100/day it is not the main lever.
Caveat: The 5% bid-tweak gain and 10–20% buying lift are the presenter's estimates, not measured benchmarks.
Caveat: CRO-first emphasis is a strong opinion from the source, not a universal rule.
